findings.conditions_text: By varying Zst at constant Tad
findings.quantity: extinction scalar dissipation rate relative to fuel-air counterparts
findings.statement: High-stoichiometric-mixture-fraction diffusion flames can remain soot-free at any strain rate and can have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts.
findings.safety_implication: Flame designs that reduce soot must still be assessed for extinction behavior under their operating conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Inert-gas distribution between fuel and oxidizer streams is a design variable for controlling soot and flame extinction behavior.
findings.source_quote: By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction
findings.statement: Prior studies of nonpremixed flames indicate there is a stoichiometric mixture fraction at which the flame is most resistant to extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Combustor operating conditions should account for mixture-fraction-dependent differences in flame extinction resistance.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere and fuel-oxidizer mixture design can affect the flame's resistance to extinction.
findings.source_quote: Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: employing inert exchange to vary Zst
findings.statement: Prior findings suggest that varying stoichiometric mixture fraction through inert exchange can shift peak temperature to the radical-production location, allowing a flame to burn at much lower temperatures.
findings.source_quote: These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: at moderate flow rates; as the flow rate was increased
findings.statement: The ACME sintered spherical burner did not maintain perfect spherical symmetry: at increasing flow rates, the flame center shifted farther from the burner center, likely toward the supply tube, limiting the symmetry of Flame Design data.
findings.source_quote: ACME’s sintered spherical burners did not always yield spherically symmetric flames which are centered on the burner’s center, where that combination is important for true spherical symmetry. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center became increasing offset from the burner center as the flow rate was increased. It is very likely that the sintered attachment of the sphere to the supply tube is more porous than the sintered sphere itself because the flame is seen to be shifted toward the supply tube.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: replaced mid-way through round 1
findings.statement: Replacing spherical burner 1002 with burner 1003 significantly improved flame symmetry, although the symmetry remained imperfect.
findings.source_quote: There was significant improvement when the starting burner (serial number 1002) was replaced mid-way through round 1 with an alternate burner (serial number 1003), which continued to be used for spherical flame testing throughout the remainder of ACME operations. Nonetheless, the symmetry was not perfect, which is a shortcoming of the Flame Design data.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer
findings.statement: ACME mass flow controllers did not always provide steady flow rates or the intended flow values; the resulting effects on flame behavior were tentatively assumed to be minor.
findings.source_quote: ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer did not always perform adequately, where the flow rates were not always appropriately steady or at the intended value. However, the resulting effects on the flame behavior are tentatively assumed to be minor.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: at atmospheric pressure; fuel is ethylene with nitrogen diluent, and the oxidizer is an oxygen/nitrogen mixture
findings.quantity: critical extinction temperature and reactant mass flux
findings.statement: For ethylene spherical diffusion flames in microgravity at 1 bar, normal flames radiatively extinguished at a critical temperature of 1130 K and a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s; inverse flames extinguished at 1130 K and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s.
findings.safety_implication: A spacecraft fire-control model for these flames should account for radiative extinction and the distinct extinction mass fluxes of normal and inverse configurations.
findings.equipment_implication: Extinction-control analyses should use the reported critical temperature and configuration-specific mass flux thresholds for ethylene flames.
findings.source_quote: All the ISS flames observed by this project extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and at a fuel mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and at an oxygen mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: in the presence of radiation heat loss
findings.statement: Steady-state gaseous ethylene spherical diffusion flames can exist in microgravity with radiation heat loss when the steady flame is smaller than its radiative-extinction size and develops fast enough to avoid cooling below 1130 K.
findings.safety_implication: Steady operation cannot be assumed safe solely from flame existence; flame size and development rate determine whether radiative extinction is avoided.
findings.equipment_implication: Operational limits for sustained combustion should account for flame size and development rate relative to radiative extinction.
findings.source_quote: Steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist in the presence of radiation heat loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinction, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: at constant reactant flow rate
findings.statement: In microgravity ethylene spherical diffusion flames at constant reactant flow rate, radiative extinction occurs as the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches chemical heat release; partial extinction and reformation may oscillate and grow until complete extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Flame oscillations and partial extinction can precede complete extinction, so transient flame behavior should not be mistaken for a stable extinguished state.
findings.equipment_implication: Flame-monitoring and suppression logic should account for intermittent partial extinction before final flameout.
findings.source_quote: Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, a flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release. Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations grow in magnitude until complete extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: in the spherical, infinite domain configuration
findings.quantity: characteristic time to effectively reach steady state
findings.statement: The characteristic time for a diffusion-controlled spherical flame system in an infinite domain to effectively reach steady state is on the order of 105 s.
findings.source_quote: In the spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion-controlled system to effectively reach steady-state is found to be on the order of 105 s.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: spherical diffusion flames in microgravity
findings.statement: In microgravity, spherical diffusion flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-risk assessments for spacecraft should account for flame size changing with both reactant flow and ambient oxygen concentration.
findings.equipment_implication: Oxygen-control assessments should account for its effect on spherical diffusion flame size.
findings.source_quote: Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: very small flames - just above their kinetic extinction limits; larger flames
findings.statement: Very small microgravity spherical diffusion flames just above their kinetic extinction limits have low radiative heat loss and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior; larger flames grow until radiative heat loss exceeds chemical heat release and they extinguish.
findings.safety_implication: Flame size and heat-loss behavior may affect how long a microgravity flame persists before extinction, so suppression assumptions should not treat small and large flames as equivalent.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression evaluations should distinguish small flames near kinetic extinction from larger flames that undergo radiative extinction.
findings.source_quote: Radiative heat loss scales with flame size such that very small flames - just above their kinetic extinction limits - have low radiative loss, and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior. Larger flames increase in size over time until the rate of radiative heat loss exceeds the rate of chemical heat release, and the flame extinguishes via radiative extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: before total extinction occurs in these flames
findings.statement: Before total radiative extinction, microgravity spherical diffusion flames can partially extinguish and reform in an oscillatory mode that grows in magnitude until total extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Intermittent flame weakening or reformation should not be assumed to indicate that the fire is fully out.
findings.equipment_implication: Extinction monitoring should distinguish temporary partial extinction from confirmed total extinction.
findings.source_quote: Before total extinction occurs in these flames, they experience an unstable, oscillatory mode, in which they partially extinguish and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude until total extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: For constant ambient oxygen concentration; larger flames (with higher fuel flow rates) and smaller flames (with lower flow rates)
findings.statement: At constant ambient oxygen concentration, larger microgravity spherical diffusion flames with higher fuel flow rates radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames with lower flow rates.
findings.safety_implication: The observed faster extinction of larger flames should not be taken to mean they pose less risk, because the report also associates them with higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release during extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Extinction evaluations should consider fuel flow and flame size together rather than infer persistence from either alone.
findings.source_quote: For constant ambient oxygen concentration, larger flames (with higher fuel flow rates) radiatively extinguish faster than smaller flames (with lower flow rates) due to higher radiative losses and decreasing chemical heat release.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: For the small flame sizes that are necessary to achieve steady-state flames
findings.statement: For the small microgravity spherical diffusion flames examined, fiber temperatures increased with time as the burner heated and its cooling effect on the flame diminished.
findings.source_quote: For the small flame sizes that are necessary to achieve steady-state flames, the burner acts as a heat sink, and as the burner temperature increases, its cooling effect on the flame diminishes, and the flame temperature increases. Accordingly, fiber temperatures measured using two-color ratio pyrometry showed increasing temperature with time for the flames examined.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: after the initial ignition transient
findings.statement: In the cited study, OH* flame emissions at 310 nm in the examined microgravity spherical diffusion flames showed steady intensity after the initial ignition transient.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported steady OH* signal after ignition is relevant to evaluating optical flame-monitoring approaches, though the cited result alone does not establish a fire-detection capability.
findings.source_quote: Flame emissions of OH* (310 nm) measured with a photomultiplier tube and a bandpass filter showed a steady intensity after the initial ignition transient.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: the flames investigated
findings.statement: The microgravity spherical flames examined appeared to approach a steady-state size and temperature, but burner heating prevented a decisive conclusion.
findings.source_quote: The flames investigated appear to be asymptotically approaching a steady-state size and temperature, however, a decisive conclusion cannot be made because of burner heating.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: shifting the nitrogen from the air (or oxygen/nitrogen mixture) to the fuel stream
findings.statement: Flame Design reports that shifting nitrogen from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream can produce permanently blue, soot-free hydrocarbon diffusion flames at all flow conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Soot-control strategies for spacecraft combustion systems can consider redistributing inert gas between fuel and oxidizer streams, while verifying that flame stability is maintained.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere and fuel-stream controls could use nitrogen exchange to reduce soot, subject to validating flame stability and operating limits.
findings.source_quote: Such nitrogen exchange has enabled the production of the flames that are soot-free at all flow conditions, i.e., which are ‘permanently blue.’
findings.earth_application: Nitrogen redistribution may inform design of low-soot non-premixed burners on Earth, where emissions and equipment fouling matter.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: Preliminary analysis of the HiBMs images
findings.statement: The report identifies soot-cloud light emission and dissymmetry as factors that may make accurate soot volume fraction measurements difficult in the Flame Design images.
findings.equipment_implication: Optical soot-measurement systems need to account for soot emission and cloud asymmetry before their measurements can support quantitative safety decisions.
findings.source_quote: Preliminary analysis of the HiBMs images suggests that significant emission of light from soot particles and dissymmetry of the soot cloud will make acquiring accurate soot volume fraction measurements difficult, if possible.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: ACME end-of-test-day procedure
findings.statement: An end-of-test-day igniter check was added to ACME operations to reduce recurrence of igniter failures that could prevent flames from being ignited on a subsequent test day.
findings.safety_implication: A pre-test-day igniter check can help ensure fire-safety experiments or operations that depend on ignition are not delayed by an unnoticed igniter failure.
findings.equipment_implication: Include an igniter check in the end-of-test-day procedure to identify failures before the next test day.
findings.source_quote: An igniter check was subsequently added to the ACME end-of-test-day procedure to avoid such recurrences.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary
findings.statement: Flame Design experiments observed steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, despite a finite boundary.
findings.safety_implication: A persistent flame can remain established for many minutes in microgravity, so crew response and suppression planning should not rely on rapid self-extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression systems and crew procedures should account for microgravity flames persisting for at least the reported observation period.
findings.source_quote: Despite a narrow range of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: Steady-state flames are simulated using the numerical model for over 100,000 s.
findings.statement: Steady-state microgravity spherical diffusion flames were simulated for over 100,000 s using the numerical model.
findings.source_quote: Steady-state flames are simulated using the numerical model for over 100,000 s.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: nearly spherical flames created in normal gravity using hydrogen as a fuel and supplied in the ambient
findings.statement: Nearly spherical flames can be produced in normal gravity using hydrogen and inert dilution, but their Richardson number remains on the order of unity, so natural convection is still present.
findings.source_quote: Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: maximum percentage of distortion allowed in the experiment (10 here); for the four flames of Table 1.1
findings.statement: The analysis predicts that keeping flame distortion to a maximum of 10% requires gravity levels on the order of 10 μg for the four flames analyzed.
findings.source_quote: By specifying the maximum percentage of distortion allowed in the experiment (10% here), the acceptable gravity level is determined, and this result is given in Fig. 2.1 for the four flames of Table 1.1. As shown, the required g levels are on the order of 10 μg.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: fuel issuing into an ambient of air; normal gravity coflow flames
findings.statement: In normal-gravity flames where fuel issues into ambient air, buoyancy drives flow from oxidizer to fuel in the lower flame regions and from fuel to oxidizer in the upper regions, making flow direction ambiguous as Zst varies.
findings.source_quote: For example, it is well known that for fuel issuing into an ambient of air, buoyancy accelerates the flow field and causes the streamlines to be from oxidizer to fuel in the lower regions of the flame and from fuel to oxidizer in the upper regions (Santoro et al., 1987). The importance of buoyancy to the flow field will vary with Zst because the velocity and thus Ri are strongly affected by dilution.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: microgravity gas jet flames in quiescent surroundings observed in drop towers and the Space Shuttle
findings.statement: Microgravity gas-jet flames observed in drop towers and the Space Shuttle showed significant differences in sooting behavior, suggesting that the drop-tower results were far from steady state.
findings.source_quote: Microgravity gas jet flames in quiescent surroundings have been observed in drop towers and the Space Shuttle and the results have revealed significant differences between the two in terms of sooting behavior, suggesting that the drop tower results were far from steady state (Urban et al., 1998).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: 40% oxygen and high fuel concentrations; in 21% oxygen
findings.statement: Constantly sooting flames were observed only with 40% oxygen and high fuel concentrations; at 21% oxygen, small flames did not soot because of heat loss to the burner, while large flames did not soot because radiative losses rapidly lowered flame temperature below the sooting limit.
findings.safety_implication: Soot formation depended on oxygen level, fuel concentration, flame size, and heat loss, so soot observations alone may not reliably indicate the presence or severity of a flame across operating conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Soot-based fire detection or monitoring should be validated across oxygen concentrations and flame sizes because flames may not produce soot under the reported conditions.
findings.source_quote: Constantly sooting flames were only observed in 40% oxygen and high fuel concentrations. In 21% oxygen, small flames did not soot because of heat loss to the burner and large flames did not soot because high radiative losses caused the flame temperature to quickly drop below the sooting limit.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: Compared to the test points on GMT 115, these tests were conducted with higher flow rates
findings.statement: In microgravity, gaseous ethylene flames from a porous spherical burner grow larger and burn for shorter durations at higher flow rates than at the lower-flow test points on GMT 115.
findings.source_quote: Compared to the test points on GMT 115, these tests were conducted with higher flow rates, which resulted in larger flames of shorter durations.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: example Flame Design flame
findings.quantity: soot visibility, flame behavior, and extinction progression
findings.statement: In the example microgravity ethylene flame, visible soot largely disappeared over time as the flame expanded and dimmed; the flame base retreated from the burner tube because of heat loss, and base oscillation preceded near-extinction from radiative heat loss.
findings.safety_implication: The observed fading and flame-base oscillation may provide visual indicators of a microgravity flame approaching extinction, but the report does not establish them as validated detection criteria.
findings.equipment_implication: Visible soot reduction and flame-base oscillation are candidate features for evaluating optical flame-monitoring methods in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: (c) The visible soot has mostly disappeared, and the flame has further grown and dimmed. The base of the flame has retreated from the burner tube because of heat loss. (d) The fiber array has begun translating with the first ceramic fiber at the edge of flame, where its glow is visible at the top of the image.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: air (21% oxygen/79% nitrogen)
findings.statement: In microgravity air at 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen, a spherical flame almost completely extinguished, then flashed back and reestablished before finally extinguishing.
findings.safety_implication: A flame that appears extinguished in spacecraft air may temporarily re-ignite, so fire-response procedures should account for flashback before declaring the hazard controlled.
findings.equipment_implication: Extinction controls and atmospheric management should be evaluated for preventing re-ignition after apparent flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: This test point was performed in a chamber environment of air (21% oxygen/79% nitrogen). The flame almost completely extinguishes but then dramatically flashes back reestablishing the spherical flame before finally extinguishing.
findings.earth_application: The result is relevant to aircraft, spacecraft analogs, and enclosed industrial environments where buoyancy is weak or airflow is limited and apparent extinction may be followed by flashback.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: ACME Flame Design test conditions; non-premixed flames
findings.statement: Microgravity ethylene flames can continue producing soot after ignition, and the experiment found that soot production depends on the conditions in non-premixed flames.
findings.safety_implication: Soot production can alter radiant heating and particulate signatures, so fire detection and thermal-hazard assessments should account for soot-producing flame states.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke and optical fire detectors should be evaluated against the particle and radiation signatures of soot-producing microgravity flames.
findings.source_quote: On GMT 156, ACME Flame Design test conditions resulted in flames which continued to produce soot following ignition, yielding new information for this study of soot processes.
findings.earth_application: The result can inform smoke-detector and combustion-emissions studies for enclosed terrestrial environments, although the microgravity particle behavior is not directly transferable.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: long residence time resulting from the microgravity condition
findings.statement: In microgravity, soot clusters in an ethylene flame become especially large because of the long residence time.
findings.safety_implication: Larger soot aggregates may change particulate transport and optical signatures, which can affect the performance of smoke and particle detection systems.
findings.equipment_implication: Particle and optical detector testing should include the larger soot-cluster distributions produced under microgravity residence times.
findings.source_quote: With the long residence time resulting from the microgravity condition, the clusters become especially large.
findings.earth_application: The observation can inform particulate-transport and smoke-detection research in low-flow or enclosed terrestrial environments.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: flame extinction oscillations
findings.statement: In one spherical flame case, extinction oscillations lasted about 30 seconds and occurred at roughly 1 Hz, with the frequency slowing as the oscillations grew stronger.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction-related flame oscillations can persist for tens of seconds, leaving a measurable interval during which monitoring and suppression systems must continue operating.
findings.equipment_implication: Flame-monitoring systems should capture low-frequency, decaying oscillations rather than treating a brief reduction in signal as confirmed extinction.
findings.source_quote: In the example shown in the graph, the flame’s oscillations lasted about 30 seconds and occurred at roughly 1 Hz, but they slowed in frequency as they grew in strength.
findings.earth_application: The signal behavior may inform optical flame-monitoring systems for industrial burners and enclosed terrestrial fires.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.statement: Before flame oscillations began, CH* chemiluminescence was relatively steady while OH* emission was decaying, and the report identifies this difference for further study of flame extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Different optical emission channels may provide earlier or more reliable indication of impending extinction than a single flame signal.
findings.equipment_implication: Multichannel optical flame detectors using CH* and OH* emissions could improve discrimination of stable burning, impending extinction, and recovery.
findings.source_quote: Interestingly, the graph shows that the CH* measurement was relatively steady before the start of the oscillations in comparison with the decaying OH* emission. This difference will be further examined to improve our understanding of flame extinction.
findings.earth_application: The finding can inform optical monitoring of terrestrial burners and industrial fire signatures where chemiluminescence sensing is practical.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: chamber pressure of 1.3 atm with varying oxygen concentrations of 34 to 40% oxygen (the remainder was nitrogen)
findings.statement: For diluted ethylene flames at 1.3 atm and 34-40% oxygen, the elevated oxygen concentration and pressure can enhance soot production.
findings.safety_implication: Oxygen enrichment combined with elevated pressure can increase soot production, potentially changing particulate and radiant-heat hazards in spacecraft atmospheres.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits and detector qualification should consider the combined effects of oxygen concentration and pressure on soot production.
findings.source_quote: The elevated oxygen and pressure can enhance the production of soot, where this research is focused on understanding the conditions that lead to sooty and soot-free flames.
findings.earth_application: The result is relevant to oxygen-enriched industrial, aviation, and vehicle environments where pressure and oxygen concentration influence soot and smoke generation.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: inverse flame; oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner into a combustion chamber filled with an ethylene/nitrogen mixture
findings.statement: A spherical inverse ethylene flame in microgravity was sustained for over 14 minutes, compared with the typically shorter-than-two-minute durations of ACME experiments and the previous longest duration of under six minutes.
findings.safety_implication: The result shows that a microgravity flame may persist far longer than typical test durations, so fire-response planning should not assume rapid self-extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew response procedures should account for the possibility of a sustained flame lasting many minutes.
findings.source_quote: For one of these tests, we observed our longest sustained flame, which burned for over 14 minutes. At that time, operational constraints required its termination. For comparison, flame durations for all ACME experiments are typically shorter than two minutes with the longest—until now—under six minutes.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: spherical flames; higher burner flow rates or flow rate too low
findings.statement: For microgravity spherical flames at higher burner flow rates, the flames grow with time and extinguish due to radiative heat loss; at flow rates that are too low, their small size leads to excessive burner heating.
findings.safety_implication: Flame persistence and extinction depend on burner flow, so airflow changes may not reliably suppress a flame and can shift it into a different failure mode.
findings.equipment_implication: Ventilation or burner-flow controls should account for both radiative-loss extinction at higher flow and excessive burner heating at too-low flow.
findings.source_quote: We have found with higher burner flow rates that flames grow with time and extinguish due to radiative heat loss. If the flow rate is too low, the flame’s small size leads to excessive burner heating. But under the right conditions, the flame can burn for minutes and perhaps even tens of minutes.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: under the right conditions
findings.statement: Under suitable conditions, a microgravity spherical flame can burn for minutes and possibly tens of minutes.
findings.safety_implication: Microgravity flames may remain burning for extended periods, making continued monitoring and active response important rather than relying on spontaneous extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire monitoring and crew response procedures should support sustained observation and intervention over many minutes.
findings.source_quote: But under the right conditions, the flame can burn for minutes and perhaps even tens of minutes.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames; oxidizer flow rate varied while concentrations of oxidizer and fuel in the chamber atmosphere were the same
findings.quantity: flame size and oscillatory quenching behavior
findings.statement: For inverse flames, increasing oxidizer flow rate produced larger flames with greater radiative heat loss, making them dimmer and causing them to quench sooner with fewer oscillations.
findings.safety_implication: The observed link between flow rate, heat loss, and quenching may inform how airflow changes affect flame persistence in spacecraft atmospheres.
findings.equipment_implication: Airflow-control assessments should account for its effect on flame size and radiative heat loss, not just reactant supply.
findings.source_quote: The higher flow rate resulted in a larger flame. However, a flame's radiative heat loss increases with its size, so the larger flame was dimmer.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: three inverse flames; oxidizer flow rates compared
findings.statement: Among the three inverse flames compared, the largest flame at the highest oxidizer flow rate quenched after less than 10 seconds of oscillating, while the smallest flame at half that flow rate oscillated for almost 40 seconds before quenching.
findings.safety_implication: Flame oscillation duration varied substantially with flow rate in these tests, so transient flame behavior may matter when assessing whether a flame is approaching extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Ventilation evaluations should consider that flow changes can alter how long a flame oscillates before quenching.
findings.source_quote: The graph shows the largest flame with the highest flow rate (red) quenched after less than 10 seconds of oscillating; whereas, the smallest flame with half the flow rate (blue) oscillated for almost 40 seconds before quenching.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames at two different chamber pressures
findings.statement: For ethylene inverse flames, lower chamber pressure produced a brighter flame and subtle signs of soot, while higher pressure reduced light emission from the flame.
findings.safety_implication: Flame brightness alone may not provide a pressure-independent indication of combustion intensity or soot formation.
findings.equipment_implication: Optical flame-detection approaches should account for pressure-dependent emission brightness when interpreting flame signals.
findings.source_quote: The flame at lower pressure is much brighter because at higher pressures light-emitting molecules are more likely to be extinguished due to molecular collisions. Also, the low-pressure flame shows subtle signs of soot formation.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: inverse spherical flame growing to consume oxygen flowing from the porous spherical burner
findings.quantity: flame temperature and radiative heat loss
findings.statement: In an inverse spherical flame, growth increased radiative heat loss, weakening and dimming the flame while its temperature dropped.
findings.safety_implication: Flame growth can be followed by thermal weakening, which is relevant when evaluating whether a developing flame may extinguish without intervention.
findings.equipment_implication: Monitoring and airflow-control assessments should account for the observed progression from flame growth to increased heat loss and declining temperature.
findings.source_quote: As the flame grew bigger, the radiative heat loss increased, which caused the flame to weaken and become dimmer. The flame's temperature dropped, which is indicated by the hue of the glowing ceramic fibers, where yellow is hotter than orange, which in turn is hotter than red.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: at atmospheric pressure; normal flames and inverse flames
findings.quantity: critical extinction temperature and reactant mass flux
findings.statement: Ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at atmospheric pressure extinguished at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.
findings.safety_implication: These extinction limits can inform operating margins for systems that rely on gaseous diffusion flames in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Use the reported limits to inform atmospheric operating envelopes and procedures for avoiding unintended flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Despite a range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame
findings.statement: For atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flames, flame growth leading to radiative extinction is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion-limited system as it approaches steady state and to reduced transport properties as flame temperature drops with increasing flame radiation.
findings.safety_implication: The reported mechanism indicates that radiative heat loss and flame growth should be considered when assessing extinction behavior over time.
findings.source_quote: Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: hydrocarbon diffusion flames; location relative to stoichiometry
findings.statement: In hydrocarbon diffusion flames, full equilibrium of the overall water-gas-shift reaction occurs on the oxidizer side of stoichiometry, while apparent equilibrium can occur on the fuel side.
findings.source_quote: For a given fuel type it was shown that the two scenarios can be separated by the location of stoichiometry. On the oxidizer side, full equilibrium of the overall WGS reaction is achieved, while on the fuel side, apparent equilibrium can occur.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion flames; mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature
findings.quantity: agreement of predicted and measured flame lengths
findings.statement: For normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion flames under the reported conditions, the Roper model predictions matched measured flame lengths with an R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91.
findings.source_quote: For normal flames the agreement is best for a mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature. This contrasts to values used by Roper for methane/air flames of 20 mm2/s and 1500 K, respectively. For the present conditions the predictions match the measurements with a R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: steady methane/oxygen/nitrogen jet flames; 3.0 mm coflowing burner; fixed fuel flow rate
findings.statement: For steady methane/nitrogen/oxygen jet flames on a 3.0 mm coflowing burner, adding inert to the fuel stream increased flame length at fixed fuel flow rate, but the effect was negligible when the fuel mole fraction exceeded 0.5.
findings.source_quote: For fixed fuel flow rate, inert addition to the fuel stream is found to increase flame length, but this effect is negligible for fuel mole fractions above 0.5.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame; atomic ratios C, N, H, and O measured by laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy
findings.statement: In an ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame, LIBS measurements produced atomic-ratio distributions across the flame, from which elemental mass fractions and mixture-fraction distributions were obtained; numerical results showed excellent agreement with the experimental results.
findings.source_quote: Then the atomic ratio distributions along the centerline of an ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame were measured to demonstrate the capability of LIBS to measure atomic ratios between different elements throughout the entire flame. The elemental mass fractions for C, H, N, O can be thus obtained from atomic ratio profiles. The mixture fraction distribution was calculated from elemental mass fractions. Numerical results were compared to the experimental results and showed excellent agreement.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: For the same heat release rate
findings.statement: In modeled spherical hydrogen-air diffusion flames, inverse flames were smaller and 290 K hotter than normal flames at the same heat release rate.
findings.source_quote: For the same heat release rate, inverse flames were found to be smaller and 290 K hotter than normal flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: spherical hydrogen-air diffusion flames; normal (H2 flowing into quiescent air) and inverse (air flowing into quiescent H2) configurations
findings.quantity: overall heat release rate at quenching
findings.statement: Modeled spherical hydrogen-air flames quenched at an overall heat release rate of 0.25 W for the weakest normal flame and 1.4 W for the weakest inverse flame.
findings.safety_implication: These modeled limits can inform expectations for flame persistence, but should not be treated as validated operational thresholds without matching the spacecraft configuration.
findings.equipment_implication: Do not use the modeled heat-release limits as standalone crew-response or shutdown thresholds.
findings.source_quote: The weakest normal flame that could be achieved before quenching has an overall heat release rate of 0.25 W, compared to 1.4 W for the weakest inverse flame.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: near extinction; smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron
findings.statement: Modeled normal and inverse spherical hydrogen-air diffusion flames had extensive ambient-reactant leakage near extinction, producing a premixed-flame regime except for the smallest burners, with radii on the order of 1 micron.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction behavior may depend on reactant leakage and mixing, so suppression assumptions based only on diffusion-flame behavior may not apply near quenching.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression evaluations should account for the modeled transition toward premixed behavior near extinction.
findings.source_quote: There is extensive leakage of the ambient reactant for both normal and inverse flames near extinction, which results in a premixed flame regime for diffusion flames except for the smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: counterflow diffusion flames; for a given fuel
findings.quantity: flame-zone and critical-reaction locations in C/O ratio space
findings.statement: Numerical results for counterflow diffusion flames indicate that, for a given fuel, flame-zone and critical-reaction locations in C/O ratio space are invariant with stoichiometric mixture fraction and strain rate.
findings.source_quote: Numerical results with detailed chemical kinetics also indicate that C/O ratio space is a fundamental variable in the sense that, for a given fuel, the location of the flame zones and critical reactions is invariant with Zst and strain rate.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: high temperature side of the soot precursor zone
findings.statement: In numerical counterflow diffusion-flame results, the high-temperature-side onset threshold of soot precursors C6H5 and C6H6 was characterized by depletion of radicals.
findings.source_quote: The onset threshold of soot precursors (C6H5 and C6H6) for the high temperature side of the soot precursor zone is characterized by the depletion of radicals.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: water/alcohol mixtures sprayed into a swirl-stabilized burner
findings.statement: For the reported water/alcohol spray-combustion system, preferential vaporization of ethanol over water enhanced flame stability.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel-water mixtures can retain flame stability through preferential fuel vaporization, so dilution alone may not guarantee reduced fire persistence.
findings.equipment_implication: Assess the volatility and preferential vaporization of fuel mixtures when evaluating their fire stability.
findings.source_quote: The results revealed that preferential vaporization of ethanol over water plays an important role in enhancing flame stability.
findings.earth_application: The reported spray-combustion behavior may inform terrestrial burner and fuel-mixture fire-safety assessments.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: bi-component droplet vaporization; diffusion limit and distillation limit modes of liquid mass transfer
findings.statement: For the reported ethanol-water spray-combustion system, modeling vaporization appropriately required accounting for the mixture's non-ideal solution behavior.
findings.source_quote: The model also demonstrated that for this experimental system, droplet vaporization was better characterized by the distillation limit mode with enhanced mass transfer by convection.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures
findings.statement: Increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures are methods considered for reducing soot in non-premixed hydrocarbon combustion, but they generally weaken the flame and can lead to extinction and substantial performance penalties.
findings.safety_implication: Soot-control strategies should be assessed for their impact on flame stability so that reducing emissions does not create a greater risk of flame extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control strategies that reduce pressure or add inert gas should account for the associated loss of flame stability.
findings.source_quote: Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties.
findings.earth_application: The tradeoff is relevant to terrestrial combustor design, where soot reduction methods can affect flame stability and performance.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion processes
findings.quantity: molecular oxygen presence at the location of maximum temperature
findings.statement: In non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion, appreciable molecular oxygen can be present at the location of maximum temperature, a flame-structure result relevant to understanding soot formation.
findings.source_quote: The presence of appreciable molecular oxygen at the location of maximum temperature has been observed and modeled in non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion processes. This work was published in one journal paper. This is significant for understanding soot formation in flames.
findings.earth_application: May inform terrestrial combustor designs intended to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emissions.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar; extinction occurred during unsteady flame conditions
findings.quantity: peak temperature at radiative extinction onset
findings.statement: In transient microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene or propane at 0.98 bar, radiative extinction onset occurred at peak temperatures of about 1100 K, significantly lower than for kinetic extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction temperatures can depend on the extinction mechanism, so a single temperature threshold may not reliably characterize whether these flames will persist.
findings.source_quote: Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: transient radiating spherical diffusion flames; except at very low flow rates
findings.quantity: dependence of extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction on flow rate
findings.statement: For transient radiating microgravity spherical diffusion flames, extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction were independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates.
findings.safety_implication: Changing flow rate may not provide a reliable way to control extinction under most tested conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Flow-control strategies should not assume that modest flow-rate changes will substantially alter extinction behavior.
findings.source_quote: Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: normal and inverse coflow flames; varying Zst and fuel stream velocity
findings.quantity: flame temperature at the sooting limit and its dependence on fuel stream velocity
findings.statement: In ethylene normal and inverse coflow flames, the measured temperature at the soot-ingestion limit increased with stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst), and the soot-inception limit temperature depended on fuel-stream velocity in both configurations.
findings.safety_implication: Soot-risk limits depend on flame configuration and operating velocity, so soot-control limits should be established for the relevant operating conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustion controls that adjust dilution and fuel-stream velocity should account for their effect on soot inception.
findings.source_quote: The flame temperature at the sooting limit is found to increase with Zst for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time are also investigated, and the sooting limit inception temperature is found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configurations.
findings.earth_application: The results can inform soot-reduction strategies in terrestrial diffusion combustors.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms
findings.quantity: critical local C/O ratio and soot-limit inception temperature
findings.statement: For ethylene, comparison of the soot-inception model with experimental data yielded a critical local carbon-to-oxygen ratio of 0.53 and a soot-limit inception temperature of 1640 K for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms.
findings.safety_implication: These model-derived thresholds provide condition-specific criteria for assessing when ethylene flames may begin producing soot.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustion designs using ethylene can use these condition-specific criteria when evaluating dilution and soot-control conditions.
findings.source_quote: By comparing the model to experimental data, a critical local C/O ratio of 0.53 and a sooting limit inception temperature of 1640 K (for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms) were determined for ethylene.
findings.earth_application: The authors describe the soot-reduction model as applicable to oxy-fuel combustion.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion flames at high Zst
findings.quantity: oxygen presence and relative location of maximum temperature
findings.statement: In computational analysis of non-premixed ethylene oxygen-enhanced combustion flames at high Zst, appreciable oxygen remained at the location of maximum temperature, which was displaced from the location of oxygen depletion.
findings.source_quote: Results demonstrate that the location of O2 depletion occurs in the vicinity of global stoichiometry for flames of any Zst and that the presence of appreciable O2 at the location of maximum temperature for high Zst flames is caused by a shift in the location of maximum temperature relative to the location of O2 depletion.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: residence times longer than 200 ms; where C/O = 0.6
findings.statement: For modeled sooting-limit spherical diffusion flames with residence times longer than 200 ms, temperatures were near 1190 K where C/O = 0.6; shorter-residence-time flames required higher temperatures.
findings.source_quote: Sooting-limit diffusion flames with residence times longer than 200 ms were found to have temperatures near 1190 K where C/O = 0.6, whereas flames with shorter residence times required increased temperatures.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: modeled spherical diffusion flames
findings.statement: Acetylene was found to be a reasonable surrogate for soot precursor species in the modeled spherical diffusion flames, with peak mole fractions of about 0.01.
findings.source_quote: Acetylene was found to be a reasonable surrogate for soot precursor species in these flames, having peak mole fractions of about 0.01.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: model combines C/O ratio and finite-rate chemistry boundaries
findings.quantity: limit inception temperature and critical C/O ratio
findings.statement: A model combining carbon-to-oxygen-ratio and finite-rate-chemistry boundaries estimated a soot-formation limit inception temperature of 1640 K and a critical C/O ratio of 0.53.
findings.source_quote: By utilizing measured limit temperature data with the model we found the limit inception temperature for soot formation to be 1640 K and the critical carbon to oxygen ratio to be 0.53.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: steady spherical diffusion flame supported by a porous burner; single-step, overall, irreversible high-activation-energy Arrhenius reaction and optically thin radiation model
findings.quantity: effect of radiation intensity on extinction and steady burning
findings.statement: Analytical analysis of a steady spherical diffusion flame supported by a porous burner found that higher radiation intensity makes the flame easier to extinguish, and that steady burning is not possible above a maximum radiation intensity.
findings.safety_implication: Radiative heat-loss conditions can reduce flame stability, so suppression assessments should account for radiation intensity.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression-system analyses for comparable flames should account for radiative heat loss when assessing extinction and continued burning.
findings.source_quote: Results show that the flame is easier to extinguish when the radiation intensity is higher, as expected, and there exists a maximum radiation intensity above which steady burning is not possible.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: normal-gravity experiments using counterflow diffusion flames; nitrogen exchange (increased stoichiometric mixture fraction)
findings.statement: Normal-gravity counterflow diffusion flames can be made permanently blue and resistant to extinction for many hydrocarbon fuels by nitrogen exchange that increases stoichiometric mixture fraction.
findings.safety_implication: Nitrogen-exchange strategies may help reduce soot while preserving flame stability in hydrocarbon combustion systems.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustor atmosphere design can use nitrogen exchange to alter stoichiometric mixture fraction and promote soot-free, extinction-resistant flames.
findings.source_quote: Recent normal-gravity experiments using counterflow diffusion flames have shown that permanently-blue flames (which are devoid of soot regardless of strain rate) and extinction-resistant flames can be produced for many hydrocarbon fuels by nitrogen exchange (increased stoichiometric mixture fraction).
findings.earth_application: The document identifies terrestrial power generation as an application for combustion approaches that reduce pollutants and improve efficiency.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: normal-gravity counterflow diffusion flames; a unique stoichiometric mixture fraction; compared with the standard hydrocarbon/air flame with the same flame temperature
findings.quantity: extinction temperature difference and strain rate ratio
findings.statement: For normal-gravity counterflow diffusion flames, a unique stoichiometric mixture fraction can produce an extinction temperature up to 200 K lower and a strain rate up to four times greater than a standard hydrocarbon/air flame at the same flame temperature.
findings.safety_implication: Combustion-system designs may be able to combine higher strain tolerance with extinction at a lower temperature, but the reported result is from terrestrial counterflow experiments and is not itself a spacecraft operating limit.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustor mixture design and flow conditions may be adjusted to pursue higher strain tolerance and lower-temperature extinction.
findings.source_quote: Furthermore, there is a unique stoichiometric mixture fraction wherein the flame temperature at extinction can be up to 200 K lower and the strain rate up to four times greater than that for the standard hydrocarbon/air flame with the same flame temperature.
findings.earth_application: The document identifies terrestrial power generation as an application for combustion approaches that reduce pollutants and improve efficiency.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: normal spherical diffusion flames
findings.statement: Numerical modeling indicates that some normal spherical ethylene-air diffusion flames may reach steady state.
findings.source_quote: The numerical modeling of spherical diffusion flames has progressed. This indicates that some normal flames of ethylene burning in air may be able to reach steady state.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: spherical diffusion flames
findings.statement: Numerical modeling predicts that some spherical diffusion flames can continue burning with peak temperatures as low as 1000 K.
findings.safety_implication: A temperature-based fire-extinction criterion should not assume that a spherical diffusion flame is extinguished once its peak temperature falls below 1100 K.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew or automated procedures that use temperature to confirm flame extinction should account for modeled burning at peak temperatures as low as 1000 K.
findings.source_quote: Furthermore, flames that continue burning with peak temperatures as low as 1000 K are observed. Previously no flames were predicted with these temperatures below 1100 K.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: inverse diffusion flames with CO2 as diluent in both fuel side and oxidizer side; IDFs with Ar and He as diluent
findings.statement: Inverse diffusion flames tested with CO2 as a diluent on both the fuel and oxidizer sides did not show double luminous zones, while tests with Ar and He showed the most remarkable double luminous zones observed to date.
findings.source_quote: At UMD we tested IDFs (inverse diffusion flames) with CO2 as diluent in both fuel side and oxidizer side. These did not have double luminous zones. We also tested IDFs with Ar and He as diluent. These had the most remarkable double luminous zones we have seen to date.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction
findings.statement: Existing predictive methods were significantly deficient for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames near extinction, limiting confidence in predictions at these flame-condition extremes.
findings.safety_implication: Models used to assess flame stability and extinction in spacecraft should be treated cautiously for highly sooting or near-extinction conditions until validated for those regimes.
findings.equipment_implication: Flammability test methods and models should be validated against sooty pure-fuel and near-extinction flame conditions before being relied on for safety assessments.
findings.source_quote: Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: For some cases of the ethylene flames; more heavily sooting cases
findings.statement: Ethylene flames have higher laminar flame speeds than methane flames, producing lift-off heights approximately half as large; heavily sooting ethylene flames can consequently transfer moderate heat to the burner.
findings.safety_implication: Burner heating in heavily sooting ethylene flames could affect thermal assumptions used to assess flame behavior.
findings.source_quote: The laminar flame speed of ethylene is higher than that of methane, causing lift-off heights to decrease by approximately a factor of two. For nonsooting flames, this decrease in lift-off height does not create any burner heating. However, the more heavily sooting cases have been observed to cause moderate heat transfer to the burner, which becomes a problem in the ethylene flames since they have a higher propensity to soot, particularly at microgravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: By increasing the fuel flow rate by a factor of 2 (as shown in Test #’s 106-111 in Table 5.1.5)
findings.statement: Doubling the fuel flow rate increased the overall amount of soot and the size of the sooting region in ethylene flame tests at 1 g.
findings.safety_implication: Higher fuel flow can increase soot production, which may increase particulate loading in spacecraft fire environments.
findings.equipment_implication: Flow-control settings should account for the observed increase in soot with higher fuel flow.
findings.source_quote: By increasing the fuel flow rate by a factor of 2 (as shown in Test #’s 106-111 in Table 5.1.5), the overall amount of soot and the size of the sooting region are increased (at 1 g), with the sooting region substantially higher off the burner surface to prevent burner heating.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: under microgravity conditions relative to 1 g conditions
findings.statement: Under microgravity, the lift-off height of the sooting region decreases relative to 1 g conditions because axial diffusion becomes more important.
findings.safety_implication: The reduced separation from the burner under microgravity makes burner heating a greater concern for sooting flames.
findings.source_quote: Raising the sooting region further off the burner surface becomes more important under microgravity conditions as the lift-off height decreases relative to 1 g conditions due to the increased importance of axial diffusion.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: SOFBALL experiment (STS-83, STS-94, and STS-107); hard shutoff at 5 minutes
findings.statement: In the SOFBALL experiment, flames were still burning when tests ended at the 5-minute hard shutoff, so the test duration could not be extended until a subsequent spaceflight.
findings.equipment_implication: Experiment procedures should allow test duration to be extended when flames remain burning beyond the expected duration.
findings.source_quote: For example, the SOFBALL experiment (STS-83, STS-94, and STS-107) initially had a hard shutoff at 5 minutes because it was fully expected that the flames would extinguish by that time. However, that assumption was found to be faulty and the tests terminated while flames were still burning diminishing the scientific return.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

findings.conditions_text: in low-g and in normal gravity
findings.statement: Drop-tower tests cited in the document found that a material's maximum oxygen concentration flammability limit can differ between low gravity and normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Normal-gravity flammability screening alone may not establish whether a material is safe in spacecraft conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Material qualification and oxygen-limit testing for spacecraft should account for gravity conditions.
findings.source_quote: Drop tower testing has demonstrated the MOC flammability limits of a material can be different in low-g than in normal gravity [3-5].
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III

findings.conditions_text: design of spacecraft fire safety systems using terrestrial fires and fire standards
findings.statement: The authors state that relying on terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire-safety systems creates inherent vehicle risk because of significant uncertainty.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire-safety design should reduce reliance on terrestrial evidence by obtaining data relevant to reduced-gravity conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Terrestrial fire standards should not be treated as sufficient evidence for spacecraft fire-safety design without addressing the stated uncertainty.
findings.source_quote: The use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III

findings.quantity: validity of the moment method with a lognormal distribution assumption
findings.statement: For aerosol produced from the five tested materials, the moment method with a lognormal distribution assumption was found to be a valid and effective way to characterize aerosol encountered in space vehicles.
findings.safety_implication: Reliable characterization of smoke aerosol can inform spacecraft smoke-detection decisions.
findings.source_quote: Based on the results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: ground testing; TEM analysis counted all particles without thresholding
findings.statement: In ground lamp-wick smoke measurements, TEM and SMPS volume distributions had similar spread but differed in peak location; counting faint particles without thresholding lowered the TEM geometric mean diameter and increased its geometric standard deviation relative to SMPS.
findings.safety_implication: Particle-size estimates used to characterize smoke detection may depend on the measurement method and on whether faint particles are included.
findings.equipment_implication: TEM and SMPS measurements produced different distribution peak locations.
findings.source_quote: For this size distribution analysis, all particles were counted without thresholding, so the small faint particles were included in the totals, which reduced the geometric mean diameter and caused σgn to be quite a bit larger than the SMPS results. The SMPS and TEM volume distributions have a similar spread but do not agree well in the peak location.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.statement: Kapton smoke particles produced in the SAME-R tests were smaller than the other observed particle types and rarely agglomerated.
findings.source_quote: Kapton particles are smaller but rarely agglomerated.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: considering both the conservative 700 nm limit and the 1000 nm limit
findings.quantity: particle size distribution captured by SMPS
findings.statement: The SMPS measured 98% to 100% of the Kapton smoke particle size distribution for both the conservative 700 nm upper limit and the 1000 nm limit.
findings.equipment_implication: The SMPS measurement range captures nearly all of the Kapton distribution in these tests.
findings.source_quote: For example, considering both the conservative 700 nm limit and the 1000 nm limit, the bar graph indicates that 98% to 100% of the distribution has been measured.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: high temperature (369.2 °C) unaged Silicone smoke; SMPS upper size limits of 1000 nm and 700 nm
findings.statement: For high-temperature unaged Silicone smoke, the SMPS captured only 40% of the volume distribution at a 1000 nm upper limit and approximately 20% at a 700 nm upper limit.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke-monitor sizing based on this instrument range may substantially underrepresent silicone aerosol volume, limiting characterization of this smoke for detection-system assessment.
findings.equipment_implication: The SMPS measurement range misses a substantial portion of the Silicone volume distribution.
findings.source_quote: Particularly in the volume distribution in Fig. 23 (right graph), the black bar representing a 1000 nm upper size limit is only at 40%, indicating that 60% of the distribution is missed by the instrument, but when losses are considered and a range of 700 nm is relied upon, approximately 20% of the distribution is captured (the white bar).
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.statement: Kapton and lamp-wick smoke particle size distributions can be considered lognormal, whereas silicone smoke particle size distributions should not be considered lognormal.
findings.safety_implication: A lognormal assumption is unsuitable for silicone smoke sizing, so aerosol characterization and conversions for that material should use a method that does not rely on that assumption.
findings.source_quote: Overall, the qualitative comparison of these diameters strongly suggests that the smoke particle size distributions for Kapton® and lamp wick can be considered lognormal and silicone should not.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Kapton smoke at these temperatures
findings.quantity: agreement between TEM and moment-method particle diameters
findings.statement: Kapton smoke generated at the tested temperatures had good agreement between TEM and moment-method diameters and was well suited to measurement by the moment method.
findings.safety_implication: Moment-method measurements can support smoke-particle characterization for Kapton, but the reported suitability should not be assumed for other smoke types.
findings.equipment_implication: The moment method was suitable for measuring Kapton smoke particle size under the tested conditions.
findings.source_quote: As expected, Kapton has good agreement with most moment method diameters, as it has a lognormal size distribution. The TEM diameters from the size analysis and the converted values are very consistent as well. Thus, it can be concluded that Kapton smoke at these temperatures is very well suited to measurement by the moment method.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Flight data; ionization detector first-moment measurement
findings.quantity: calibration-range limitation and its effect on moment-method calculations
findings.statement: Many smoke aerosols exceeded the ionization detector's calibration range for first-moment measurements, which strongly influence the resulting moment-method calculations; Kapton was unaffected because it consists of smaller particles.
findings.safety_implication: Particle-size estimates from the moment method may be unreliable for aerosols outside the first-moment detector's calibration range, potentially limiting smoke characterization for spacecraft monitoring.
findings.equipment_implication: The ionization detector's calibration range constrained first-moment measurements for many smoke aerosols.
findings.source_quote: Although meticulous calibrations were performed, many smoke aerosols exceeded the calibration range for the ionization detector which measures the first moment. As evident in equations (12) and (13), error in the first moment measurement has the largest influence on the resulting calculations. Kapton consists of smaller particles and was not affected by this shortcoming, so these tests provided the most reliable moment method results.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Flight data
findings.statement: For lamp wick, Kapton, and Pyrell smoke in flight data, the moment method provided a reasonably good measurement of diameter of average mass compared with TEM.
findings.safety_implication: The moment method can provide a useful average-mass particle-size measure for these smoke types, supporting aerosol characterization when TEM comparisons are unavailable.
findings.equipment_implication: The moment method provided a reasonably good measurement of diameter of average mass for the three materials shown.
findings.source_quote: For the three materials in this graph, the moment method provides a reasonably good measurement for the diameter of average mass. Thus it can be concluded that the zeroth and third moment instruments maintained their calibration sufficiently to quantify one of the moment average diameters from flight data.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Flight Dynamic diluter
findings.statement: For the Flight Dynamic diluter, actual sample flow was correlated to the commanded flow by actual flow (ccm) = 0.9474*command value (ccm) -1.2395 (ccm).
findings.safety_implication: Using commanded flow without this measured correction could bias aerosol concentration calculations used to interpret smoke measurements.
findings.equipment_implication: A measured flow correction was reported for the Flight Dynamic diluter.
