findings.source_quote: The correlation between actual sample flow and commanded flow to LFE for the Flight Dynamic diluter is: actual flow (ccm) =  0.9474*command value (ccm) -1.2395 (ccm).
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Engineering Dynamic diluter
findings.quantity: availability of a validated flow correlation
findings.statement: The SAME-R Engineering Dynamic diluter had no valid test results establishing a flow correlation, so the Flight Dynamic diluter correlation was to be used for it if needed.
findings.safety_implication: Applying a correlation from a different diluter leaves uncertainty in Engineering-unit aerosol concentration estimates.
findings.equipment_implication: No valid flow-correlation test results were available for the Engineering Dynamic diluter.
findings.source_quote: There are no valid test results to give such a correlation for the Engineering Dynamic diluter. Thus the above correlation will be used for the engineering Dynamic diluter if needed.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Same Rt/R0 across samples
findings.statement: For the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature could differ by as much as 30 degrees Celsius between samples.
findings.safety_implication: Matching tests by Rt/R0 alone may not ensure equivalent smoke-generation temperatures, which can confound comparisons of smoke properties.
findings.equipment_implication: Rt/R0 alone did not uniquely ensure the same actual heating temperature across samples.
findings.source_quote: After the heating temperatures were obtained, it is surprising that for the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature difference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.material: Lamp wick, silicone rubber, Pyrell, and Teflon
findings.conditions_text: Baseline runs; aged 720 s
findings.statement: After aging for 720 s, smoke particle diameters increased for lamp wick, silicone rubber, and Pyrell, while Teflon’s count mean and geometric mean diameters decreased slightly and its diameter of average mass increased.
findings.source_quote: The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diameters.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.material: Teflon, Kapton, lamp wick, and silicone rubber
findings.conditions_text: Baseline runs; aged cases
findings.statement: In the tested baseline runs, Teflon and Kapton smoke particles were small, while lamp wick and silicone rubber had substantially larger average-mass diameters, especially after aging; detecting the smaller particles with light-scattering devices is challenging.
findings.safety_implication: A spacecraft smoke detection system may miss or respond weakly to smoke from Teflon or Kapton unless it can distinguish particle sizes.
findings.equipment_implication: Light-scattering detectors need particle-size discrimination to detect small-particle smoke without excessive nuisance alarms from large dust.
findings.source_quote: Overall, the Teflon and Kapton particles were very small.  The lamp wick and silicone results exhibited substantially larger diameters of average mass, particularly for the aged cases.  As reported previously10, the Dust Trak results for lamp wick and silicone demonstrated substantial portions of the particle distribution possessed aerodynamic diameters larger than 1 micrometer.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Particle diameter plotted versus duct velocity
findings.statement: Smoke particle size increased as duct air velocity decreased for lamp wick, Kapton, and Teflon; smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure is therefore expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detectors should be evaluated under low-flow enclosure conditions because smoke particle size, and hence detector response, may differ from ventilated-area conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Validate detector response at low airflow representative of avionics enclosures.
findings.source_quote: These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates.  This indicates that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Correlation processing of MPASS output using other SAME measurements as reference
findings.statement: With appropriate processing, the two-moment MPASS output can be proportional to either particle number concentration or mass concentration across a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions, and can distinguish smoke concentration from a strong signal caused by large dust particles.
findings.safety_implication: A two-moment detector can reduce false smoke alarms from large dust particles while retaining sensitivity to smoke across varying particle sizes and compositions.
findings.equipment_implication: Use two particle-size moments with appropriate signal processing to estimate either number or mass concentration and discriminate dust from smoke.
findings.source_quote: Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions.  This independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Aging; TEM images
findings.statement: Aging increased average smoke particle size, but the most visible change in TEM images was disappearance of the smallest particles.
findings.source_quote: As seen in Table 1, aging did increase the average particle size, however this level of change is not readily visible in the TEM images, instead the most visible change is the disappearance of the smallest particles.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: MPASS measures two approximate aerosol moments, the 3rd and 2nd moments
findings.quantity: particle-size correction of smoke detector signal
findings.statement: The report describes the MPASS two-moment aerosol sensor as enabling smoke-detector alarms to be less sensitive to larger particles typical of dust, by correcting the detector signal for particle size.
findings.safety_implication: Reducing alarms triggered by larger dust particles could help crews distinguish smoke from dust and preserve confidence in spacecraft fire alarms.
findings.equipment_implication: Two-moment aerosol sensing can compensate the alarm signal for particle size, unlike single-moment spacecraft smoke detectors.
findings.source_quote: The underlying assumption is that by measuring two moments of the aerosol it is possible to correct the smoke detector signal for the particle size, unlike previous spacecraft smoke detectors which are limited to a single moment measurement10. This will enable the alarm to be less sensitive to larger particles that are typical of dust.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.statement: The much smaller smoke particles from Kapton and Teflon are challenging for light-scattering devices to detect, and detection against background particles requires a system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.
findings.safety_implication: A single-moment light-scattering detector may miss or misclassify smoke from these materials in a particle-background environment.
findings.equipment_implication: Use particle-size discrimination or multi-moment measurement for smoke detection across differing particle sizes.
findings.source_quote: This suggests that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: Correlation derived from SAME measurements across test points with signal to noise ratio greater than 2
findings.quantity: relative variance of smoke concentration response
findings.statement: With appropriate processing, the MPASS could estimate either smoke number concentration or mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions, reducing relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 compared with a conventional single-output sensor.
findings.safety_implication: Multi-moment processing can provide a more reliable smoke concentration indication across different aerosols than a single-output response.
findings.equipment_implication: MPASS multi-moment processing can estimate number or mass concentration and distinguish smoke from large dust particles.
findings.source_quote: Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.material: silicone rubber and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick
findings.conditions_text: TEM imaging of samples collected on grids using the thermal precipitator
findings.statement: Silicone rubber and dibutyl-phthalate smoke samples produced no particles visible by TEM, presumably because condensed liquid particles evaporated before imaging.
findings.safety_implication: TEM imaging may fail to characterize smoke from these materials if condensed liquid particles evaporate before analysis.
findings.equipment_implication: Interpret TEM non-detection cautiously for potentially volatile liquid smoke particles.
findings.source_quote: Overall, silicone rubber and DBP presented no particles that were visible via TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the TEM.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests
findings.statement: For all tested materials, the diameter of average mass of smoke particles was 30% to 40% larger in zero-flow microgravity tests than in tests with flow.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke-detection systems should be assessed with low-gravity, zero-flow smoke because its larger particles may be detected differently than smoke produced under flow.
findings.equipment_implication: Assess detector performance against larger-particle smoke produced under low-gravity zero-flow conditions.
findings.source_quote: It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: zero-flow condition; case with a flow of 8 cm/s
findings.statement: In microgravity zero-flow conditions, Pyrell smoke changed from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres at 8 cm/s airflow to spherical particles.
findings.source_quote: A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13).
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.conditions_text: For the conditions of the SAME experiment
findings.statement: The five tested spacecraft materials produced substantially different smoke particle size distributions, and spacecraft overheat events may produce broad distributions because materials and flow and temperature conditions vary.
findings.safety_implication: Detector performance should be assessed across broad particle size distributions representative of varied spacecraft materials and overheat conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Evaluate detector response across a broad range of smoke particle sizes.
findings.source_quote: The results from the SAME experiment  indicate that substantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft materials that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.quantity: detector response to particle size range and nuisance sources
findings.statement: The report concludes that detection methods measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution may detect a broader particle range and reject nuisance-source false alarms more successfully than single-moment detectors.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire detection designs should consider multi-moment sensing to improve response across varied smoke sizes while limiting nuisance alarms.
findings.equipment_implication: The prototype 2-moment detector MPASS showed potential for broad particle response and false-alarm avoidance.
findings.source_quote: These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors. The results from the prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance sources.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.material: silicone rubber, lampwick, Pyrell, Teflon, and Kapton
findings.conditions_text: for a fixed wire temperature
findings.statement: For a fixed wire temperature, increasing convective flow produced mixed aerosol mass concentration trends across materials: silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increased slightly, while Teflon and Kapton decreased.
findings.source_quote: Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

findings.material: cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, and Teflon; dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick was used as a reference
findings.conditions_text: samples were heated to temperatures below the ignition point
findings.statement: For the spacecraft materials tested in microgravity, a substantial portion of the smoke particles produced by heating below ignition were smaller than 500 nm in diameter.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors should be evaluated for sensitivity to submicron particles from overheated materials.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector design and qualification should account for smoke particles below 500 nm from the tested spacecraft materials.
findings.source_quote: The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.statement: In the SAME smoke transport model, mixing dominated smoke transport, resulting in longer detection time lags than in normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detector placement and alarm-response assumptions for spacecraft should account for slower smoke transport and longer detection delays in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft detector layouts and response planning should account for mixing-dominated transport and longer detection lags than in normal gravity.
findings.source_quote: The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: STS background aerosol measurements using two cascade impactors
findings.statement: STS background aerosol measurements showed a bimodal particle-size distribution, with about 40% of particles in each of the 2.5 µm to 10 µm and greater-than-100 µm ranges; the other measured ranges were very lightly populated.
findings.safety_implication: Fire detection thresholds for spacecraft should distinguish fire aerosols from substantial ambient particle populations in these size bands.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector discrimination should be evaluated against spacecraft background aerosol distributions, not only clean-air baselines.
findings.source_quote: The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 2.5 μm to 10 μm and >100 μm ranges. The other two ranges <2.5 μm and 10 μm to 100 μm were very lightly populated.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: STS measurements compared with typical indoor measurements
findings.statement: STS background aerosol concentrations in the two most populated size ranges were more than five times typical indoor measurements.
findings.safety_implication: Alarm discrimination strategies designed around ordinary indoor aerosol backgrounds may not transfer directly to spacecraft environments.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft detector calibration should reflect measured spacecraft background concentrations, which exceeded typical indoor levels in key size ranges.
findings.source_quote: These results showed substantially higher concentrations than typical indoor measurements (over a factor of 5 for the two most populated size ranges).
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: STS light-scattering measurements at 12 locations
findings.statement: STS light-scattering measurements reported mass concentrations from 50 μg/m3 to 70 μg/m3 in all 17 measurements across 12 locations.
findings.source_quote: These data were supported by the light scattering instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 locations, all of these reported mass concentrations ranging from 50 μg/m3 to 70 μg/m3.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: ISS US Lab, Increment 10; DAFT feasibility experiment
findings.statement: ISS background particle counts measured during the DAFT feasibility experiment were below 5 particles/cm3, at the instrument noise level.
findings.safety_implication: The noise floor limits confidence in interpreting low-level spacecraft aerosol backgrounds, so detector validation needs adequate sensitivity below the expected background range.
findings.equipment_implication: Aerosol instruments used to characterize spacecraft backgrounds need a noise floor low enough to resolve counts below 5 particles/cm3.
findings.source_quote: The measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm3).
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: In the SAME experiment
findings.quantity: instrument signal correlation with aerosol moments
findings.statement: In the SAME smoke-aerosol measurements, instrument signals correlated well with the corresponding moments except for the third moment, whose value depended on both the DustTrak output and particle diameters; determining the best-fit geometric mean diameter and geometric standard deviation therefore required an iterative procedure.
findings.equipment_implication: Optical aerosol measurement equipment used to estimate particle-size distributions should account for particle diameter when calibrating or interpreting its signal as a third moment.
findings.source_quote: The results of these calibrations showed that the instrument signals correlate well with corresponding moments except for the third moment. The third moment was found to be a function of the DustTrak output and the particle diameters.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: ground calibration with monodisperse DOP droplets
findings.statement: During ground calibration of the P-Trak with monodisperse DOP droplets, particle diameter affected its number-count output more noticeably as number concentration increased, so separate correlations were used for different particle sizes when analyzing flight data.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detector or particle-monitor readings may require particle-size-aware calibration to avoid mischaracterizing smoke concentrations.
findings.equipment_implication: Particle counters used to assess smoke should be calibrated for the particle-size range expected in service.
findings.source_quote: As the number concentration increases, the effect of the particle diameter becomes more evident. Separate correlations were developed for each particle size and the closest correlation was used to analyze the flight data based on the initial estimates of the average particle size.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: ground calibration across particle sizes
findings.quantity: ion chamber response dependence on particle size
findings.statement: In ground calibration, the ion chamber's response showed very little dependence on particle size, so a single correlation was used for all particle sizes.
findings.safety_implication: The ion chamber's particle-size-insensitive calibration may support more consistent smoke detection across varying aerosol sizes.
findings.equipment_implication: Ion-chamber smoke detectors may need less particle-size-specific calibration than the P-Trak for the tested aerosol sizes.
findings.source_quote: The first moment device, the ion chamber, showed very little effect of particle size, as seen in Fig 8. Consequently a single correlation was used for all particle sizes.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Typical ISS runs; silicone rubber and Teflon smoke
findings.quantity: smoke detector response to particle-size distribution
findings.statement: During ISS tests, silicone rubber smoke contained a substantial fraction of aerosol mass in particles larger than 1 μm, while Teflon smoke consisted primarily of particles smaller than 1 μm; the ISS and STS smoke detectors responded differently to these particle-size distributions.
findings.safety_implication: A detector that responds weakly or erratically to one smoke particle-size range could provide less reliable warning for fires producing that smoke.
findings.equipment_implication: Evaluate smoke detectors against the particle-size distributions expected from different spacecraft materials, rather than relying on a single smoke type.
findings.source_quote: This shows that the smoke detectors used in STS and ISS have different response to particle size range.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: 720 second aging runs
findings.statement: During an ISS smoke-aging run, particle number concentration decreased substantially while mass concentrations remained relatively steady, a pattern consistent with particle coagulation and limited wall loss.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke aging can change particle number without a comparable change in aerosol mass, so detection performance may depend on how long smoke has been transported before reaching a sensor.
findings.equipment_implication: Assess detector response over smoke-aging times representative of the expected transport path to the sensor.
findings.source_quote: Figure 13 shows that the effect of is a substantial decrease in the number concentration (Ptrak) while the mass concentrations (DustTraks) remain relatively steady. This behavior is consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.material: Kapton, Teflon, lamp wick, and silicone
findings.conditions_text: SAME flight tests; smoke particle sizes across the range seen in SAME and CSD
findings.quantity: smoke particle size and detector response
findings.statement: In SAME, smoke from Kapton and Teflon had small particle diameters that make detection challenging for light-scattering devices, while lamp-wick and silicone smoke produced larger light-scattering signals; detecting smoke across the range seen in SAME and CSD while discriminating against dust likely requires particle-size discrimination.
findings.safety_implication: A spacecraft smoke-detection system should be evaluated across varied smoke particle sizes and against dust to reduce missed detections and false alarms.
findings.equipment_implication: Use detectors that measure more than one moment of the particle size distribution or classify particles into size ranges.
findings.source_quote: In combination with the knowledge gained from previous CSD experiment, it becomes obvious that the detection of smoke across the size range seen in SAME and CSD, while still discriminating against dust (which tends to be large), will probably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size distribution to at least a limited degree.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Smoke aging; aging considered representative of smoke emerging from a closed volume
findings.statement: In the SAME tests, aged smoke particle sizes increased substantially, with aged silicone's diameter of average mass rising to over 1 μm; for smoke emerging from a closed volume, such as an avionics enclosure, fire sensors must account for large particles as well as the smaller particles seen with Kapton.
findings.safety_implication: Sensors monitoring enclosed spacecraft volumes should remain effective as smoke particles grow during aging, rather than relying only on response to small particles.
findings.equipment_implication: Design or qualify fire sensors to detect both small particles and the larger particles that can occur in aged smoke.
findings.source_quote: The aging results show substantial increase in the average particle sizes with them rising to over 1 m for the aged silicone diameter of average mass. Since the aging can be considered to be representative of smoke emerging from a closed volume (e.g. an
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Non-flaming overheat; pre-fire conditions
findings.quantity: ionization detector response and smoke particle size
findings.statement: The CSD experiment reported poor detection by the Space Shuttle ionization detector for non-flaming overheat smoke from cellulose and silicone rubber, indicating larger particle sizes; SAME's authors note that under some reasonable pre-fire conditions smoke size distributions can extend beyond those observed in SAME.
findings.safety_implication: Detector qualification should include non-flaming overheat smoke, which may produce particle sizes outside the range represented by SAME.
findings.equipment_implication: Test ionization smoke detectors against non-flaming overheat smoke from cellulose and silicone rubber, including potentially larger particles.
findings.source_quote: The CSD experiment5 reported poor detection by the Space Shuttle detector for non-flaming overheat of cellulose and silicone rubber (indicating larger particle sizes). The reduced signal on the Space Shuttle detector for CSD suggests that under some reasonable pre-fire conditions the smoke size distribution can extend to diameters beyond those seen in the SAME experiment.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.material: Kapton®, Teflon®, lamp wick, and silicone rubber
findings.quantity: smoke particle size and size distribution
findings.statement: Smoke particle size depended on the tested material: Kapton® and Teflon® produced small particles that are challenging for light-scattering detection, while lamp-wick and silicone-rubber smoke included substantially larger particles and may require detectors capable of measuring more than one particle-size moment.
findings.safety_implication: A spacecraft smoke detector designed around one particle-size response could miss or mischaracterize smoke from some materials.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector qualification should account for material-dependent particle sizes and evaluate more than one particle-size moment.
findings.source_quote: The small diameters for the Kapton® and Teflon® will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices; on the other hand, the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone rubber would generate very large signals on a light scattering system, suggesting that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.statement: Combining two particle-sensor measurements of different moments can provide an inexpensive assessment of aerosol particle size.
findings.equipment_implication: Two-moment particle sensing is a cited approach for adding particle-size information to smoke detection.
findings.source_quote: This is similar to the approach suggested by Litton et al. who demonstrated that by combining two simple particle sensors that measure different moments, an inexpensive assessment of the particle size could be achieved.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: low-g combustion particulate
findings.statement: Direct knowledge of low-gravity combustion particulate is needed for confident spacecraft smoke-detector design rather than extrapolation from 1-g data.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft detector designs based solely on normal-gravity smoke data may not reliably represent smoke encountered in orbit.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft smoke-detector design should use direct measurements of low-g combustion particulate.
findings.source_quote: The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.statement: In some SAME measurement cases, the iterative scattering model did not converge, so the geometric mean particle diameter could not be determined; a bimodal particle-size distribution was suggested as a possible cause.
findings.equipment_implication: Particle-sizing algorithms based on this model may fail to return a diameter for some measured smoke distributions.
findings.source_quote: In some cases, convergence was not obtained and for these cases, the geometric mean diameter can not be determined. This non-convergence is currently under investigation but may be due to the presence of a bimodal particle size distribution.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Low-gravity smoke particle size data were not available when the existing systems were designed
findings.statement: Existing ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors, designed using 1-g smoke data, generally have non-overlapping particle-size sensitivities, while low-gravity smoke particle sizes were not available to their designers.
findings.safety_implication: Detector coverage may be incomplete for smoke particle sizes produced in microgravity, so spacecraft detection designs need validation against low-gravity smoke data.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft smoke detector design should account for measured low-gravity particle-size distributions rather than rely only on 1-g data.
findings.source_quote: Low-gravity smoke particle size data were not available when the existing systems were designed, consequently the designers used 1-g smoke detector designs. These design decisions led to detectors on the ISS and the Space Shuttle Orbiter that, in general, have non-overlapping particle size sensitivities.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: low-gravity
findings.statement: Prior CSD experiment results suggested that liquid smoke particles from several spacecraft materials in low gravity could exceed 1 μm, while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range.
findings.safety_implication: Detector performance should be assessed for both larger liquid droplets and smaller solid particles because one sensing principle may not cover both size ranges.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector selection and calibration should cover the distinct particle-size ranges of liquid smoke and solid particulate in low gravity.
findings.source_quote: Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment [2] which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: STS and ISS background aerosol measurements compared with typical normal-gravity fires
findings.statement: The low particle levels below 2.5 μm in the STS measurements and low overall particle counts on the ISS suggest an opportunity for spacecraft fire detection in a size range where typical normal-gravity fires produce substantial particulate, although more complete particle-size statistics are needed.
findings.safety_implication: A low-background particle-size range may support sensitive spacecraft fire detection, but the limited background statistics leave uncertainty in detector design.
findings.equipment_implication: Explore detector sensitivity below 2.5 μm while obtaining more complete spacecraft background particle-size statistics.
findings.source_quote: The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection since typical normal gravity fires produce substantial particulate in this size range[2,7]. However more complete particle size statistics are needed.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: log-normal distribution with Dg=1.0 μm and σg=2.0
findings.statement: For a log-normal aerosol size distribution with Dg=1.0 μm and σg=2.0, the count mean diameter D0.5 is 1.27 μm and the diameter of average mass D1.5 is 2.06 μm.
findings.source_quote: As an example, for a log-normal distribution with Dg=1.0 μm and σg=2.0, the corresponding values of D0.5 and D1.5 are 1.27 μm and 2.06 μm, respectively.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: unaged results; count mean diameter (CMD) is 227 nm
findings.statement: For silicone rubber smoke in microgravity, DustTrak signals indicated that a substantial portion of aerosol mass was in particles larger than 1 µm, and almost half the particle mass was larger than 1000 nm despite a count mean diameter of 227 nm.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detectors and particle monitors should not rely on count mean diameter alone to characterize the aerosol mass that may be present.
findings.equipment_implication: Evaluate smoke-monitor response across particle-size distributions that include a substantial mass fraction above 1 µm.
findings.source_quote: Consequently, although the CMD for silicone rubber is 227 nm, almost half the particle mass is larger than 1000 nm, as evidenced by the ratio of the DustTrak instruments.
findings.earth_application: Smoke-monitor calibration for terrestrial fires should account for cases where particle count statistics underrepresent the mass contribution of larger particles.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Teflon smoke comprised primarily of particles having diameters less than 1 micron
findings.statement: For Teflon smoke composed primarily of particles with diameters below 1 micron, the STS detector gave a strong signal while the ISS detector signal was more erratic.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detection performance can vary with aerosol particle size, so detector selection and validation should include fine-particle smoke.
findings.equipment_implication: Validate detector response using fine-particle smoke representative of the reported Teflon aerosol.
findings.source_quote: For the Teflon smoke comprised primarily of particles having diameters less than 1 micron as shown in figure 9, the STS detector provided a strong signal. Conversely, the signal from the ISS detector was more erratic.
findings.earth_application: Terrestrial smoke-alarm evaluation can include fine-particle aerosols because detector response differed for the reported submicron smoke.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.material: Silicone rubber, Teflon, lamp wick (cellulose), and Kapton
findings.conditions_text: For the conditions of the SAME experiment
findings.statement: For the four materials tested in the SAME experiment, smoke particle size distributions differed substantially, and all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particles that are better detected by ionization smoke detectors.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft detection systems should include sensitivity to sub-micron smoke rather than relying only on response to larger particles.
findings.equipment_implication: Ionization detection is important for sensing the sub-micron particles produced by the tested materials.
findings.source_quote: The preliminary results from the experiments indicate that substantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the four materials that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are better detected using an ionization smoke detector.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: credible pre-fire overheat events; depending on the conditions
findings.statement: Considering SAME and CSD results, credible pre-fire overheat events in low gravity can produce broader smoke particle size distributions depending on the conditions, and detection methods measuring more than one moment of the distribution may improve detection and alarm rejection compared with single-moment detectors.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke alarm designs should account for varying particle sizes to improve detection while limiting false alarms from non-fire aerosols such as dust.
findings.equipment_implication: Use particle-size-sensitive detection, such as measuring multiple moments or classifying particles into size ranges.
findings.source_quote: Considering the results from both the SAME and CSD experiments, the only two fire detection experiments conducted in low-gravity, broader smoke particulate size distributions can be produced from credible pre-fire overheat events, depending on the conditions. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and alarm rejection than single moment detectors.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: particulate produced by low-gravity flames
findings.statement: Prior low-gravity studies reported that soot or unburned fuel particles from low-gravity flames tend to be larger than particles produced in normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors should be validated against low-gravity particle sizes rather than relying only on normal-gravity fire data.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector sizing and response should account for the larger particles reported in low gravity.
findings.source_quote: The salient result on smoke particle size determination in low-gravity reported by Urban et al.9 is that particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.material: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick
findings.conditions_text: similar conditions in normal gravity
findings.statement: Smoke particulate produced in microgravity was typically about 50% larger in count mean diameter than under similar normal-gravity conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detector response may differ between spacecraft microgravity and ground-test conditions, so ground testing alone may not fully characterize on-orbit detection.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector evaluation should account for the larger particle sizes measured in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than similar conditions in normal gravity.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.material: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick
findings.conditions_text: Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity
findings.statement: Smoke particles produced in the experiments were all below 300 nm, suggesting that detection in the sub-micrometer range could help distinguish spacecraft smoke from dust.
findings.safety_implication: A detector strategy that distinguishes sub-micrometer smoke from spacecraft dust could reduce missed fire indications or nuisance alarms.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported result supports evaluating detector technologies that discriminate particles in the sub-micrometer range.
findings.source_quote: The resultant sizes were all below 300 nm suggesting that discriminating smoke from spacecraft dust possibly could be achieved by detecting in the sub-micrometer range.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS
findings.statement: Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the ISS US Lab predicted that detection times could be quite long and strongly dependent on source location and the presence of obstructions.
findings.safety_implication: Detector placement and installed equipment can create location-dependent delays, so coverage should be assessed across likely fire locations and obstructed flow paths.
findings.equipment_implication: The modeled delays support assessing detector placement and smoke transport with representative onboard obstructions and ventilation conditions.
findings.source_quote: Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Smoke Points in Coflow
findings.statement: For non-buoyant jet diffusion flames, increasing co-flow velocity increases the laminar smoke-point length (LSP) and decreases soot formation time.
findings.equipment_implication: Co-flow velocity affects smoke-point length and soot formation time, so airflow conditions should be considered when interpreting smoke-related fire behavior.
findings.source_quote:
Increasing ua
increases LSP.
– Decreases soot
– Decreases soot 
formation time.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: Smoke Point Luminous Lengths
findings.statement: The luminous smoke-point length depends primarily on mass fuel flow rate (mf) and stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst).
findings.source_quote:
LSP depends 
primarily on mf and 
Zst.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: In microgravity conditions
findings.statement: In microgravity, increasing coflow velocity or decreasing burner diameter increased the smoke-point flame length of the tested coflow diffusion flames.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke-point length changes with airflow and burner size, so smoke-based fire assessments in microgravity should account for both conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detection and ventilation assessments for microgravity flames should account for coflow velocity and burner diameter.
findings.source_quote: In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm; unconfined coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm
findings.quantity: smoke-point length response to coflow velocity
findings.statement: For normal-gravity coflow flames using 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm burners, smoke-point length increased as coflow velocity increased; with an unconfined 13.7 mm burner, length decreased for ethylene and propylene and increased for propane.
findings.safety_implication: The effect of airflow on smoke-point behavior depends on burner configuration and fuel, so a single airflow-based smoke expectation may not generalize across sources.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detection and ventilation evaluations should consider fuel and burner configuration when interpreting smoke-point changes with airflow.
findings.source_quote: In normal earth gravity coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane flames.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: non-reacting flows; relatively weak coflows
findings.statement: A simplified prediction of centerline jet velocity did not produce residence-time-based criticalities or collapse the microgravity smoke-point data, and non-reacting-flow simulations showed it predicted velocity decay only for relatively weak coflows.
findings.source_quote: A simplified prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows showed that the simplified centerline velocity prediction was able to predict velocity decay for only relatively weak coflows.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.quantity: temperature at which soot nucleation becomes significant
findings.statement: Prior work reported that soot nucleation becomes significant at 1250 K.
findings.source_quote: Sunderland and Faeth24 determined soot nucleation to become significant at 1250 K.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: buoyant diffusion flame; at the flame tip
findings.quantity: temperature at which smoke burnout ceases
findings.statement: Prior work reported that smoke burnout in buoyant diffusion flames ceases when the flame tip cools to approximately 1300 K.
findings.source_quote: Kent and Wagner25 found that smoke burnout in the oxidative region of the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame at its smoke point
findings.quantity: temperature at the luminous flame tip
findings.statement: Prior work reported that the luminous tip of a nonbuoyant microgravity flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point.
findings.source_quote: Urban et al.26 found that the luminous tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: typically at the smoke point flame height
findings.quantity: radiative heat loss from the flame as a fraction of total heat release rate
findings.statement: Prior work reported that soot radiation accounts for about 30% of the total heat release rate in flames typically at the smoke-point flame height.
findings.source_quote: Also corroborating what was mentioned previously about a limiting temperature at which soot oxidation ceases, typically at the smoke point flame height, the radiative heat loss from the flame by soot radiation is about 30% of the total heat release rate of the flame.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: diffusion flames
findings.statement: Prior work reported that fuel sooting propensity in diffusion flames decreases in the order aromatics, alkynes, alkenes, then alkanes.
findings.source_quote: For diffusion flames, work by Schalla and McDonald34 showed that fuel sooting propensity decreases with hydrocarbon family in the following order: aromatics > alkynes > alkenes> alkanes.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames; inert added to the fuel stream
findings.statement: In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, adding inert to the fuel stream typically reduces sooting propensity and lengthens the smoke point.
findings.source_quote: In over-ventilated coflow diffusion flames, addition of inert to the fuel stream typically reduces sooting propensity. Longer smoke points result.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: buoyant and nonbuoyant jet flames
findings.statement: In buoyant flames, soot nucleated near the flame sheet is drawn into the fuel-rich core, while in nonbuoyant flames soot moves outward more directly toward the flame sheet and downstream oxidative region.
findings.source_quote: Therefore in a buoyant flame, once soot is nucleated in the soot production region near the flame sheet, it is drawn into the fuel rich core, allowing continued growth. In a nonbuoyant flame as the flow is drawn outwards, the soot moves in a more direct path to the flame sheet and oxidative region downstream.16
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.material: fuel and burner diameter combinations, including propylene mixtures
findings.conditions_text: For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter
findings.statement: For nonbuoyant coflow flames, increasing coflow velocity generally increases smoke-point luminous flame length for a given fuel and burner diameter.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke-point behavior in reduced-gravity coflow flames depends on ventilation velocity, so spacecraft smoke and soot assessments should account for airflow conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke and soot detection assessments for coflow environments should account for changes in coflow velocity and the associated smoke-point flame length.
findings.source_quote: For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: propylene with the 0.41 mm burner; testing on different days
findings.statement: For the 0.41 mm burner with propylene, smoke points varied between testing days when the duct exit became partially clogged; the lowest smoke points occurred with the relatively clogged exit, and the highest after it was vacuumed clean.
findings.safety_implication: Soot buildup or restrictions in airflow paths can affect smoke-point measurements, so airflow-path condition should be controlled when interpreting results used for spacecraft fire assessments.
findings.equipment_implication: Maintain and verify duct-exit cleanliness and coflow uniformity when using smoke-point measurements to characterize ventilation or smoke behavior.
findings.source_quote: The present smoke points were found to be repeatable, except for propylene with the 0.41 mm burner. Testing on different days yielded different smoke points for this combination.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: nonbuoyant coflow flames
findings.statement: For nonbuoyant coflow flames, smoke-point luminous flame length increases as burner diameter decreases, with a stronger difference between 0.76 and 0.41 mm burners than between 1.6 and 0.76 mm burners.
findings.safety_implication: Burner-scale effects can alter soot-related flame dimensions, so fire characterization using one burner diameter may not represent other source sizes in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke-related flame characterization and test protocols should account for burner diameter, particularly across the 0.76 to 0.41 mm range.
findings.source_quote: Figure 4.2 reveals that smoke points of nonbuoyant coflow flames increase with decreasing burning diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: increasing the N2 content of propylene
findings.statement: Increasing the N2 content of propylene increases smoke-point flame length.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel dilution changes soot-related flame behavior, so smoke-point characterization for fuel mixtures should not be assumed to represent the undiluted fuel.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke and soot assessments should characterize the actual fuel dilution rather than extrapolating from pure propylene.
findings.source_quote: The effect of fuel dilution can also be seen, with an increase in smoke point flame length with increasing the N2 content of propylene.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: flames with high initial fuel velocities relative to the surrounding coflow; LSP and 0.41 mm propylene data compared with 1.6 mm burner data
findings.quantity: slope ratio of corrected luminous flame-length correlation
findings.statement: For microgravity flames with high initial fuel velocity relative to surrounding coflow, flame-length data correlated more closely with the still-air flame-length relation than with the coflow relation; the reported slope for the LSP and 0.41 mm propylene data was approximately 1.44 times that of the 1.6 mm burner data.
findings.source_quote: The slope of the gray points (LSP and 0.41 mm propylene, neglecting possible outlier point indicated in the figure) is approximately 1.44 times the slope of the 1.6 mm burner points. It could be concluded that flames with high initial fuel velocities relative to the surround coflow would better correlate with the length correlation predicted by Equation (2.5) for flames in air still.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.material: ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen
findings.conditions_text: air coflow aboard the International Space Station; burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s
findings.quantity: luminous flame length and smoke-point fuel flow rate
findings.statement: In microgravity air-coflow diffusion flames using ethylene, propane, propylene, and 50% or 75% propylene mixtures in nitrogen, increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame length while shifting the smoke point to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
findings.safety_implication: Airflow changes can alter both visible flame extent and soot onset, so spacecraft fire assessments should account for ventilation conditions when evaluating flame behavior and smoke production.
findings.equipment_implication: Ventilation controls and material screening should be evaluated across the expected airflow range because coflow changes smoke-point behavior.
findings.source_quote: Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
findings.earth_application: The result can inform aircraft, vehicle, and building fire assessments where ventilation affects flame length and smoke production.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.material: ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen
findings.conditions_text: air coflow aboard the International Space Station; burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s
findings.statement: In microgravity coflowing diffusion flames, smaller burner diameters produce longer smoke-point flame lengths.
findings.safety_implication: Small-scale fuel outlets can sustain longer luminous flames before reaching the smoke point, so burner geometry should be included in spacecraft fire-risk assessments.
findings.equipment_implication: Burner and outlet designs should be tested at representative diameters rather than extrapolated from larger hardware.
findings.source_quote: Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames.
findings.earth_application: The finding may inform fire testing of small fuel jets and fuel-system components in aircraft and industrial equipment.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.material: ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen
findings.conditions_text: nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the International Space Station
findings.statement: The luminous flame lengths of the tested microgravity coflow diffusion flames generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, while increasing slightly as air velocity decreases.
findings.safety_implication: Flame-length predictions used in spacecraft fire analysis should include fuel mass flow, mixture stoichiometry, and coflow velocity.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire-model inputs and test procedures should measure both fuel flow and coflow velocity when estimating flame extent.
findings.source_quote: The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases.
findings.earth_application: The correlation may support flame-length and heat-exposure estimates for ventilated fires in aircraft, vehicles, and buildings.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: SPICE operation in the Microgravity Science Glovebox
findings.statement: Soot accumulated in the SPICE outlet screen and changed the flow behavior in the duct, requiring crew cleaning with a vacuum.
findings.safety_implication: Soot deposition can degrade ventilation performance during combustion experiments, so airflow paths require monitoring and a defined cleaning response.
findings.equipment_implication: Ventilation systems should provide fouling detection or inspection access and a procedure for restoring flow after soot accumulation.
findings.source_quote: SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in the duct. This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the outlet screen on June 15.
findings.earth_application: The finding is relevant to soot fouling of ventilation ducts and filters in aircraft, vehicles, and industrial fire-test systems.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: coflowing nonbuoyant flames; data extrapolated to ua = 0
findings.statement: In microgravity coflowing nonbuoyant flames, smoke point length increases as burner diameter decreases; extrapolation to zero coflow velocity gives only a weak dependence on burner diameter, consistent with cited normal-gravity observations.
findings.source_quote: Figure 2 reveals that smoke points of coflowing nonbuoyant flames increase with decreasing burner diameter. This differs from previous observations of microgravity flames in still air [17,18], whose smoke points are only weakly dependent on burner diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: fixed burner diameter and coflow velocity
findings.quantity: sooting propensity inferred from smoke point length
findings.statement: For fixed burner diameter and coflow velocity, the tested fuels' sooting propensity generally increases in the order propane, ethylene, 50% propylene, 75% propylene, then propylene; at the 0.76 mm burner, ethylene instead has a longer smoke point length than propane.
findings.source_quote: The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from changes in smoke point length for fixed burner diameter and coflow velocity, is generally propane < ethylene < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. (This is consistent with unpublished normal gravity results in the same apparatus.)
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: at the 13 mm Station and 56 mm Station; 6 Fan Dial Settings
findings.statement: In the SPICE flow duct, measured air velocity at 13 mm downstream of the nozzle was lower on the centerline than above and below, and this difference increased with fan settings; at 56 mm, the vertical profile became nearly linear with higher velocity at the bottom.
findings.safety_implication: Nonuniform local airflow near the nozzle can affect flame behavior, so duct or fan assessments should not rely only on an average airflow value.
findings.equipment_implication: Ventilation assessments should account for spatial airflow differences near the nozzle, not only average air velocity.
findings.source_quote: It can be seen that at the 13 mm Station, the air velocity on the centerline (downstream of the nozzle) is lower than those above and below. The velocity difference increases with fan settings (average air velocity), whereas at the 56 mm Station, this center-dipping velocity profile evolves to a near linear profile with higher velocity at the bottom.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: The nozzle ID in all the three cases is 1.6 mm and the average air velocity in the nozzle remains to be 50 cm/s; coflow velocity 25 cm/s
findings.statement: COMSOL modeling of the SPICE nozzle flow predicted that at 25 cm/s co-flow, air velocity decreases with radius near the nozzle and then increases before dropping again near the flow-duct wall; this profile extends downstream.
findings.safety_implication: Local airflow around a flame can differ substantially from the co-flow setting, which matters when assessing flame behavior under spacecraft ventilation conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Flow assessments should account for co-flow-dependent velocity distributions near the nozzle rather than treating co-flow as spatially uniform.
findings.source_quote: When the coflow velocity increases to 25 cm/s, a boundary layer around the nozzle becomes significant. Near the nozzle, in the radial direction the air velocity decreases with radius and then increases. As radius further increases to get near to the flow duct wall, the air velocity drops again.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: nonbuoyant coflowing flames
findings.statement: For microgravity nonbuoyant coflowing flames, smoke-point lengths decrease as burner diameter increases; extrapolating the measurements to zero coflow velocity diminishes the burner-diameter dependence.
findings.source_quote: Figure 18 reveals that smoke points of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. This behavior also can be attributed to effects of residence time, as fuel velocity is proportional to d–2 when fuel mass flow rate is constant.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: microgravity flames near and beyond their smoke points
findings.statement: In microgravity tests, smoke points of propane and ethylene were generally identified by gradual dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip, whereas propylene and propylene-mixture flames typically transitioned rapidly to open-tipped flames when smoke points were exceeded.
findings.safety_implication: Visual monitoring criteria for smoke-point transitions may need to account for the fuel, since the flame-tip cue differs across fuels.
findings.equipment_implication: Flame or video monitoring criteria should recognize both gradual dimming and rapid open-tip transitions as fuel-dependent cues.
findings.source_quote: Some smoke points (particularly for propane and ethylene) were identified by the onset of gradual dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames (particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming and reddening near their tips, except when much longer than their smoke points. For these flames, smoke points were identified by the rapid transition to open-tipped flames.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: when smoke points are far exceeded
findings.statement: Microgravity open-tipped flames occur when smoke points are far exceeded and are associated with centerline flame extinguishment and soot escaping in an annular shell.
findings.safety_implication: A dark or open flame center does not by itself indicate that combustion products have stopped escaping into the surrounding cabin environment.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke monitoring should account for soot emissions from open-tipped flames even when the flame centerline is extinguished.
findings.source_quote: Open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded4 and are associated with flame extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: 75% C3H6 flames shown in Fig. 17
findings.statement: The measured luminous flame lengths near smoke point were more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity in the illustrated 75% propylene flames.
findings.source_quote: The luminous lengths of the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: smoke-point flames plotted with respect to ṁf / Zst; matched conditions with low ua / uf
findings.statement: A reasonably good single correlation describes measured smoke-point luminous flame lengths across the tested fuels when plotted against fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction; at otherwise matched conditions, flames with low coflow-to-fuel velocity ratios are generally longer.
findings.source_quote: This choice of axes yields a reasonably good single correlation of the luminous lengths of all fuels. These results are similar to those of Lin and Faeth1 in that flames with low ua / uf are generally longer than those at otherwise matched conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air
findings.statement: For microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air, increasing coflow velocity increases smoke-point length.
findings.equipment_implication: Coflow velocity changes the smoke-point length, which should be considered when evaluating how airflow affects smoke production in comparable flame conditions.
findings.source_quote: An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air
findings.statement: For microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air, decreasing burner diameter increases smoke-point length.
findings.source_quote: A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: present fuel mixtures in microgravity; comparison with normal gravity
findings.statement: In microgravity, the sooting propensity of the tested fuel mixtures increased in the order ethylene, propane, 50% propylene, 75% propylene, and propylene; the order matched normal gravity except that ethylene and propane exchanged positions.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel choice can affect smoke production, so spacecraft fire-risk assessments should account for the tested fuel's sooting propensity under the relevant gravity conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Material and fuel selection assessments should consider the reported differences in sooting propensity and its gravity-dependent ranking.
findings.source_quote: The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: luminous length at the smoke point; ua / uf decreases
findings.statement: For the tested microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames, luminous length at the smoke point was proportional to fuel mass flow rate, with a slight increase in luminous length as ua / uf decreased.
findings.source_quote: Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as ua / uf decreases.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: present smoke point lengths; diameter and coflow velocity varied
findings.statement: For the present microgravity smoke-point flames, smoke-point length scales with d –0.91 uair 0.41; decreasing burner diameter or increasing coflow velocity decreases residence time and radiative loss fraction, leading to a longer smoke point.
findings.equipment_implication: Airflow changes can affect smoke-point length and should be considered when assessing ventilation effects on smoke production in comparable systems.
findings.source_quote: The present smoke point lengths scale with d –0.91 uair 0.41. Either a decrease in diameter or an increase in coflow velocity decreases residence time and radiative loss fraction, which in turn leads to a longer smoke point.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: present smoke points
findings.statement: For the present smoke points, residence time helps explain the observations but does not provide quantitative correlations of smoke points.
findings.source_quote: Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations of smoke points.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.conditions_text: conditions of low overall flame velocity
findings.statement: In microgravity, low-overall-velocity laminar jet diffusion flames can be dominated by radiative heat losses, extinguish at the flame tip, and emit soot; the smoke-point phenomenon can differ substantially from normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detection should account for soot emissions from low-velocity flames that extinguish at the tip, rather than relying solely on normal-gravity expectations.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detection for spacecraft should be evaluated against soot-emission behavior under microgravity, including flame-tip extinction at low overall flame velocity.
findings.source_quote: Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted.
findings.investigation_title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

findings.statement: Simulated microgravity smoke (no buoyancy, no settling) is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (>40 µm), while in Earth gravity settling limits maximum particle size to ~40 µm and mode size to ~5 µm.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detectors calibrated for terrestrial smoke may under-respond to the larger particles formed in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors must be sensitive to particles well above 10 µm, not only the ~5 µm terrestrial mode.
findings.source_quote: Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼ 40 µm and the mode particle size to ∼ 5 µm. Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm).
findings.earth_application: Better modeling of how smoke particle size depends on airflow and walls can improve placement and calibration of smoke detectors in low-airflow buildings and enclosed vehicle compartments.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: At 8 cm/s the microgravity size distribution has two maxima (5 µm and 30 µm); Earth gravity has only one at 5 µm and no particles above 40 µm, which settle out.
findings.source_quote: The Case 1MG distribution contains two local maximums: one at 5 µm and another at 30 µm. The Case 1EG distribution contains only one local maximum at 5 µm.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Earth gravity smoke contains orders of magnitude more particles <5 µm than microgravity smoke.
findings.source_quote: Case 1EG contains orders of magnitude more particles < 5 µm than Case 1MG.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Removing particle settling from the 1g simulation widens the distribution (nm to 100 µm) and creates a second maximum near 35 µm, like microgravity: settling is the main reason 1g smoke lacks large particles.
findings.source_quote: Eliminating the settling mechanism has expanded the size distribution to include both smaller and larger particles, and has also introduced a new local maximum in the size distribution near 35 µm.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Thermophoresis keeps particles away from the hot source surface; without it, particles reach the hot surface and evaporate, giving about 5x more peak-number particles and fewer large ones.
findings.source_quote: the peak number density in Case 1MG-NT is greater than Case 1MG by approximately a factor of five
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Rotating the heated source 90° shrinks the wake; the microgravity mode becomes 10 µm (about twice the other cases) and the 30 µm peak disappears — smoke size depends strongly on geometry.
findings.source_quote: The most frequent particle diameter for Case 1MG-R is dp = 10 µm – approximately two times larger than Cases 1MG, 1EG, and 1EG-R.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Microgravity cases show larger, darker smoke regions in the wake; Earth-gravity smoke appears more sensitive to small changes in flow speed.
findings.source_quote: Visual inspection also suggests the Earth gravity smoke to be more sensitive to small perturbations in flow speed than the microgravity smoke
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: In 1g, gravitational settling eliminates all particles >35 µm downstream of the wake; the 8 cm/s Earth case is unimodal at 5 µm, unlike microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter > 35 µm.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Three mechanisms make microgravity smoke larger: different recirculation (longer hot, vapor-rich residence), no settling of large particles, and (in 1g) buoyant transport of vapor to cool surfaces.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detection on spacecraft must expect larger particles, especially where hot recirculation zones form behind overheating components.
findings.equipment_implication: Choose detector size sensitivity and placement considering recirculation zones near likely smoke sources.
findings.source_quote: Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: The differences are material- and geometry-dependent; microgravity and 1g smoke should be more similar without stable recirculation, with small non-settling particles, or in open spaces without cool surfaces.
findings.source_quote: In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: A quiescent, enclosed system is where Earth-gravity and microgravity smoke are expected to differ most — recommended for future work.
