findings.safety_implication: Enclosed, low-ventilation spaces (e.g., stowage or racks) are where terrestrial smoke-detection assumptions are least reliable.
findings.source_quote: a quiescent, enclosed system is a relevant case where Earth gravity and microgravity smoke are hypothesized to differ significantly
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Cited measurements indicate microgravity smoke particles are 2–8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles.
findings.source_quote: Measurements suggest microgravity smoke particles to be 2 − 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005).
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Smoke detection systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities.
findings.safety_implication: Terrestrial-calibrated smoke detectors may miss or under-report fires on spacecraft such as the ISS.
findings.equipment_implication: Design mission-critical smoke detectors for the particle sizes seen in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Cited ISS-era data show particles >100 µm at ten times terrestrial mass concentration, and total particulate mass more than five times greater in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Cabin air filtration must handle larger and more persistent particulates in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Total particulate mass concentrations are also more than five times greater in microgravity
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Simulated SAME-like conditions: 0.08 m/s (8 cm/s) inlet air (the SAME flow), heated sample at 473.2 K releasing DBP at 8.4e-5 kg/m²·s.
findings.source_quote: We consider two inlet velocities: Uo = 0.08 m/s, the velocity considered in the SAME experiments, and a slightly faster flow of Uo = 0.10 m/s.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.statement: Earth-gravity nucleation peaks at ~1e14 vs ~1e12 in microgravity; in 1g buoyancy carries hot vapor to the cool upper wall, creating a high-nucleation zone there.
findings.source_quote: Nucleation occurs at a higher rate, ∼ 1014 m3 · s−1, in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: at time t = 7 seconds
findings.statement: In the DBP-vapor simulation, nucleation was higher in Earth gravity than in microgravity: approximately 10^14 m^-3·s^-1 in Case 1EG versus approximately 10^12 m^-3·s^-1 in Case 1MG.
findings.safety_implication: Gravity-dependent smoke-particle formation may affect how smoke detection performance observed on Earth translates to microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector evaluations intended for spacecraft should account for the predicted difference in particle nucleation between gravity conditions.
findings.source_quote: Panel (b) shows two primary zones of nucleation in Case 1EG: downstream of the upper wake vortex and in the region downstream and above the upper wake vortex, near the upper surface. Nucleation occurs at a higher rate, ∼1014 [m3 · s]−1, in Case 1EG than in Case 1MG.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: at time t = 7 seconds
findings.statement: The simulation predicted different particle-density distributions for DBP smoke in microgravity and Earth gravity: Case 1MG had approximately 10^10 m^-3 at wake-vortex centers and approximately 10^11 m^-3 downstream, while Case 1EG had nearly 10^12 m^-3 near the upper surface and fewer particles in its wake than Case 1MG.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke sampling locations and alarm response may differ between microgravity and Earth gravity because the predicted particle concentrations are distributed differently.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft smoke-detection assessments should consider particle concentration both in the wake and near chamber surfaces, rather than assuming a uniform distribution.
findings.source_quote: Panel (a) shows a particle number density of ∼1010 m−3 at the center of each counter-rotating wake vortex. Thermophoretic forces prevent particles from contacting the downstream surface of the heated vapor source (this will be demonstrated in Section 4.8), resulting in a void of particles between the heated vapor source and the particle-dense wake vortices.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: at time t = 7 seconds
findings.statement: The simulated DBP aerosol had a diameter of average mass typically between 10 and 20 µm in both microgravity and Earth gravity.
findings.source_quote: The diameter of average mass is typically 10 − 20 µm in both cases.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: Simulated smoke formation and growth in microgravity and Earth gravity; SAME geometry; flow speeds of 8 cm/s and 10 cm/s.
findings.statement: In the simulated dibutyl phthalate (DBP) smoke, microgravity produced larger particles than Earth gravity: the microgravity distribution could have a larger mode above 35 µm or a single mode at 10 µm, while the terrestrial distribution had effectively zero particles above 35 µm and a mode at 5 µm.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detectors or particle-measurement systems intended for spacecraft should not assume that terrestrial smoke particle-size distributions represent microgravity smoke.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft smoke detection performance should be assessed against particle-size distributions that include the larger microgravity modes reported here.
findings.source_quote: Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, while the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: 8 cm/s Earth gravity case; downstream of the wake; comparison with a case without particle settling.
findings.quantity: maximum particle diameter and particle size distribution
findings.statement: In the simulated 8 cm/s Earth-gravity DBP case, gravitational settling eliminated particles larger than 35 µm downstream of the wake; omitting settling produced a bimodal distribution with maxima comparable to the microgravity case.
findings.source_quote: Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling eliminates all particles with diameter > 35 µm. Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5 µm. Without particle settling, a bimodal distribution results with two local maximums at particle diameters comparable to the microgravity case.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: The authors identify material- and geometry-dependent mechanisms and discuss open environments and quiescent, enclosed systems.
findings.statement: For the modeled DBP smoke, the differences between microgravity and Earth-gravity particle distributions depend on material and geometry; the authors hypothesize greater similarity when nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, particles are too small to settle, or cool surfaces are absent, and significant differences in quiescent enclosed systems.
findings.safety_implication: Predictions based on this DBP configuration should not be generalized to spacecraft smoke from other materials or flow and enclosure geometries without further validation.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector assessments should account for the tested material and flow/enclosure geometry rather than treating the reported particle distributions as universal.
findings.source_quote: However, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: In Earth gravity
findings.statement: In the Earth-gravity simulations of dibutyl phthalate smoke, buoyancy created asymmetries in the flow and particle fields and increased vapor-to-particle conversion near room-temperature surfaces at the upper boundary.
findings.source_quote: In Earth gravity, buoyancy produces asymmetries in all fields of interest and amplifies vapor-to-particle conversion near room temperature surfaces at the upper boundary of the simulation domain.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: In Earth gravity
findings.statement: In the simulations, gravitational settling removed large particles from the dibutyl phthalate aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to approximately 40 µm and the mode size to approximately 5 µm.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors calibrated to terrestrial particle sizes may not detect microgravity smoke reliably.
findings.equipment_implication: Particle-size sensitivity for spacecraft smoke detection should account for the different particle sizes produced in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Gravitational settling removes large particles from the aerosol, limiting the maximum particle size to ∼40 µm and the mode particle size to ∼5 µm.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: Without buoyancy or settling
findings.statement: Without buoyancy or particle settling, the simulated microgravity dibutyl phthalate smoke plume was spatially symmetric and contained particles larger than 40 µm.
findings.safety_implication: Terrestrial smoke detector calibration may not transfer to spacecraft because microgravity smoke can contain much larger particles.
findings.equipment_implication: Spacecraft detector design and calibration should account for large particles in microgravity smoke.
findings.source_quote: Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity smoke plume is spatially symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 µm).
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: When prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source
findings.statement: In the simulated microgravity flow with prominent recirculation behind the hot vapor source, the dibutyl phthalate aerosol had a bimodal particle-size distribution: large particles greater than 20 µm associated with long-residency, vapor-rich, high-temperature recirculation, and smaller particles under 10 µm formed farther downstream.
findings.source_quote: A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source. The distribution is comprised of large particles (> 20 µm) associated with long residency time, vapor rich, high temperature recirculation, and smaller particles (< 10 µm) that originate farther downstream of the hot vapor source.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: Without recirculation
findings.statement: In simulated microgravity dibutyl phthalate smoke without prominent high-temperature recirculation, no distinct large-particle mode appeared, but large particles remained; the mode particle diameter was approximately 10 µm, about twice that of terrestrial smoke.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detector sizing and calibration for spacecraft should account for a larger characteristic particle size than terrestrial smoke.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector particle-size sensitivity should reflect the larger mode diameter reported for microgravity smoke.
findings.source_quote: A distinct large particle mode does not appear in microgravity flows that do not have prominent high temperature recirculation, although the aerosol still contains large particles. Without recirculation, the mode particle diameter in microgravity is ∼10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: Future experiments
findings.statement: The authors recommend that future experiments quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor to control geometry-dominated features of the particle-size distribution.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector development based on these simulations should use experiments that characterize surface interactions and hot-vapor recirculation effects on particle sizes.
findings.source_quote: Results show that future experiments should carefully consider and quantify surface interactions and the presence of hot, recirculating vapor, in order to control geometry-dominated features of the particle size distribution.
findings.investigation_title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

findings.conditions_text: n-dodecane droplets burning in air; (do = 4.00 mm)
findings.statement: For n-dodecane droplets burning in air, the cool-flame extinction diameter decreases as pressure increases and is absent at 3 atm, where the droplet burns to completion following warm-flame combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction assessments for pressurized spacecraft environments should account for pressure-dependent cool-flame behavior and the possibility of continued warm-flame combustion.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control and fire-risk assessments should account for pressure effects on cool-flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Both hot and cool flame extinction diameter has a non-linear dependence on pressure. de,CF decreases as pressure is increased, and is absent at 3 atm as the droplet burns to completion following a “Warm” flame combustion
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: three fuels
findings.quantity: cool-flame extinction properties and hot-flame extinction behavior
findings.statement: For the three n-alkane fuels, larger molecules exhibited more robust, higher-temperature cool flames and smaller extinction diameters; hot-flame extinction behavior was predicted to be similar across the fuels.
findings.safety_implication: Cool-flame extinction expectations should be fuel-specific; similarity in hot-flame behavior does not establish similar cool-flame behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Fuel-specific extinction assessments should include cool-flame behavior rather than infer it from hot-flame results.
findings.source_quote: Hot flame characteristics of all three fuels indicate that predicted extinction phenomena are all very similar. Cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the n-alkane molecular weight, and the chain length of the n-alkane has significant effect on the cool flame reactivity - larger n-alkane exhibited more robust cool flame (i.e., higher temperature) and hence smaller extinction diameters.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: each fuel
findings.quantity: cool-flame extinction diameter versus initial droplet diameter
findings.statement: For each fuel, cool-flame extinction diameter varied linearly with initial droplet diameter, but these relationships did not collapse to a single function across fuels, unlike the hot-flame relationships.
findings.source_quote: Universally, de,CF for each fuel varies linearly with initial droplet diameter, but unlike de,HF these relationships do not collapse to a single function.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: ambient pressures above one atmosphere
findings.statement: For n-dodecane droplet combustion, single two-stage hot-cool flame transitions changed to multi-cycle combustion above one atmosphere and eventually to a hot-to-warm flame transition as ambient pressure increased.
findings.safety_implication: Combustion behavior established at one pressure may not predict droplet flame transitions at higher operating pressures.
findings.equipment_implication: Pressure-dependent combustion modes should be considered when assessing spacecraft atmosphere operating conditions.
findings.source_quote: n-Dodecane droplet combustion reveal a strong dependence of observations on ambient pressure. Single, two-stage hot-cool flame combustion transitions to a multi-cycle combustion behavior at ambient pressures above one atmosphere, and eventually into a hot - “Warm” flame transition.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: Xenon LOI grows with droplet size: about 4%, 5% and 6% O2 for 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm droplets.
findings.source_quote: The LOI for xenon was found to be ~4%, 5% and 6% for 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm droplet sizes respectively.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: The exceptionally low thermal diffusivity of xenon (slow diffusive heat loss) is the main reason for its higher peak gas temperature and very low LOI.
findings.equipment_implication: When screening suppressant gases, prioritize high heat capacity and high thermal diffusivity, not just inertness.
findings.source_quote: The exceptionally low thermal diffusivity of xenon is primarily responsible for the significantly higher peak gas temperature and remarkably low LOI
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: This analysis led NASA to postpone testing and investment in xenon as a microgravity fire suppressant on the ISS; numerical droplet combustion can screen untested suppressants before costly flight tests.
findings.equipment_implication: Use validated droplet-combustion simulations to screen new gaseous suppressants before flight tests.
findings.source_quote: NASA also realized the possible drawbacks of xenon as a micro- gravity fire suppressant and postponed testing and investing resources on it.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: CFD predictions of methanol droplet burning in xenon agreed well with ISS (FLEX) experiments.
findings.source_quote: The CFD predictions are compared against the ISS experiments with the good agreement
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: Droplet combustion simulations found that the Sarathy et al. butanol model burned too fast because of isomer-specific transport (Lennard-Jones) parameters; after the authors updated them, predictions improved.
findings.source_quote: Following the recommendations from our studies to update fuel specific transport parameters, the model was revised by its authors, the prediction performances improved significantly for both gas and liquid phase targets.
findings.earth_application: Better kinetic models for renewable butanol fuels support engine and combustor design using bio-derived fuels.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.statement: Cool flames of n-alkane droplets matter for engine knock, spark/compression ignition and HCCI engines; the thesis models ozone-assisted direct cool-flame ignition of 0.5 mm n-heptane/n-decane droplets to enable ground drop-tower tests.
findings.source_quote: Because of its applied importance to engine knock and ignition in spark and compression ignition engines respectively, and potential for homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) engines
findings.earth_application: Cool-flame chemistry informs engine knock control and HCCI engine design.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Do = 0.56 mm, 1 atm, 21% O2/balance N2
findings.quantity: droplet diameter regression agreement with measurements
findings.statement: The detailed and reduced kinetic models predicted n-Butanol droplet-diameter regressions that agreed well with measurements up to approximately 50% of burn-time; after that, deviations grew, with the reduced model deviating more than the detailed model.
findings.source_quote: Up to approximately 50% of the burn, predictions from the model are almost identical and are in very good agreement with the measured data. However, beyond 50% of the burn-time slight deviation between the predictions and measurements start to exist. The discrepancy with the measurements increases when the reduced kinetic model is employed compared to the detailed kinetic model, as expected since reduced kinetic models removed possibly finer kinetic aspects during the process of reduction.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Spherically symmetric, isolated n-Butanol droplet combustion
findings.quantity: combustion completion and soot shell formation
findings.statement: Experimentally studied isolated n-butanol droplets burned to completion without a soot shell; numerical predictions also showed complete combustion and no flame extinction.
findings.safety_implication: The observed resistance to extinction suggests that small n-butanol droplets could remain burning rather than self-extinguish in comparable environments.
findings.source_quote: The experiments show no presence of a soot shell during the combustion process and droplets are observed to burn to completion unlike other smaller C1–C3 alcohols.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter sized n-Butanol droplets
findings.statement: For sub-millimeter n-butanol droplets, numerical analysis predicted a limiting oxygen index as low as 10%, and the authors concluded that flame extinction is unlikely in practical applications.
findings.safety_implication: Oxygen reduction alone may not reliably prevent or extinguish n-butanol droplet flames under comparable conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control and suppression strategies should not assume that reducing oxygen below ordinary ambient levels will extinguish n-butanol droplet flames.
findings.source_quote: The numerical analysis predicts that for sub-millimeter sized n-Butanol droplets, the limiting oxygen index is as low as 10% suggesting that flame extinction for n-Butanol is unlikely in practical applications.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: standard atmosphere conditions; isolated droplets with diameters ranged from 0.52 mm to 0.56 mm
findings.quantity: burning rate and flame stand-off ratio
findings.statement: For isolated butanol-isomer droplets under standard-atmosphere conditions, measured iso- and sec-butanol burning rates were very close to n-butanol's, while flame structure differed; n-butanol had smaller flame stand-off ratios than the isomers, and tert-butanol had the largest.
findings.safety_implication: Similar burning rates across these isomers do not imply identical flame geometry, so hazard assessments should account for the fuel isomer as well as burning rate.
findings.equipment_implication: Material and fuel hazard evaluations should distinguish butanol isomers because their flame structures and stand-off ratios differ.
findings.source_quote: The experimental data showed that the burning rates of iso- and sec-butanol are very close to that of n-butanol, differing only in flame structure. The flame stand-off ratios (FSR) for n-butanol flames are smaller than those for the isomers, while tert-butanol flames exhibited the largest FSR.
findings.earth_application: The measured combustion behavior can inform hazard assessment of butanol-isomer fuels used in ground transportation.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: isolated droplet burning characteristics under standard atmosphere conditions
findings.quantity: model accuracy for burning rates and flame stand-off ratios
findings.statement: For butanol-isomer droplet combustion, the Sarathy et al. kinetic-model predictions overestimated burning rates and flame stand-off ratios for all isomers except n-butanol, while Merchant et al.-based predictions agreed better with experiment, with larger discrepancies for tert-butanol.
findings.source_quote: DNM predictions based on the kinetic model of Sarathy et al. over-predict the droplet burning rates and FSRs of all the isomers except n -butanol. Predictions using a kinetic model based on the  work of Merchant et al. agree much better with the experimental data, though relatively higher discrepancies are evident for tert-butanol simulation results.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: For an individual isomer, respective simulations are performed under the same level of initial ignition energy. Ambient condition for simulation: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K.
findings.quantity: predicted gas-temperature rise and maximum gas temperature
findings.statement: For sec-, iso-, and tert-butanol droplet simulations at the same initial ignition energy, the LLNL model predicted earlier temperature rises than the MIT model, while both predicted nearly the same maximum gas temperature after ignition except during flame-out.
findings.source_quote: It is perceptible from the figure that the LLNL model ignition chemistry for each of the isomers is more sensitive than its counterpart model. Therefore, the rise in temperature for LLNL model is consistently earlier than that of MIT model. Surprisingly, immediately after the ignition transient, both the model approaches to the same maximum temperature throughout the lifetime of the burning droplet (i.e., at least till LLNL model predicted lifetime), both profiles remain almost the same except the flame-out phase.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter droplets; during the droplet burning history
findings.statement: In sub-millimeter droplet combustion, tert-butanol had the largest flame stand-off ratio (FSR) among the four butanol isomers, while n-butanol had the lowest; sec-butanol was slightly higher than iso-butanol.
findings.source_quote: It is evident that n-butanol has the lowest FSR along the combustion history. With the FSR of sec-butanol slightly higher than that of iso-butanol, tert-butanol exhibits the largest FSR among all four isomers.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: initial diameters (0.54 ±0.02 mm); ignoring the initial ignition transient and flame-out dynamics
findings.statement: For sec-, iso-, and tert-butanol droplets with initial diameters near 0.54 mm, experimental FSR values, excluding ignition and flame-out transients, ranged approximately from 5.0 to 9.0 during burning.
findings.source_quote: It is seen from the figure that irrespective of the butanol isomers, all of them show a similar trend in term of FSR evolution. By ignoring the initial ignition transient and flame-out dynamics, their overall values evolve in between ∼5.0 and 9.0.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter droplets; FSR evolution during burning
findings.quantity: agreement of kinetic-model FSR predictions with experiments
findings.statement: For sec-, iso-, and tert-butanol droplet combustion, the MIT kinetic model reproduced FSR evolution, particularly with the maximum-heat-release-rate marker, while the LLNL model consistently overpredicted FSR from the start of burning.
findings.source_quote: For sec-, iso- and tert-butanol isomers, the MIT model correctly simulated the FSR evolution, especially with HRRmax approach. Although the model’s prediction capability is laudable for sec- and iso-butanol, disagreement for tert-butanol at the latter part of the burn time is noticeable. Surprisingly, for all the isomers reported here, LLNL model consistently over-predicts the FSR evolution from initial burn time with similar FSR trend throughout its burning period and ultimately exhibiting almost the same extinction/flame-out temporal location (t/( Do)2 ∼1.20-1.25 s/mm2).
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: tert-butanol droplet combustion (Do = 0.52 mm)
findings.quantity: effect of model parameter exchange on predicted combustion behavior
findings.statement: For tert-butanol droplet combustion, exchanging isomer-specific transport property data caused the LLNL model to reproduce the MIT model prediction; exchanging thermodynamic property data or elementary reaction kinetics did not produce a distinguishable difference from the LLNL base run.
findings.source_quote: As evident in Figure 5.10, reaction kinetics and thermodynamic expression exchange do not contribute to distinguishable difference than its base run reported earlier (cf. Figures 5.4, 5.5 and 5.7). However, for the case of transport property data exchange, the LLNL model prediction reproduces the model prediction of MIT model.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: droplet burning under reduced gravity (O~10-4 g)
findings.statement: Under reduced gravity of approximately 10^-4 g, n-, iso-, and sec-butanol droplets had nearly identical D² histories, while tert-butanol had noticeably lower burning rates.
findings.source_quote: Experimental results of droplet burning under reduced gravity (O~10-4 g) show that D2 histories of n-, iso-, and sec- butanol are almost identical while tert-butanol has noticeably lower burning rates.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: droplet burning under reduced gravity (O~10-4 g)
findings.statement: For reduced-gravity butanol droplet combustion, n-butanol had the smallest flame spread rate, while the other three butanol isomers had similar flame spread rates.
findings.source_quote: FSR results suggest that n-butanol has the smallest FSR with the other three butanol isomers having FSRs close to each other.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: droplet combustion under reduced gravity
findings.quantity: model prediction accuracy for D² history, burning rate, and flame spread rate
findings.statement: For butanol-isomer droplet combustion, the LLNL model predicted n-butanol D² and flame spread rate well but overpredicted burning rates and flame spread rates for the other three isomers; the MIT model best predicted iso-butanol droplet-diameter evolution and acceptably predicted the other isomers, but neither model aligned as well with tert-butanol data.
findings.source_quote: The LLNL model does a good job predicting the D2 and FSR of n -butanol, but it overshoots the burning rates and FSRs of the other three isomers. The MIT model best predicts the evolution of droplet diameter for iso-butanol and provides acceptable predictions for the other isomers.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: computationally investigated for atmospheric and higher operating pressure (25 atm) conditions with varying levels of ozone (O3) mole fractions in the surroundings
findings.quantity: cool-flame burning mode and transition to hot flames
findings.statement: For computationally modeled sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets, cool-flame regime and transition behavior depended on ozone loading, pressure, diluent, initiation-source strength, and fuel vapor pressure; sustained cool burning without transition to a hot flame was possible over some combinations of ozone concentration, pressure, and droplet diameter, while sufficiently high ozone concentrations led to hot-flame transition after initiation.
findings.safety_implication: Ozone contamination and operating conditions can change whether a droplet sustains cool combustion or transitions to a hot flame, so these conditions matter when assessing ignition hazards around these fuels.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere controls and operating procedures involving ozone and pressure should account for their modeled influence on cool-to-hot flame transitions.
findings.source_quote: Comprehensive parametric computations show that the regime of the cool flame burning mode and the transition from cool to hot flames are sensitive to the changes of O3 loading, pressure, diluent variation, the strength of initiation source, and the influence of fuel vapor pressure at the ambient condition.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter sized droplets; over a range of O3 concentrations in the ambient; over some range of O3 concentrations, operating pressure, and drop diameter
findings.quantity: sustained cool-flame burning and transition to hot flame
findings.statement: Computations predict that sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets can sustain cool-flame burning across a range of ambient ozone concentrations, and that some ozone-concentration, pressure, and droplet-diameter conditions permit continuous self-sustaining cool flames without hot-flame transition.
findings.safety_implication: A cool flame can persist without becoming a hot flame, so absence of hot-flame transition does not by itself establish that combustion has ended.
findings.equipment_implication: Operational assessments should distinguish sustained cool-flame combustion from hot-flame transition when evaluating ozone and pressure conditions.
findings.source_quote: For both fuels and over a range of O3 concentrations in the ambient, sustained cool flame burning can be directly produced, even for sub-millimeter sized droplets. Over some range of O3 concentrations, operating pressure, and drop diameter, a self-sustaining, continuous cool flame burn can be produced without incurring a hot flame transition.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sufficiently high O3 concentrations
findings.quantity: transition from cool flame to hot flame
findings.statement: The computations predict that sufficiently high ozone concentrations cause combustion initiation in n-heptane and n-decane droplets to be followed by a hot-flame transition.
findings.safety_implication: High ozone conditions may turn initiated droplet combustion into a hot flame, which should be considered when evaluating ignition hazards in ozone-containing environments.
findings.equipment_implication: Ozone-control limits and operating procedures should account for the predicted hot-flame transition at sufficiently high ozone concentrations.
findings.source_quote: For sufficiently high O3 concentrations, combustion initiation is always followed by a hot flame transition.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: in the air at atmospheric pressure
findings.quantity: droplet diameter associated with transition to cool-flame diffusive burning
findings.statement: In ISS experiments at atmospheric pressure, n-heptane droplets larger than approximately 4 mm initially undergo hot-flame radiative behavior that transitions to cool-flame diffusive burning; smaller n-heptane droplets exhibit only hot-flame burning, followed by diffusive extinction or complete liquid consumption.
findings.source_quote: For example, in experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS), large n-heptane (n-C7H16) droplets (Do > ~ 4 mm) ignited in the air at atmospheric pressure the hot flame phenomena occurring initially radiatively transitions to a cool flame diffusive burning mode [2]. For smaller n-heptane droplets that do not have an overwhelming radiative loss from the flame, only hot flame burning is observed, leading to diffusive extinction or complete liquid phase consumption.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: n-decane droplets (Do ~ 4 mm); controlling the hot wire initiation energy– current amplitude and duration
findings.statement: For approximately 4 mm n-decane droplets, controlling hot-wire initiation energy through current amplitude and duration can produce either direct cool-flame burning or hot-flame burning; numerical analyses attribute this control to modulation of flammable fuel-air mixture formation near the droplet surface.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures for n-decane droplets can use hot-wire current amplitude and duration to select between direct cool-flame and hot-flame burning modes.
findings.source_quote: However, in more recent ISS experiments using n-decane (n-C10H22) droplets (Do ~ 4 mm) [5], cool flame behavior was able to be achieved directly by controlling the hot wire initiation energy– current amplitude and duration. Numerical analyses reveal that as a result of the high flashpoint of n-decane (319.3 K [8]), modulation of the initiation energy can be utilized to control the formation rate of partially premixed flammable fuel/air mixtures near the drop surface, and hence, control the heat release associated with vapor phase reaction.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: two initial droplet diameters (Do = 0.1 and 0.5 mm) and two ambient air pressures (1 and 30 atm) seeded with different levels of O3
findings.statement: For sub-millimeter n-heptane and n-decane droplets, the study computationally evaluates whether adding ozone can directly induce cool-flame burning at initial diameters of 0.1 and 0.5 mm and ambient pressures of 1 and 30 atm; this passage reports the study objective and conditions, not the outcomes.
findings.source_quote: The primary objective of this study is to computationally evaluate the potential of O3 addition to directly induce cool flame burning for sub-millimeter sized low and high flash point fuels, i.e. for n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, respectively. Below, we investigate two initial droplet diameters (Do = 0.1 and 0.5 mm) and two ambient air pressures (1 and 30 atm) seeded with different levels of O3.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: 0.5 mm initial droplet; 3% O3; prescribed thermal ignition source compared with hot-ambient approach
findings.statement: For a 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet at 1 atm with 3% O3, simulations predicted that the prescribed thermal ignition source initiated and stabilized the cool flame faster than the hot-ambient ignition approach.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition method can affect observed ignition timing, so comparisons of ignition behavior should control or document the method used.
findings.equipment_implication: Combustion-test procedures should specify the ignition-energy deposition method when comparing ignition times.
findings.source_quote: Therefore, for the remainder of this article, all results and discussions are based on the prescribed thermal ignition source.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter sized low flash point fuels such as n-C7H16
findings.statement: For sub-millimeter n-heptane droplets, ozone-stimulated oxidation of initially present fuel vapor and initiation energy help establish sustained cool-flame burning, but heat release from that vapor can limit or prevent it.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition controls for low-flash-point fuels should account for fuel vapor already present near the droplet, since it can alter whether cool-flame burning is sustained.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for both initiation energy and the availability of fuel vapor when assessing cool-flame establishment.
findings.source_quote: In summary, the combined effects of initiation energy, and ozone-stimulated chemical heat release from initially present fuel vapor oxidation play key roles in establishing a sustained cool flame droplet burning behaviors for sub-millimeter sized low flash point fuels such as n-C7H16.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: large diameter n-decane droplets on board the ISS; ambient temperatures are below the flash point
findings.statement: Experiments with large n-decane droplets in the ISS showed that when ambient temperature is below the fuel's flash point, ignition behavior depends more strongly on the applied thermal initiation energy; changing its deposition rate led to either hot-flame radiative extinction followed by prolonged cool-flame burning or direct cool-flame establishment.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition-energy delivery can change whether a droplet transitions through a hot flame or establishes a cool flame directly, which matters when evaluating ignition and flame-extinction behavior in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures and tests should account for the rate of thermal energy deposition when assessing cool-flame outcomes for fuels below their flash point.
findings.source_quote: Recent experiments with large diameter n-decane (n-C10H22) droplets on board the ISS demonstrated that for fuels and conditions where ambient temperatures are below the flash point, the overall ignition characteristics are significantly more dependent on the thermal initiation energy that is applied.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: sub-millimeter sized n-C10H22 droplets; simulated
findings.quantity: droplet surface temperature at establishment of steady cool-flame combustion
findings.statement: In simulations of n-decane droplets, an initial cool-flame attempt consumed fuel without establishing steady combustion while fuel-vapor supply was insufficient; oscillatory cool flames followed, and steady cool-flame combustion became possible when the droplet surface approached ~ 400 K and evaporation increased.
findings.safety_implication: A transient flame or ignition event may not indicate sustained burning when vapor supply is limited, while subsequent droplet heating can enable steady combustion.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition assessments should distinguish transient cool-flame activity from sustained combustion as the droplet heats and vapor production changes.
findings.source_quote: Therefore, oscillatory cool flames are triggered (cf. Figure 6.6 (a), 7 (f) and 8 (d)) similar to those observed for large diameter droplets [4, 33]. By the time the second dumped cool flame reappears, liquid phase droplet surface temperature approaches ~ 400 K at which enhanced fuel evaporation is established which is sufficient to establish a steady cool flame combustion (cf. Figure 6.6 (a) and 7 (e)).
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: stable cool-flame mode of operation
findings.statement: In the simulations, n-decane droplets burned at an ever-increasing burning rate until the droplet burned to completion, with a relatively slowly evolving flame stand-off ratio.
findings.source_quote: Contrary to the n-C7H16 droplet, n-C10H22 burns at an ever-increasing burning rate (Figure 6.6 (b)) with relatively slow-evolving FSR until the droplet burns to completion.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: 0.5 mm droplet at 1 atm (3% O3, producing cool flame) and 25 atm (0.5% O3)
findings.statement: For 0.5 mm n-heptane droplets, numerical simulations indicate that raising pressure from 1 atm to 25 atm shifts burning toward hot ignition, with elevated pressure making the H2O2 decomposition pathway to OH more important.
findings.source_quote: At atmospheric pressure, the relative importance of H2O2 in transitioning the gas phase reactive mixture to hot ignition via H2O2 (+M) = OH + OH (+M) is much less pronounced than the elevated pressure scenario where the O3 loading is purposely made small. At higher pressure, the drastic consumption of H2O2 and the evolution of gas phase temperature and OH radicals (cf. subplots in bottom row) manifest the impact of pressure in shifting the system to hot ignition.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Isolated n-alkane droplet combustion; low and high flashpoint fuels
findings.statement: For isolated n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, the initiation-energy requirements differ: partially premixed vapor combustion helps sustain low-flashpoint fuel burning as it transitions to diffusion burning, while high-flashpoint n-C10H22 liquid must first be heated above its flash temperature and the energy must also sustain that transition.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition strategies for liquid fuels should account for fuel flashpoint and vaporization because the energy needed to initiate and sustain burning differs between fuels.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for fuel-specific flashpoint and vaporization behavior.
findings.source_quote: The required initiation energy for igniting low and high flashpoint (relative to ambient temperature) fuel droplets differ as a result of combustion of partially premixed flammable vapor present in the low flashpoint case.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Without ozone present
findings.statement: Without ozone, n-C7H16, the low-flashpoint fuel case, is difficult to keep from transitioning to hot-flame conditions because of the vapor temperature needed for ignition and the rate and duration of droplet vaporization.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition of low-flashpoint liquid fuels without ozone may produce hot flames rather than a controlled cool-flame state.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for the difficulty of avoiding hot-flame conditions in the low-flashpoint case without ozone.
findings.source_quote: Without ozone present, the fuel/vapor temperature required to initiate the burning of the low flash point fuel and the rate and duration of vaporization of the droplet makes it difficult to avoid the transition to hot flame conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Without ozone present; limited vaporization typical of high flash point fuels
findings.statement: Without ozone, limited vaporization in the high-flashpoint fuel case allows the initiation energy's rate and duration to be controlled to achieve cool-flame burning without hot-flame conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel volatility and control of ignition energy can affect whether ignition produces cool-flame or hot-flame burning.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures should account for fuel vaporization and control the rate and duration of initiation energy.
findings.source_quote: Without ozone present, and with the limited vaporization typical of high flash point fuels, the initiation energy can be controlled in terms of rate and duration to achieve cool flame burning without incurring hot flame conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: O3 seeded into the surrounding air
findings.quantity: initiation temperature and energy release rate
findings.statement: For n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets, ozone seeding reduces the temperature, and therefore the initiation energy, required to initiate gas-phase reactions; the ozone amount affects the rate of energy release at and after reaction initiation.
findings.safety_implication: Ozone concentration can alter ignition requirements and subsequent energy release, so it is a relevant atmospheric condition when assessing ignition behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere assessments should account for ozone concentration because it affects both initiation requirements and energy release after ignition.
findings.source_quote: The seeding of O3 into the surrounding air offers an ability to reduce the temperature (and therefore initiation energy required) to initiate gas phase reactions of the flammable vapor/air mixtures. The amount of O3 seeding affects the rate of energy release occurring at and subsequent to reaction initiation.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: At elevated pressure (here, 25 atm)
findings.quantity: maximum O3 concentration threshold for hot ignition
findings.statement: For n-C7H16 and n-C10H22 droplets at elevated pressure (25 atm), the maximum ozone concentration threshold associated with hot ignition decreases significantly, attributed to pressure dependence in reactions forming HO2 and especially H2O2 (+M) = OH + OH (+M).
findings.safety_implication: Higher pressure can make hot ignition possible at a lower ozone threshold, so ignition risk assessments should consider pressure and ozone together.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere hazard assessments should account for the interaction of pressure and ozone concentration when evaluating ignition regimes.
findings.source_quote: At elevated pressure (here, 25 atm), the requirement for threshold maximum O3 concentration that drives the system to hot ignition decreases significantly due to the pressure dependence of reactions forming HO2 and especially the H2O2 (+M) = OH + OH (+M).
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: For XO2=21% and a range of selective ozone seeding
findings.statement: In simulations of an isolated 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet at 21% oxygen and atmospheric pressure, selective ozone seeding produced near-quasi-steady cool-flame burning without hot-flame initiation or radiative extinction.
findings.source_quote: For XO2=21% and a range of selective ozone seeding,  near-quasi-steady cool flame burning is achieved directly (without requiring hot flame initiation and radiative extinction).
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Under low oxygen index conditions, with 5% ozone seeding (v/v)
findings.statement: At low oxygen index with 5% ozone seeding, a 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet initially develops a nearly quasi-steady cool flame that transitions to oscillatory cool-flame burning until the droplet is consumed.
findings.source_quote: Under low oxygen index conditions, with 5% ozone seeding (v/v), a nearly quasi-steady cool flame is initially established that then transitions to a dynamically oscillating cool flame burning mode until the droplet is completely consumed.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: 5% ozone seeding (v/v); low oxygen index conditions
findings.statement: The simulated oscillation of a cool-burning n-heptane droplet begins when the fuel-vapor/oxidizer layer near its surface is depleted and dynamically re-established by vaporization and transport.
findings.source_quote: It is found that the oscillation is initiated by the depletion of fuel vapor-oxidizer layer evolving near the droplet surface and its dynamic re-establishment through liquid vaporization and vapor/oxidizer transport.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: oscillatory burning mode
findings.statement: In the simulated oscillatory cool-flame mode, the reaction kinetics dynamically pass through conditions associated with the negative-temperature-coefficient turnover temperature between low-temperature and NTC kinetic regimes.
findings.source_quote: The coupled flame dynamics and kinetics suggest that in the oscillatory burning mode, kinetic processes dynamically cross through conditions characterizing the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) turnover temperature separating low temperature and NTC kinetic regimes.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: initial droplet diameter of 0.5 mm; atmospheric conditions (1 atm, 298 K); XO3 = 5%; reduced oxygen index cases; oxygen index well below the LOI conditions
findings.quantity: cool flame induction time and temperature
findings.statement: In simulations of 0.5 mm n-heptane droplets at 1 atm and 298 K with 5% ozone seeding, reducing ambient oxygen below the approximately 13% limiting oxygen index still allowed a quasi-steady cool flame to establish, after an induction time of about 0.12 s; its predicted temperature was about 710 K.
findings.safety_implication: Oxygen levels below the cited limiting oxygen index should not be treated as preventing all combustion when reactive ignition products or comparable ignition conditions are present.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should account for ignition conditions that can sustain cool-flame burning below the nominal oxygen index limit.
findings.source_quote: For the reduced oxygen index cases, a QSS cool flame is predicted to occur after an induction time of ~0.12 s, with a discernibly lower cool flame temperature of ~710 K.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: n-heptane droplet (Do = 0.5 mm); Ambient conditions: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K; same ozone seeding level (5%); reduced oxygen index cases compared with 21% oxygen index
findings.quantity: flame stand-off ratio, peak gas temperature, and burning rate
findings.statement: For 0.5 mm n-heptane droplets at atmospheric conditions with 5% ozone seeding, lowering ambient oxygen increased flame stand-off ratio and significantly decreased peak gas temperature and burning rate relative to the 21% oxygen case.
findings.source_quote: Lowering the ambient oxygen level increases the FSR and as a consequence, Tmax and Ko decrease significantly from the values for 21% oxygen index.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: near-limit cool flame burning of an isolated sub-millimeter sized droplet
findings.quantity: critical local O2 mole fraction for oscillation inception
findings.statement: In simulations of near-limit n-heptane droplet combustion, cool-flame oscillation begins when local O2 falls below 12%, prompting the flame to move outward to reach the O2 needed for a spherical diffusion flame.
findings.source_quote: The inception of oscillation is initiated by the local depletion of O2 below the critical mole fraction of 12%. This reduction of O2 compels the flame to grow outside to meet the O2 requirement for spherical diffusion flame.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: fiber-supported droplets; alternative established Nusselt number correlations
findings.quantity: sensitivity of burning characteristics to Nusselt number correlation
findings.statement: For fiber-supported droplet combustion simulations, the overall burning rate, extinction diameter, and extinction time were each less than 1% sensitive to the adopted Nusselt number correlation.
findings.source_quote: In addition, other established Nusselt number correlations has been adopted [8, 9] and the overall droplet burning characteristics (burning rate, extinction diameter, and extinction time) were found to be sensitive less than 1% [3].
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: statistical narrow band correlated-k radiation model
findings.statement: The SNB-CK radiation model is reported to provide better predictability than the Curtis-Godson correlation for the combustion-radiation modeling discussed.
findings.source_quote: This yields better predictability over Curtis-Godson  correlation.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: xenon (Xe) enriched environments
findings.statement: Numerical simulations predict that methanol droplets burning in xenon-enriched environments have a reduced burning rate, larger extinction diameter, and prolonged burning time compared with other ambient conditions studied.
findings.safety_implication: The prolonged burning time and larger extinction diameter mean xenon enrichment may not reliably shorten the hazard period or promote extinction in reduced-gravity fire scenarios.
findings.equipment_implication: Xenon should not be assumed to be an effective fire-suppression diluent for reduced-gravity applications.
findings.source_quote: It is found that xenon augmented ambient results in reduced burning rate, larger extinction diameter and counter-intuitively, prolonged burning time.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: xenon, argon, carbon dioxide or helium as diluents
findings.statement: Numerical analyses find that the limiting oxygen index for methanol combustion in xenon is significantly lower than in argon, carbon dioxide, or helium, with xenon's lower thermal diffusivity identified as the principal cause.
findings.safety_implication: An atmosphere containing xenon may support methanol combustion at lower oxygen levels than these alternative diluents, so oxygen thresholds should not be transferred across diluent choices.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should account for the diluent because xenon has a lower predicted limiting oxygen index than argon, carbon dioxide, or helium.
findings.source_quote: The limiting oxygen index (LOI) for xenon is found be significantly lower than argon, carbon dioxide or helium. The numerical analyses also indicate that the lower thermal diffusivity of xenon is the principal factor responsible for the remarkably lower LOI.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: xenon as a diluent in reduced gravity applications
findings.statement: The authors conclude that xenon is unsuitable as a fire-suppression diluent for reduced-gravity applications because its associated elevated peak gas temperature, exceptionally slow diffusive heat loss, and lower limiting oxygen index detract from its suppression utility.
findings.equipment_implication: The authors advise against relying on xenon as a suppressive diluent in reduced-gravity fire-safety applications.
findings.source_quote: It is concluded that the combined observation of elevated peak gas temperature, exceptionally slow diffusive heat loss and the lower LOI value associated with xenon as a diluent all detract from its utility for suppressing fire concerns in reduced gravity applications.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: For an ignition energy lower than 0.4 J
findings.quantity: minimum ignition energy for quasi-steady burning
findings.statement: For methanol droplets in microgravity, numerical predictions found that ignition energy below 0.4 J did not establish quasi-steady burning.
findings.safety_implication: Ignition-system qualification should account for the possibility that insufficient ignition energy may prevent a stable burn, rather than treating ignition as a reliable proxy for sustained combustion.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures and test setups should distinguish successful ignition from establishment of quasi-steady burning.
findings.source_quote: For an ignition energy lower than 0.4 J, quasi-steady burning could not be established, as also found in an earlier analysis [33] for similar droplet initial diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: at increased loading condition (i.e. low oxygen concentration)
findings.quantity: quasi-steady combustion behavior with diluent gas
findings.statement: For methanol droplets in the predicted cases, higher xenon displacement promoted rather than degraded quasi-steady combustion at low oxygen concentration, unlike helium and carbon dioxide dilution.
findings.safety_implication: Low oxygen concentration alone may not predict whether a droplet flame persists; the identity of the diluent can change the combustion response.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control analyses should treat xenon, helium, and carbon dioxide as distinct diluents rather than interchangeable oxygen-displacement agents.
findings.source_quote: Unlike the results for other diluents (helium, carbon dioxide), at increased loading condition (i.e. low oxygen concentration), higher xenon displacements promote rather than degrade quasi-steady combustion [4].
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: at t ~1 s for 21% O2
findings.statement: In numerical predictions at 1 atm and 298 K, a 1.0 mm methanol droplet in 21% O2 had a peak temperature of 2212 K at about 1 s, compared with 2020 K for a 2.0 mm droplet, a difference of about 190 K.
findings.source_quote: For instance, at t ~1 s for 21% O2, 1 mm droplet exhibits a peak temperature of 2212 K while the 2 mm droplet yields 2020 K, a difference of ~ 190 K.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: 21% O2/79% Xe composition during the quasi-steady burn period; xenon mole fraction raised to 93% from 79% (Do = 2.0 mm)
findings.statement: For predicted microgravity combustion of methanol droplets, flame stand-off ratio depended weakly on initial droplet size and strongly on ambient gas composition; at 2.0 mm, increasing xenon from 79% to 93% raised FSR from about 5.0 to about 6.4.
findings.source_quote: For 21% O2/79% Xe composition, the FSR during the quasi-steady burn period was found to be ~ 5.0 for Do = 2.0 mm which then increased to ~5.5 for Do = 1.0 mm. However, when xenon mole fraction is raised to 93% from 79% (Do = 2.0 mm), the FSR escalates to ~ 6.4.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: xenon-rich environment
findings.quantity: burning time and flame temperature compared with other diluents/extinguishers
findings.statement: In microgravity methanol combustion, xenon-rich environments produced longer burning times and higher flame temperatures than other tested diluents or extinguishers, and supported hot flames at lower oxygen content.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon may be a poor choice for spacecraft fire suppression because it can prolong burning and sustain hot flames at lower oxygen levels.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported combustion behavior argues against adopting xenon as a next-generation microgravity fire suppressant.
findings.source_quote: The comprehensive analysis revealed that xenon promotes longer burning time and higher flame temperature compared to existing other diluents/extinguishers and can support hot flame with much lesser oxygen content than its counterparts.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: droplet combustion experiments at atmospheric conditions
findings.statement: At atmospheric conditions, simulations using the Sarathy et al. butanol-isomer kinetic model predicted faster burning and a larger flame diameter in droplet combustion; perturbation analysis attributed the faster burning tendency to isomer-specific species transport parameters.
findings.source_quote: The numerical simulation of the butanol droplet combustion experiments at atmospheric conditions predicted the faster burning rate and larger flame diameter using the above model.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: submillimeter-sized droplets (Do = 0.5 mm); varying the ignition energy
findings.quantity: possibility of achieving direct cool-flame burn
findings.statement: For n-heptane and n-decane droplets with a diameter of 0.5 mm, droplet dimensionality statistically reduced the possibility of achieving direct cool-flame burning by varying ignition energy alone.
findings.source_quote: It has been found that the dimensionality of the droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) statistically reduces the possibility of achieving direct cool flame burn for the droplet by simply varying the ignition energy initiation.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: identical ambient; ozone-augmented ambient
findings.quantity: initial cool-flame dynamics and ozone requirement
findings.statement: Under identical ambient conditions, n-decane, the higher-flash-point fuel, is more likely than n-heptane to undergo initial dumped cool-flame oscillation and requires higher ozone loading for direct cool-flame initiation.
findings.source_quote: Higher flash point fuel (here, n-C10H22) is likely to undergo initial dumped cool flame oscillation than its lower value counterpart (n-C7H16) and will require higher O3 loading under identical ambient.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: near-limit condition; directly introduced cool flame
findings.statement: Near the limit, directly introduced cool flames in the modeled n-alkane droplets did not attain steady burning and instead developed continuously evolving oscillations.
findings.source_quote: In the near-limit condition, such directly introduced cool flame fails to attain a steady burn and enters into a continuously evolving oscillatory cool flame.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: 1 atm, 298 K; initial droplet diameters of 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm; xenon-enriched ambient
findings.statement: For numerically modeled methanol droplets at 1 atm and 298 K, the limiting oxygen index in xenon-enriched ambient increased with initial droplet diameter: it was approximately 4% for 1.0 mm droplets, 5% for 1.5 mm droplets, and 6% for 2.0 mm droplets.
findings.safety_implication: Oxygen-control limits for droplet combustion should account for fuel droplet size; a single limiting oxygen value may not protect against larger droplets.
findings.equipment_implication: Oxygen-control criteria should account for the larger-droplet LOI reported in these simulations.
findings.source_quote: The LOI for Do values of 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm were found to be ~ 4%, 5%, and 6%, respectively.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: increasing ambient xenon content (decreasing oxygen); initial droplet diameters of 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm
findings.statement: In numerical predictions for methanol droplets, increasing xenon content in the ambient reduced the average burning rate; the text attributes this to reduced thermal diffusivity and diminished heat feedback to the droplet surface.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon enrichment can reduce modeled droplet burning rates, but this result alone does not establish a safe oxygen limit or guarantee extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Xenon-based atmosphere controls may reduce droplet burning rates, but require validation against extinction and oxygen-limit criteria.
findings.source_quote: It can be seen in Figure 3.3 (a) that an increase in the ambient xenon content (i.e., decrease in oxygen) reduces Ko,avg. The presence of xenon reduces the thermal diffusivity of the ambient gas significantly, as evidently shown in Table 3.1.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Do = 1.5 mm, XO2 = 21% and balance diluent; ambient condition-1 atm, 298 K
findings.quantity: burning rate, extinction diameter and burn time
findings.statement: For modeled 1.5 mm methanol droplets at 21% oxygen, helium produced the highest burning rate, largest extinction diameter, and shortest burn time among the compared diluents, while carbon dioxide produced the lowest burning rate.
findings.safety_implication: The diluent identity affects both burning behavior and extinction, so oxygen concentration alone is not sufficient to characterize atmosphere-related fire risk.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control assessments should evaluate the specific diluent, since equal oxygen fractions did not yield equivalent modeled combustion behavior.
findings.source_quote: Helium is found to produce the maximum burning rate, largest extinction diameter, and shortest burn time. The higher thermal diffusivity (c.f. Table 3.1) of helium leads to increased heat transfer to both the droplet surface as well as to the far-field (i.e., a thicker flame structure).
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: Do = 1.5 mm at 1 atm; xenon compared with nitrogen under similar ambient condition
findings.statement: The document reports that the xenon limiting oxygen index for a 1.5 mm methanol droplet at 1 atm was lower by a factor of 2.2 than the nitrogen value of 11% cited for the similar ambient condition.
findings.safety_implication: Do not transfer oxygen-limit criteria between diluents without accounting for the diluent-specific difference reported here.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should be established for the intended diluent rather than inferred from nitrogen data.
findings.source_quote: In contrast to the LOI results found for nitrogen (e.g., 11% for Do = 1.5 mm at 1 atm [4]), the LOI for xenon under the similar ambient condition is reduced by a factor of 2.2.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: For instance, LOI for Do =1.5 mm was found to be 5%, 8%, 21% and 21% for xenon, argon, helium and carbon dioxide respectively.
findings.statement: For methanol droplets with an initial diameter of 1.5 mm in microgravity, xenon had a lower limiting oxygen index (5%) than argon (8%), helium (21%), and carbon dioxide (21%), and its longer burn times indicate that xenon is a poor fire-suppressant diluent under these conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon dilution should not be relied on to suppress methanol droplet flames in microgravity, because flames can persist at substantially reduced oxygen concentrations.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression and atmosphere-control strategies should not treat xenon as an effective diluent for methanol droplet fires under these conditions.
findings.source_quote: For instance, LOI for Do =1.5 mm was found to be 5%, 8%, 21% and 21% for xenon, argon, helium and carbon dioxide respectively. The combination of a very low LOI and longer burn times points to xenon being a poor choice as a ‘fire suppressant’ diluent under microgravity conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: at the respective LOI conditions for Do = 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm; efficiency factors relative to argon of 0.5, 1, and 2
findings.quantity: average burning rate sensitivity to xenon collision efficiency
findings.statement: In simulations of methanol droplets at their respective limiting oxygen index conditions, predicted average burning rates were insensitive to xenon third-body collision efficiency factors of 0.5, 1, and 2 relative to argon.
findings.source_quote: The predictions show that the average burning rates of the individual cases are insensitive to the variation in the collision efficiency factor.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: increasing xenon content (i.e. decreasing O2) for a fixed droplet diameter
findings.statement: In the microgravity methanol-droplet simulations, increasing xenon content reduced droplet regression rate and caused earlier flame extinction at larger extinction diameters.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon enrichment may shorten burning but does not by itself establish that a xenon-based atmosphere will improve overall fire safety.
