findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control assessments should account for the coupled changes in burning rate and extinction diameter as xenon content changes.
findings.source_quote: The droplet regression rate decreases with increasing xenon content (i.e. decreasing O2) for a fixed droplet diameter contributing reductions in burning rate and earlier flame extinction at larger extinction diameters.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: reduced gravity environments; xenon diluent
findings.statement: The authors concluded that xenon is not an effective choice for improving fire-safety characteristics in reduced-gravity environments, considering its longest burn time, maximum peak gas temperature, and lowest LOI conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Xenon should not be treated as an effective fire-safety diluent for reduced-gravity spacecraft atmospheres based on these simulations.
findings.equipment_implication: Xenon-based atmosphere control or suppression strategies should not be selected as a fire-safety improvement on the basis of these results.
findings.source_quote: The unified understanding of longest burn time, maximum peak gas temperature, and lowest LOI conditions clearly suggests that xenon is not an effective choice to improve fire safety characteristics in reduced gravity environments.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: xenon, argon, carbon dioxide, and helium diluents
findings.statement: In the simulations, extinction of methanol droplets in xenon and argon was primarily influenced by water dissolution and re-gasification, while extinction with carbon dioxide and helium was heat-loss-driven.
findings.source_quote: Contrary to the heat loss driven extinction phenomena observed with carbon dioxide and helium diluent, extinction in xenon and argon are found to be primarily influenced by water dissolution and it’s re-gasification effects.
findings.investigation_title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

findings.conditions_text: after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames
findings.statement: In CFI-G tests, non-premixed cool flames occurred after normal hot flames self-extinguished, but their presence was not recognized during testing and the tests were terminated, shortening cool-flame combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Fire monitoring and test procedures that detect only hot flames could miss ongoing low-temperature combustion after apparent flame extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Detection systems and operating procedures should account for cool flames persisting after hot-flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing. During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition; closest thermocouple approximately 1 cm from burner surface
findings.statement: In two CFI-G tests with the long/near thermocouple, a platinum-containing exposed type-B thermocouple about 1 cm from the burner surface contributed to rapid reignition during intervening low-temperature combustion, limiting its duration.
findings.safety_implication: Hot, exposed platinum-containing components near fuel flames may catalyze oxidation and undermine flame-extinction assumptions.
findings.equipment_implication: Avoid placing exposed platinum-containing thermocouples near the burner when evaluating whether low-temperature combustion persists after hot-flame quenching.
findings.source_quote: In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low-temperature combustion. It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39
findings.quantity: conditions for observing spherical cool diffusion flames
findings.statement: Normal n-butane spherical cool diffusion flames were observed on the ISS only at 2 bar and an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39; the flames were not readily produced.
findings.source_quote: Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39
findings.quantity: hot flame size relative to cool diffusion flame size
findings.statement: The hot flames that spawned spherical n-butane cool diffusion flames were 2.6 times as large as the cool diffusion flames.
findings.source_quote: The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: observed spherical cool diffusion flames
findings.statement: Observed spherical cool diffusion flames resided in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.
findings.source_quote: They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: cool diffusion flames burning near the surface of fuel pools
findings.statement: Cool diffusion flames burning near the surface of liquid n-heptane pools had measured peak temperatures of 705–760 K, corresponding to a 70 K gas-temperature increase; autoignition first occurred at 550 K.
findings.source_quote: The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism
findings.statement: Cantera autoignition simulations using the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool-flame temperature of 885 K for homogeneous mixtures, significantly higher than the observed temperatures.
findings.source_quote: Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: The first three days of testing
findings.statement: During the first three days of ISS CFI-G testing, the team found no evidence that self-sustained cool flames had been created, although momentary cool flames could not be ruled out.
findings.source_quote: The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: during Increments 64-66
findings.statement: During the CFI-G ISS experiment, researchers identified 15 cool flames among tests that ignited 280 hot flames using ethane, propane, and n-butane.
findings.source_quote: A total of 280 hot flames were ignited (or in some cases naturally reignited) for the CFI-G experiment during Increments 64-66, where 33, 225, and 22 flames were ignited in the three increments, respectively. Testing began near the end of Increment 64 and the final test day was conducted at the start of Increment 66. Cool flame evidence was seen in some tests and 15 cool flames, listed and discussed later, have been identified thus far.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: 30 vol% n-butane and 40 vol% O2, normal flames, a pressure of 2.03 bar, and mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s
findings.quantity: conditions under which cool diffusion flames were observed
findings.statement: In the ISS tests, cool diffusion flames from 30 vol% n-butane occurred only with 40 vol% O2, normal flames, a pressure of 2.03 bar, and mass flow rates between 0.75 and 1.5 mg/s.
findings.equipment_implication: These observed conditions can inform atmosphere-control studies, but the reported tests do not establish general flammability limits.
findings.source_quote: These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% n-butane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.quantity: radiant heat flux behavior and hot-cool flame transitions
findings.statement: After a hot n-butane diffusion flame underwent radiative extinction, radiant heat flux remained above zero while fuel continued flowing, indicating a cool flame; some tests then experienced repeated hot-flame reignition.
findings.safety_implication: A drop in radiant output after hot-flame extinction may not mean combustion has ended, so fire monitoring should account for persistent low-level emission and possible reignition.
findings.equipment_implication: Radiant monitoring and response procedures should consider persistent emission after apparent hot-flame extinction and the possibility of reignition.
findings.source_quote: Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped flowing. Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot-cool flame transitions.
findings.earth_application: Radiant monitoring for fires could account for continued combustion and reignition after visible flames diminish.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.quantity: relative reaction-zone breadth and flame shape
findings.statement: In the reported images, n-butane cool flames had a broader reaction zone than hot flames, while hot flames were more spherical and less attached to the burner tube.
findings.source_quote: While a flame sheet is clearly indicated in the hot flame image, the intensity of a cool flame gradually decreases from the peak along radial direction, which implies that the reaction zone of the cool flame is broader than that of the hot flame. In addition, it is noted that the hot flame is more spherical and less attached to the burner tube than the cool flame.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: in microgravity compared to normal gravity
findings.statement: For ACME CLD Flame, dilution limits were extended in microgravity compared with normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire-safety assessments should account for the possibility that flames can persist at greater dilution in microgravity than normal-gravity tests indicate.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control thresholds based on normal-gravity dilution limits may not ensure flame prevention in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to normal gravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: Steady microgravity flames
findings.statement: Steady microgravity flames in ACME CLD Flame were more stable and had lower lift-off heights than normal-gravity flames, attributed to the lack of buoyancy.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-risk evaluations for spacecraft should not rely on normal-gravity expectations for flame stability or lift-off behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew procedures and fire-response assumptions should account for the greater stability and lower lift-off of steady microgravity flames.
findings.source_quote: Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the lack of buoyancy.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K
findings.statement: At representative values of L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, the Richardson number for a spherical diffusion flame is 1300 in normal gravity; the report concludes that typical spherical diffusion flames require microgravity to make buoyancy negligible.
findings.source_quote: Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity
findings.statement: Analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free microgravity below 10-5 g is needed for spherical diffusion flames to approach quasi-steady state.
findings.source_quote: Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert
findings.statement: The report states that n-pentane testing was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack and ACME chamber insert because of its low vapor pressure, so ethane was used as an alternate.
findings.source_quote: In contrast to objective 2 (and hypothesis 3), it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: during ACME testing
findings.statement: ACME spherical burners did not always produce spherically symmetric flames, reportedly because of excess flow through the porous-sphere joint and local flame quenching from heat loss to the support tube.
findings.source_quote: Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: so far have not been observed in CFI-G testing
findings.statement: In CFI-G testing to date, gaseous-fuel cool diffusion flames had not been observed.
findings.source_quote: CFI-G’s goal is to study non-premixed cool flames using gaseous fuels, which have not been observed before and so far have not been observed in CFI-G testing.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: Due to microgravity
findings.statement: In microgravity, soot in nitrogen-diluted butane flames remains in the flame longer and forms clusters.
findings.source_quote: Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-diluted butane fuel
findings.statement: Nitrogen-diluted butane flames at 2 atm produced non-premixed cool flames after the hot flames quenched; the cool flames were detected through thermal radiation and burner-temperature measurements.
findings.safety_implication: Cool flames can persist after a hot flame quenches, so flame-out indications based only on visible heat or light may not establish that combustion has ended.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire detection intended to confirm flame extinction should account for faint post-quench cool-flame emissions or associated thermal signals.
findings.source_quote: These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-diluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after the hot flames quenched.
findings.earth_application: Vehicle-engine ignition and combustion design may benefit from understanding gaseous-fuel cool-flame chemistry.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.statement: Escaping soot clusters from a nitrogen-diluted ethane flame can increase heat loss, locally quench the flame, and create holes that permit direct fuel-oxygen mixing and enhance flammability; the flame then reforms and the process can repeat.
findings.safety_implication: Localized quenching should not be treated as proof of extinction because the resulting opening can allow fuel and oxidizer to mix and the flame to reform.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew and automated response procedures should distinguish local flame holes or quenching from confirmed extinction.
findings.source_quote: The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again due to heat loss.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: 12% ethane; 6% ethane
findings.statement: In inverse flames in an ethane/nitrogen chamber, flames in 12% ethane burned longer than flames in 6% ethane.
findings.source_quote: We observed that flames in 12% ethane burned longer than those in 6% ethane.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: same oxygen flow rate; greater nitrogen flow rate on the right; chamber filled to 3 atm with propane and nitrogen
findings.statement: In inverse flames, flame size depends on oxygen availability, the limiting reactant; with equal oxygen flow rates, propane/nitrogen flames at 3 atm had similar sizes despite different nitrogen flow rates.
findings.source_quote: This image compares two CFI-G inverse flames that had the same oxygen flow rate, but where the flame on the right had a greater nitrogen flow rate, making the oxygen more dilute and the total flow rate greater. The chamber had been filled to 3 atm with propane and nitrogen. The flames, photographed with an intensified camera, are similar in size.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent
findings.statement: For inverse flames with the same oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and chamber pressure, greater oxidizer flow rates produced larger flames; the larger flames were dimmer because radiative heat loss scales with flame size.
findings.source_quote: As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames; heat loss to the burner’s supply tube
findings.statement: In inverse flames, heat loss to the burner supply tube locally quenched the flame and created an opening where reactants mixed; the opening could oscillate and grow until extinction, although some flames remained quasi-steady despite it.
findings.safety_implication: Localized heat loss can trigger progressive flame instability and extinction, so flame persistence cannot be inferred from an initially sustained spherical flame alone.
findings.equipment_implication: Burner and feed-tube thermal design can affect flame stability and extinction behavior.
findings.source_quote: These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame. The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens of seconds.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: inverse propane flames; fourth day of testing
findings.statement: The investigators had not observed evidence of cool flames with inverse propane flames after four days of testing.
findings.source_quote: This day was our fourth day of testing with inverse propane flames, and we have yet to see evidence of cool flames with this fuel.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames; oxidizer flow rate from the burner varied
findings.statement: For inverse butane flames, increasing oxidizer flow from the burner produced a larger flame with greater radiative heat loss; radiation from the larger flame was several times greater than from the smaller flame.
findings.source_quote: In these tests, the flame size depends on the amount of fuel in the atmosphere required to consume the oxygen, so a larger flow rate results in a larger flame. However, a flame’s radiative heat loss increases with its size and the larger flame is significantly dimmer. Measurements of thermal radiation from the flame on the right were several times greater than from the flame on the left.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: 14.0% and 17.5% butane; same oxidizer mixture ratio and flow rate
findings.statement: In inverse butane flames, the flame at 14.0% butane developed heat-loss-driven oscillations that grew until it self-extinguished, while oscillations in the 17.5% butane flame did not cause extinction during the test.
findings.source_quote: The dim flame in the 14.0% butane experienced large oscillations (shown in blue on the graph) due to heat loss to the burner’s supply tube. These oscillations grew in strength until the flame self-extinguished. In contrast, the flame in 17.5% butane was much brighter.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: extra day of testing with normal flames
findings.statement: During the final normal-flame butane tests, cool flames occurred between hot-flame episodes, enabling the extinguished hot flames to reignite repeatedly.
findings.safety_implication: An apparently extinguished hot flame may not indicate that combustion has ceased if cool-flame reactions can continue and trigger reignition.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew response procedures should account for possible reignition after a hot flame appears to extinguish.
findings.source_quote: In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames.
findings.earth_application: The finding may inform vehicle-engine ignition research, where the report notes cool-flame chemistry is relevant to ignition.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: in microgravity; nearly impossible to create in Earth’s gravity
findings.statement: Cool diffusion flames burning gaseous fuels were created in microgravity, while creating such flames in Earth gravity is described as nearly impossible.
findings.safety_implication: This result alone does not establish that ordinary gaseous-fuel fires are more likely or harder to control in spacecraft.
findings.source_quote: Cool flames were first discovered aboard the space station in 2012 burning liquid fuel; more recently, the investigation created cool flames burning gaseous fuels.
findings.earth_application: The investigation may improve understanding of combustion and fires on Earth.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.statement: The investigation describes a cool flame as burning at about 600 degrees Celsius, compared with a candle at around 1,400 degrees Celsius.
findings.source_quote: A cool flame is one that burns at about 600 degrees Celsius. A candle is about two times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius.
findings.earth_application: The report says the investigation's results could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases

findings.conditions_text: Spacecraft fire prevention through improved assessment for materials selection (currently based on 1g testing)
findings.statement: NASA reported that flames can exist in microgravity when materials selected using normal-gravity (1g) testing would not indicate that behavior.
findings.safety_implication: Materials qualification based only on normal-gravity testing may miss materials that can sustain flames in spacecraft microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Materials selection and flammability assessment should account for microgravity behavior rather than relying solely on 1g testing.
findings.source_quote:
Spacecraft fire prevention through improved
assessment for materials selection (currently based on
1g testing, where flames can exist in µg and not in 1g)
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: spherical diffusion flames; radiative extinction at high flow rates and kinetic extinction at low flow rates
findings.statement: Spherical diffusion flames fueled by CH4 or H2 exhibited both radiative extinction at high flow rates and kinetic (convective) extinction at low flow rates in microgravity.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-control assessments should account for distinct extinction mechanisms across flow conditions rather than assuming that lower flow always prevents flame extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression strategies and airflow controls should be evaluated for both high-flow radiative extinction and low-flow kinetic extinction regimes.
findings.source_quote:
Both radiative and kinetic (i.e., convective) extinction of the spherical flames appear to have been observed.
Radiative extinction seems to occur at high flow rates and kinetic extinction at low flow rates.
findings.earth_application: The distinct extinction regimes may inform airflow and suppression analysis for gas diffusion fires in enclosed terrestrial settings.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: at low flow rates, flames close to the burner where velocities are highest
findings.statement: For spherical diffusion flames, kinetic extinction occurs at low flow rates when the flames are close to the burner, where velocities are highest.
findings.safety_implication: Low bulk flow should not be treated as proof that a localized flame is protected from extinction-related flow effects near a burner.
findings.equipment_implication: Evaluate local burner-region velocities, not only bulk flow rate, when assessing airflow and suppression behavior.
findings.source_quote: The latter may seem counterintuitive but at low flow rates the flames are close to the burner where the velocities are highest.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: helium, rather than nitrogen, dilution of both the fuel and oxygen
findings.statement: For spherical diffusion flames, helium dilution of both fuel and oxygen shifts the extinction limits compared with nitrogen dilution, and kinetic extinction is generally difficult to discern with helium.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction behavior established with nitrogen dilution may not transfer directly to helium-diluted atmospheres.
findings.equipment_implication: Suppression assessments for helium-diluted atmospheres should use extinction data specific to helium rather than assuming nitrogen-based limits apply.
findings.source_quote: With helium, rather than nitrogen, dilution of both the fuel and oxygen, the extinction limits are shifted and kinetic extinction is generally difficult to discern.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: sooty attached flames
findings.statement: In microgravity, sooty attached methane and ethylene flames can have soot volume fractions several times higher than comparable normal-gravity flames, and are taller and wider.
findings.safety_implication: Greater soot production and flame size may affect spacecraft fire hazard assessments and the suitability of terrestrial flame models for microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability assessments should account for the larger, sootier flames observed in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: For sooty attached flames, preliminary results have revealed that the soot volume fraction can be several times greater in microgravity flames than in comparison normal-gravity flames. These microgravity flames are also taller and wider.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: diluted flames in microgravity
findings.statement: Dilution limits for methane and ethylene flames were extended in microgravity, where increased flame stability allowed lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations.
findings.safety_implication: Terrestrial flammability limits may not fully characterize flame persistence in microgravity, so spacecraft material hazard assessments should consider the microgravity environment.
findings.equipment_implication: Flammability testing and standards intended for spacecraft should account for the extended dilution limits observed in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Meanwhile, dilution limits for both methane and ethylene flames were extended in microgravity, where the microgravity flames are more stable, allowing for lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: highly diluted flames; electric field strength varied
findings.quantity: flame stabilization and electrical discharge behavior
findings.statement: Highly diluted non-premixed flames were stabilized with very weak electric fields, while high field strengths produced corona and arc discharges.
findings.safety_implication: Electric-field flame control may introduce discharge hazards at high field strengths and should not be treated as a risk-free suppression or control method.
findings.equipment_implication: Any electric-field flame-control equipment should account for the observed corona and arc discharges at high field strengths.
findings.source_quote: It was found that highly diluted flames can be stabilized with very weak electric fields. But at high field strengths, the flames exhibited corona and arc discharges.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: ethylene and methane used to simulate condensed fuels
findings.conditions_text: low-momentum microgravity flames in the absence of an air flow or flame spread; oxygen concentration below ~25% (by volume)
findings.statement: Low-momentum microgravity flames can burn for minutes without airflow or flame spread, but self-extinguished below approximately 25% oxygen by volume.
findings.safety_implication: Still-air microgravity fires may persist for minutes at elevated oxygen levels, making atmosphere composition and oxygen limits important fire-safety controls.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere controls and material flammability assessments should account for sustained burning in still microgravity conditions and self-extinction below ~25% oxygen by volume.
findings.source_quote: It was found that low-momentum microgravity flames can burn for minutes in the absence of an air flow or flame spread. Although the flames can burn for minutes in elevated oxygen concentrations, like those being considered for future spacecraft, they were found to self-extinguish in concentrations below ~25% (by volume).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: elevated oxygen concentrations
findings.statement: In BRE tests at elevated oxygen concentrations, smaller flames could burn for minutes, larger flames generally self-extinguished within 1.5 minutes, and methane flames self-extinguished within a minute while ethylene flames could burn for minutes.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel identity and flame size affect persistence, so a single representative fuel or flame size may not adequately bound spacecraft fire duration.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire hazard evaluations should distinguish fuel type and flame size when assessing persistence at elevated oxygen concentrations.
findings.source_quote: While smaller flames can burn for minutes at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes. Although ethylene flames at elevated oxygen concentrations can burn for minutes, methane flames were seen to self-extinguish within a minute.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: normal flames; flame size varies with reactant flow rate and ambient oxygen concentration
findings.statement: In normal-flame ISS testing, larger flames grew over time and extinguished after an unstable oscillatory mode in which they partially quenched and reformed; very small flames asymptotically approached steady-state behavior, with one lasting over 14 minutes before operational termination.
findings.safety_implication: Partial quenching and reformation before extinction means a flame that appears to be weakening may remain active and should not be assumed extinguished.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire monitoring and response procedures should account for oscillatory partial quenching and reformation before full extinction.
findings.source_quote: Very small flames have low radiative loss and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior, where one flame lasted over 14 minutes until it was terminated due to operational constraints. In contrast, large flames increase in size over time until the flame extinguishes because of radiative heat loss. Before extinction, these flames experience an unstable oscillatory mode, in which they partially quench and reform.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Teflon™, Kapton™, cellulose and silicone rubber
findings.conditions_text: produced in low-gravity
findings.quantity: count mean diameter of smoke particulate
findings.statement: Smoke particulate produced in low gravity from Teflon™, Kapton™, cellulose, and silicone rubber had count mean diameters smaller than 300 nm.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors may need sensitivity to sub-micrometer particles to detect smoke from these materials.
findings.equipment_implication: Detector designs should be sensitive to small particulate while limiting response to larger dust particles.
findings.source_quote: Preliminary results indicate that the smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from the four solid materials all had count mean diameters smaller  than 300 nm, suggesting that discriminating smoke from spacecraft dust could possibly be achieved by detecting in the sub-micrometer range.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Condensed-phase fuels represented by heat of combustion and heat of gasification
findings.conditions_text: 25 mm flat disk; at a constant heat of gasification and heat of combustion
findings.statement: For a 25 mm flat disk with matched heat of combustion and gasification, the burning rate in normal gravity is approximately 3 to 4 times the microgravity burning rate.
findings.safety_implication: Ground tests may overstate burning rates relative to quiescent microgravity, so spacecraft fire assessments should use gravity-appropriate burning data.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability assessments should account for the different burning rates in normal gravity and microgravity.
findings.source_quote: As deducted from Fig. 5.4, the burning rate in normal gravity is about 3 to 4 times higher than microgravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen
findings.conditions_text: quiescent ambient; over 0.56 to 1 atm there appears to be a negligible experimental effect; theoretical analysis indicated pressure reduction expands the flammable mass burning rate
findings.statement: Reduced ambient pressure enhances the fire hazard for microgravity combustion in a quiescent ambient, although the experiments reported negligible effect over 0.56 to 1 atm.
findings.safety_implication: Reduced-pressure spacecraft atmospheres should not be assumed to reduce fire hazard; the reported theoretical result indicates they may expand the flammable burning-rate range.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere pressure limits should be assessed alongside oxygen concentration because lower pressure may expand the flammable burning-rate range.
findings.source_quote: In other words, reduced ambient pressure enhances the fire hazard in microgravity in a quiescent ambient. Quantities D, a, 1/r, n, and k are proportional to 1/p, but 𝜌D is independent of p. In the experimental presentation of this paper, it can be dug out that over 0.56 to 1 atm there appears to be a negligible effect as discussed in [21,23].
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: A steady critical flame temperature range of 1100 to 1200 K was observed that segregates the conditions of the steady and self-extinguished flames.
findings.statement: For the tested microgravity flames, a steady critical flame-temperature range of 1100 to 1200 K separated steady-burning conditions from self-extinguished conditions.
findings.safety_implication: This temperature range may help characterize when a flame can persist or self-extinguish in microgravity, but should not be treated as a universal spacecraft limit without validation for other materials and conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability assessments for microgravity should account for the reported flame-temperature criterion and validate it across relevant materials and conditions.
findings.source_quote: A steady critical flame temperature range of 1100 to 1200 K was observed that segregates the conditions of the steady and self-extinguished flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.statement: In the reported comparison, materials burned about 3 to 4 times faster on the ground than in microgravity.
findings.safety_implication: Ground-test burning rates may not represent microgravity burning behavior, so spacecraft material hazard assessments need evidence specific to microgravity conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Ground-based material screening should not be extrapolated directly to microgravity without a validated method that accounts for gravity-dependent burning rates.
findings.source_quote: A comparison between flammability of micro- and normal gravity showed that materials burn about 3 to 4 times faster on the ground.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: NASA test 1, an upward flame spread over a real material sample in a controlled environment in 1-g
findings.statement: The document states that NASA Test 1, an upward flame-spread test conducted in 1-g, has no scientific basis for extrapolating its results to microgravity conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Using NASA Test 1 results alone to qualify materials for spacecraft microgravity conditions risks missing gravity-dependent flammability behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: NASA Test 1 should not be used alone to infer microgravity material flammability without a scientifically validated extrapolation method.
findings.source_quote: The current criteria for material selection for use in spacecrafts is based on NASA test 1, an upward flame spread over a real material sample in a controlled environment in 1-g. However, there is no scientific basis to extrapolate the results of this test to microgravity condition.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: for each nominal ambient XO2; based on Dhc, and L
findings.statement: The study proposes flammability maps based on Dhc and L for each nominal ambient oxygen mole fraction, and notes these properties can be measured with the Cone Calorimeter, NASA Test 2, which is not currently used to determine flammable hazard in space.
findings.safety_implication: Using these measurable material properties in spacecraft hazard assessment could provide a route to evaluating microgravity flammability beyond current 1-g screening.
findings.equipment_implication: The document identifies NASA Test 2 measurements of Dhc and L as inputs for flammability maps, although it is not currently used to determine space flammable hazard.
findings.source_quote: This study provides a flammability map based on Dhc, and L for each nominal ambient XO2. These properties can be effectively measured by the Cone Calorimeter: NASA Test 2, not currently used to determine flammable hazard in space.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: BRE flames generated by the 25 mm BRE burner and ethylene-diluent mixture
findings.quantity: fraction of computed steady flame height
findings.statement: For ethylene-diluent flames generated by the 25 mm BRE burner, fuel-terminated flames reached an average of 0.953 of their asymptotic height before fuel termination, while self-extinguished flames were about 0.5 to 0.9 of their computed steady value at extinguishment.
findings.safety_implication: Extinction can occur before flames approach steady state, so fire-safety assessments should account for transient flame behavior rather than relying only on steady-burning conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Flammability assessments for these mixtures should distinguish self-extinguished transient flames from fuel-terminated flames used to estimate steady behavior.
findings.source_quote: It is shown that the 49 fuel terminated flames reached 0.953 of their asymptotic height before fuel termination with standard deviation of 0.019 and the results are shown in Fig. 6.1. The state of the self-extinguished flames showed that they ranged from about 0.5 to 0.9 of their computed steady value, indicating they were relatively far from being steady at extinguishment.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: at the endpoints of steady flames generated by the 25 mm BRE burner and ethylene-diluent mixture
findings.quantity: surface heat flux trend with fuel-mixture mass flux
findings.statement: For steady flames from a 25 mm BRE burner burning an ethylene-diluent mixture, measured surface heat flux decreased as fuel-mixture mass flux increased, while the center-to-offset heat-flux ratio increased.
findings.source_quote: It is shown that as the mass flux is increased the flame grows and gets further from the surface and thus the surface heat flux is decreased. The center to offset heat flux ratio is increased as mass flux is increased.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: steady flames generated by the 25 mm BRE burner and ethylene-diluent mixture
findings.quantity: radiative heat flux to the surface
findings.statement: For steady flames from the 25 mm BRE burner using an ethylene-diluent mixture, increasing fuel-mixture mass flux generally increases flame size and the fraction of total radiative heat reaching the surface, making radiative heat flux dominant at higher mass flux.
findings.equipment_implication: The result informs material-burning emulation by showing that surface radiative heating depends on fuel-mixture mass flux.
findings.source_quote: It is shown that as mass flux is increased, the flame size gets larger and in general, the portion of total radiative heat that impinges the surface is increased. It explains the reason for the radiative heat flux becoming dominant over the surface as mass flux is increased.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: As the ambient XO2 is decreased the flammable zone area is decreased and the critical extinction range is increased.
findings.quantity: flammable zone area and critical extinction range
findings.statement: For the modeled porous-burner flames, decreasing ambient oxygen concentration decreased the area of the flammable zone and increased the critical extinction range.
findings.safety_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should account for the modeled increase in extinction range as oxygen concentration falls; a smaller flammable zone does not by itself establish that a specific atmosphere is safe.
findings.equipment_implication: Use the predicted oxygen-dependent flammability maps when evaluating candidate cabin oxygen conditions.
findings.source_quote: As the ambient 𝑋9: is decreased the flammable zone area is decreased and the critical extinction range is increased.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: The radiative extinction limit shifts to the higher L, that is equivalent to lower mass burning rate, as heat of combustion is increased
findings.statement: In the modeled flammability maps, increasing heat of combustion shifted the radiative extinction limit to higher heat of gasification, corresponding to a lower mass burning rate.
findings.equipment_implication: Material-emulation assessments should account for heat of combustion when estimating radiative extinction behavior and burning rate.
findings.source_quote: The radiative extinction limit shifts to the higher L, that is equivalent to lower mass burning rate, as heat of combustion is increased resulting in a slopped line shown on the flammability maps.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: steady flames generated by ethylene-diluent mixture and 25 mm burner; nominal XO2 of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4
findings.statement: For steady flames generated by ethylene-diluent mixtures on a 25 mm burner, oxygen-enriched environments generally increase flame temperature, which the document identifies as more hazardous.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft atmosphere oxygen enrichment can increase flame thermal severity, so oxygen concentration is a fire-risk control parameter.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control limits should account for higher calculated flame temperatures at increased oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: As expected, oxygen enriched environments, generally increase the flame temperature which is more hazardous.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: XO2 of 0.4, and 0.34; XO2 of 0.265
findings.statement: The PMMA-emulated flame is predicted to burn steadily at oxygen mole fractions XO2 of 0.4 and 0.34, while at XO2 of 0.265 it falls in the extinction zone.
findings.safety_implication: PMMA-like materials may sustain burning at higher oxygen fractions even when extinction is expected at a lower fraction, so spacecraft material qualification should cover the intended atmosphere.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability tests should evaluate PMMA-like materials across the relevant oxygen fractions instead of relying on a single atmosphere.
findings.source_quote: it suggests that PMMA burns steadily at XO2 of 0.4, and 0.34. But, for the last case, XO2 of 0.265, since the PMMA point falls in the extinction zone, the region to the left of radiative extinction limit.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: XO2 decreased from 0.4, to 0.34, and 0.265, respectively
findings.quantity: minimum heat of combustion required for ignition
findings.statement: The minimum heat of combustion required for ignition was observed to rise from 10 to 12 to 13 as XO2 decreased from 0.4 to 0.34 to 0.265, respectively.
findings.safety_implication: Lower-oxygen spacecraft atmospheres may still permit ignition for materials with sufficiently high heat of combustion, so oxygen reduction alone does not establish nonflammability.
findings.equipment_implication: Material qualification should account for oxygen-dependent ignition requirements and the uncertainty in the calculated values.
findings.source_quote: Also, the horizontal double solid line indicates the minimum ∆ℎ!,  required for ignition that was observed in the experiments. It shown that the minimum ∆ℎ!, required for ignition increases slightly from 10 to 12, and 13 when XO2 is decreased from 0.4, to 0.34, and 0.265, respectively.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: materials represented by the flammability map
findings.statement: The theoretical flammability region narrows as oxygen fraction decreases, and the analysis found no flammable region at XO2 = 0.15.
findings.safety_implication: The predicted absence of a flammable region at XO2 = 0.15 is specific to this model and should not be treated as a validated spacecraft operating limit without experimental confirmation.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere limits based on this result require validation against actual materials and combustion tests before being used as control thresholds.
findings.source_quote: The same approach was used to plot the extinction limits and thus, a theoretical flammability region for XO2 = 0.15, which confirmed that there is no flammable region for that ambient condition.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: ambient conditions considered in this study; XO2 = 0.4
findings.statement: For the analyzed conditions, the maximum achievable flame temperature at XO2 = 0.4 was 1420 K.
findings.source_quote: The maximum achievable flame temperature in an ambient with XO2 = 0.4, was found to be 1420 K. In other words, for the ambient conditions considered in this study, the flame temperatures did not exceed 1420 K.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen
findings.conditions_text: nominal XO2 of 0.25, and 0.21
findings.statement: For ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen burning on the BRE in microgravity, all flames ignited at nominal oxygen mole fractions of 0.25 and 0.21 self-extinguished within 90 seconds.
findings.safety_implication: These tested oxygen conditions did not sustain BRE flames, but the result should not be treated as a general spacecraft-material oxygen limit without accounting for the burner-emulation conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: The result can inform evaluation of reduced-oxygen spacecraft atmospheres, but does not establish a standalone safe oxygen setpoint for other fuels or geometries.
findings.source_quote: All flames that were ignited at nominal XO2 of 0.25, and 0.21 self-extinguished within 90 seconds.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: small flame extinction limit; critical flame temperatures (1100 K or 1200K)
findings.statement: For the small-flame extinction limit in the BRE analysis, critical heat release rate approaches approximately 40 kW/m2 for both critical flame temperatures of 1100 K and 1200 K.
findings.source_quote: It is observed that for the small flame extinction limit, the critical heat release rate corresponding to both critical temperatures approaches ~40 kW/m2.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: At the small flame extinction limit
findings.quantity: critical mass flux dependence on oxygen mole fraction
findings.statement: At the small-flame extinction limit, the modeled critical mass flux does not change with oxygen mole fraction, while decreasing oxygen concentration narrows the combustible range of heat of combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Oxygen reduction may narrow which fuel-property combinations can sustain burning, but it does not reduce the modeled critical mass flux for combinations that remain within the combustible range.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere and material assessments should account for both the narrowed combustible range and the oxygen-independent small-flame critical mass flux.
findings.source_quote: At the small flame extinction limit, the critical mass flux does not change with XO2 except that as XO2 is decreased the combustible range for heat of combustion decreases.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: radiative extinction limit
findings.quantity: critical heat release rate dependence on oxygen mole fraction
findings.statement: At the radiative extinction limit, critical heat release rate increases significantly with oxygen mole fraction.
findings.source_quote: However, for the radiative extinction limit the critical heat release rates increase significantly with XO2 (See Fig. 6.16).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: At the radiative extinction limit
findings.quantity: critical mass flux and flammable heat-of-combustion range dependence on oxygen concentration
findings.statement: At the radiative extinction limit, critical mass flux increases with oxygen concentration for a given heat of combustion, and the flammable heat-of-combustion range also increases with oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: At the radiative extinction limit, the critical mass flux, increase with oxygen for a given  ∆ℎ!. Also, the flammable range of ∆ℎ! is increased with 𝑋9:.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26 % and above
findings.statement: For the ethylene-nitrogen Burning Rate Emulator tests in microgravity, nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26% and above could produce thin blue flames that grew slowly for minutes, and more than half of the tests lasted at least 2 minutes and up to 5 minutes.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire assessments should account for slowly growing, sustained flames in oxygen-enriched microgravity conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere control limits should consider sustained burning at nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26% and above.
findings.source_quote: Generally, it has been found that nominal oxygen mole fractions of 26 % and above can lead to steady flames which are thin blue in color and grow slowly over time for minutes.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4
findings.statement: The theoretical flammability maps for ethylene-nitrogen mixtures at nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4 were bounded by radiative and small-flame extinction limits.
findings.safety_implication: The modeled flammable region depends on extinction boundaries, so spacecraft material hazard assessments need to consider both radiative and small-flame extinction behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Flammability assessments should use maps that represent both radiative and small-flame extinction limits across relevant oxygen concentrations.
findings.source_quote: A flammability map as a plot of heat of gasification vs. heat of combustion was developed based on the measurement and theory for nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265, 0.34, and 0.4. The flammability maps were bounded by two extinction limits, radiative, and small flame
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: critical flame temperature of 1100 K or 1200 K
findings.statement: The theoretical flammability-map extinction limits for ethylene-nitrogen mixtures were obtained using critical flame temperatures of 1100 K or 1200 K.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability maps based on this analysis use 1100 K or 1200 K as critical flame-temperature criteria for extinction.
findings.source_quote: The extinction limits were theoretically obtained by applying critical flame temperature of 1100 K or 1200 K. The flammable zone consists of flames with temperatures higher than these values.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Real materials emulated using heat of combustion and heat of gasification properties
findings.conditions_text: flammability maps based on Dhc, and L, properties
findings.statement: The authors recommend NASA use Test 2 to determine flammable hazard in space, based on flammability maps developed from heat of combustion and heat of gasification properties that can be effectively measured by the Cone Calorimeter.
findings.safety_implication: Using Test 2 could provide NASA with a material-screening basis for flammable hazards in space.
findings.equipment_implication: The authors recommend Test 2 for determining flammable hazard in space using properties measurable by the Cone Calorimeter.
findings.source_quote: The development of flammability maps based on Dhc, and L, properties that can be effectively measured by the Cone Calorimeter, suggests NASA to use Test 2 to determine flammable hazard in space.
findings.earth_application: The Cone Calorimeter-measurable properties may support material fire-hazard assessment on Earth, though the stated recommendation is specifically for space.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: aboard the ISS and with the 25 mm burner
findings.statement: Methane-nitrogen flames on the 25 mm burner in ISS microgravity self-extinguished within 45 seconds.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-response planning should account for the possibility that these flames extinguish without intervention, while still allowing for a sustained burn lasting up to 45 seconds.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew response procedures should not assume immediate extinction after ignition.
findings.source_quote: All flames self-extinguished within 45 seconds.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: aboard the ISS; 50 mm burner
findings.statement: Some ethylene-nitrogen flames on the 50 mm burner in ISS microgravity burned for the full test duration, with oscillations beginning before fuel termination.
findings.safety_implication: A flame can remain present throughout a test even when its burning becomes oscillatory, so oscillations alone should not be treated as evidence of extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Flame monitoring and response procedures should distinguish oscillatory burning from extinction.
findings.source_quote: There were several tests that burned for the entire duration of the test but with oscillations started before fuel termination.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: all flame temperatures
findings.statement: Estimated flame temperatures for the ethylene-nitrogen flames were below the critical temperature range of 1100 K to 1200 K.
findings.source_quote: It was shown that all flame temperatures were below the critical temperature range of 1100 K to 1200 K.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: 5 tests conducted at normal atmosphere
findings.quantity: heat flux, flame-existence duration, flame size, and radiative heat loss
findings.statement: In normal-atmosphere tests, numerical simulations predicted heat flux, flame-existence duration, flame size, and radiative heat loss; the tests exhibited instabilities and flame oscillation before self-extinguishment.
findings.safety_implication: Flame oscillation and partial extinction can precede final extinguishment, so an apparent reduction in flame activity should not be treated as confirmation that the fire is out.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire detection and suppression controls should account for flame activity that oscillates before self-extinguishment.
findings.source_quote: Numerical simulations for 5 tests conducted at normal atmosphere was able to successfully predict, heat flux, flame existence duration, flame size and radiative heat loss. All these tests led to some instabilities, flame oscillation before self-extinguishment.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: quasi-steady data for the FT tests; no steady data for 21 % oxygen
findings.statement: For quasi-steady FT tests, local center heat flux was about 50% higher than the heat flux measured at an offset radius of 9.5 mm; both heat fluxes decreased as fuel-mixture mass flux increased and increased nearly in direct proportion to oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: Center heat flux was about 50 % higher than offset located at r = 9.5 mm. Both heat fluxes decrease as the mass flux is increased. (This is associated with the flame located further from the surface). Heat fluxes increase nearly directly proportional to oxygen concentration.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: corrected calorimeter data for quasi-steady FT tests
findings.statement: For quasi-steady FT tests, corrected average calorimeter heat flux was 20 to 70% higher than local center heat flux; average heat flux decreased with mass flux and fuel mole fraction and increased with oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: Corrected average heat flux can be 20 to 70 % higher than the local center heat flux. Heat flux decreases with mass flux, increases with XO2 and decreases with fuel mole fraction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: quasi-steady and self-extinguished microgravity flames; extinguished data include low XO2 (21 and 26.5%)
findings.statement: For quasi-steady microgravity flames, radiant fraction was nearly directly related to heat of combustion, with pure fuel having nearly twice the radiant fraction of diluted fuel mixtures; the extinguished cases showed no apparent critical radiant-loss fraction for extinction.
findings.source_quote: The radiant fraction is nearly directly related to the heat of combustion with the pure fuel nearly twice as high as the diluted fuel mixture. It might appear that “steady” flames cannot have a radiant fraction above about 60%. Extinction of microgravity flames has been associated with radiation loss and subsequent flame temperature drop.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: self-extinguished cases at low XO2 (21 and 26.5%)
findings.statement: For the self-extinguished flame cases, radiant fractions ranged from about 0.5 to 0.8 at low oxygen concentrations of 21 and 26.5%, but the data did not indicate a critical radiant-loss fraction for extinction.
findings.source_quote: The extinguished data range from about 0.5 – 0.8 for low XO2 (21 and 26.5%). While these are relatively high values of radiant loss fraction, there does not appear to be a critical value for extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.statement: Materials can burn more easily in microgravity than in normal gravity, but at much lower burning rates.
findings.safety_implication: Normal-gravity burning-rate tests may not reveal that some materials can sustain burning under microgravity conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability testing should account for the differing ease of burning and burning rates in microgravity and normal gravity.
findings.source_quote: The implication is that materials can burn more easily in microgravity than in normal gravity but with much lower burning rates.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: in microgravity; heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g
findings.quantity: material property ranges associated with burning
findings.statement: Solid materials with heats of combustion from 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.
findings.safety_implication: A broad range of solid materials may be capable of burning in spacecraft microgravity, so material screening needs to include these property ranges.
findings.equipment_implication: The document identifies NASA alternative flammability Test 2 using a Cone Calorimeter as a way to measure the relevant material properties.
findings.source_quote: One important fire safety consideration, based on the findings of this study, is that solid materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: fuel mixture on a flat burner surface
findings.conditions_text: flat surface of 25 mm diameter; atmospheres above 21 % oxygen
findings.quantity: burning duration and steady burning behavior
findings.statement: The study reports that steady burning can be achieved in microgravity for a flat surface of 25 mm diameter, with burning lasting more than 3 minutes and apparent steady blue hemispherical-like flames at oxygen concentrations above 21%.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-safety assessments should not assume that flames in microgravity are necessarily transient; sustained burning was observed under the stated conditions.
findings.source_quote: The primary conclusion from this study is that the BRE has indicated that steady burning can be achieved in microgravity for a flat surface of 25 mm diameter. Experiments have shown that burning could take place for more than 3 minutes with apparent steady blue hemispherical-like flames at atmospheres above 21 % oxygen.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: NASA alternative flammability Test 2 using the Cone Calorimeter
findings.statement: The study recommends that NASA may wish to put more emphasis into alternative flammability Test 2, using the Cone Calorimeter to measure material properties relevant to microgravity burning.
findings.equipment_implication: The authors recommend greater emphasis on Cone Calorimeter-based Test 2 as the study develops a more complete understanding of microgravity material burning.
findings.source_quote: The NASA alternative flammability Test 2 using the Cone Calorimeter can measure these material properties [77,78]. As this study develops a more complete understanding, NASA may wish to put more emphasis into Test 2.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: solids with heats of combustion from about 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification of 1 to 10 kJ/g
findings.conditions_text: 25 mm diameter surfaces
findings.statement: In microgravity, 25 mm diameter solid surfaces with heats of combustion of about 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification of 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn steadily.
findings.safety_implication: Material qualification for spacecraft should account for whether the material can sustain steady burning in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Material screening and flammability tests should consider the stated heat-property range and microgravity conditions.
findings.source_quote: The findings suggest that solids of 25 mm diameter surfaces with heats of combustion from about 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g, and heats of gasification of 1 to 10 kJ/g can steadily burn in microgravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.statement: In the reported experiments, lower fuel mole fractions or heats of combustion and higher ambient oxygen concentrations helped flames burn for longer durations.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire assessments should consider that oxygen enrichment and fuel-mixture properties can affect how long flames persist.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere controls and material assessments should account for the reported influence of oxygen concentration and fuel properties on flame duration.
findings.source_quote: Moreover, it is shown that lower fuel mole fractions (or heats of combustion) and higher ambient oxygen concentrations help flames burn for longer durations.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: ethylene and nitrogen mixtures emulating condensed-phase burning
findings.conditions_text: for the range of analyzed conditions
findings.quantity: heat of gasification and mass flux associated with steady burning; flame stability with pressure
findings.statement: Model computations predict that, across the analyzed conditions, heats of gasification of about 1 to 5 kJ/g would produce steady burning over a mass-flux range of about 1 to 6 g/m2s, and that lower pressure appears to yield more stable flames.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft material fire-safety determinations should account for the possibility of sustained, more stable burning at lower ambient pressure.
findings.equipment_implication: Microgravity material fire-safety assessments should include the predicted heat-of-gasification and mass-flux range and evaluate stability at low pressure.
findings.source_quote: It is found that for the range of analyzed conditions, heats of gasification of about 1 to 5 kJ/g, steady burning would result over a range of about 1 to 6 g/m2s. Low pressure appears to yield more stable flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: steady flames
findings.statement: For the steady flames studied, measured flame radiant fraction was primarily a function of flame height.
findings.source_quote: It was observed in the analysis of the data that the measured flame radiant fraction of the steady flames was a primary function of the flame height [51].
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Condensed fuels represented by gaseous fuel-charged burners; ethylene-nitrogen mixtures were examined
findings.conditions_text: surfaces up to 100 mm in diameter
findings.statement: The analysis predicts that microgravity burning from surfaces up to 100 mm in diameter typically has a mass flux of about 1 to 5 g/m2s.
findings.safety_implication: The predicted range can inform estimates of fuel-vapor generation when assessing how condensed fuels may sustain fires in quiescent microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Material flammability assessments for microgravity should account for the predicted mass-flux range.
findings.source_quote: It says that burning in microgravity for surfaces up to 100 mm in diameter will typically range from about 1 to 5 g/m2s.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Condensed fuels represented by gaseous fuel-charged burners
findings.conditions_text: For the analyzed microgravity burning conditions; external radiation can offset surface re-radiation heat loss.
findings.quantity: effect of radiation on mass flux and burning rate
findings.statement: The analysis identifies external radiant heat flux as a factor that can increase mass flux and contribute to substantial fire growth in microgravity, while surface re-radiation decreases burning rates.
findings.safety_implication: Fire assessments should account for radiative heating from nearby flames or external sources because it may accelerate fuel generation and fire growth.
findings.equipment_implication: Material fire evaluations should include external radiant heat exposure when estimating burning behavior.
findings.source_quote: However, external radiation can offset this effect, and increase the mass flux. As in Earth-based fires, external radiation is the key to massive fire growth; it is likely this can be an issue in microgravity as well.
findings.earth_application: Radiant heat transfer is also relevant to fire growth assessments for terrestrial fires.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.material: Condensed fuels represented by gaseous fuel-charged burners
findings.conditions_text: Lower ambient pressure; NASA seeks habitable atmospheres of lower pressure and higher oxygen levels.
findings.quantity: effect of ambient pressure on burning conditions
findings.statement: The analysis reports that ambient pressure has a minor effect on overall burning rate, but lowering pressure expands the range of burning to higher rates; the authors state that the lower-pressure, higher-oxygen atmosphere sought by NASA will enhance burning conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft atmosphere choices involving lower pressure and higher oxygen should be evaluated for their combined effect on material burning conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere control and material screening should consider that lower pressure can broaden burning conditions and the described lower-pressure, higher-oxygen atmosphere can enhance them.
findings.source_quote: Ambient pressure effects are minor, and it affects the range of burning conditions, but not the overall burning rate. The effect of dropping the atmospheric pressure tends to expand the range of burning to higher burning rates. This is significant, as NASA seeks to provide habitable atmospheres of lower pressure and higher oxygen levels.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.conditions_text: Classification based on heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and burning temperature, with ambient oxygen mole fraction, pressure, and external radiant heat flux considered.
findings.statement: The paper proposes using NASA Flammability Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, or an equivalent method to classify material properties for a science-based fire-safety evaluation methodology for spacecraft materials.
findings.safety_implication: This approach could support material screening tied to ambient conditions and radiant exposure rather than relying on a single burning condition.
findings.equipment_implication: Use NASA Flammability Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, or an equivalent method to classify material properties for spacecraft fire-safety evaluation.
