findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.statement: Simple scaling using fundamental material properties can be used to understand condensed-fuel burning and extinction in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Material-property scaling can support fire-safety screening of condensed fuels for microgravity use.
findings.source_quote:
Simple scaling with fundamental material properties 
can be used to understand g burning and extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

findings.statement: In microgravity the flame voltage-current curve has no saturation plateau (as in 1g) but a distinct peak ion current at the most compact flame — buoyancy strongly shapes 1g flames even with an electric field applied.
findings.source_quote: where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: A small electric field stabilized very weak, highly diluted microgravity flames that would otherwise quench — a surprise; electric fields might mimic buoyancy for partial-gravity studies.
findings.safety_implication: Electric fields near electronics could keep weak flames alive that would otherwise self-extinguish in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: This stabilizing feature of electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Sooting is far more significant in microgravity flames than in similar 1g flames; with soot present, electric fields cause unpredictable behaviors including soot elimination, showers of luminous particles and unstable dancing flames.
findings.equipment_implication: Expect sootier flames (more smoke particles) in microgravity hydrocarbon fires.
findings.source_quote: Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar conditions with 1-g flames.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Flame luminosity, combustion intensity and ion current are clearly correlated; the most robust burning gives the highest ion current even though the flame is most compact.
findings.equipment_implication: Ion-current sensing can indicate combustion intensity.
findings.source_quote: The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even though the flame is most compact.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Jet flames became unstable at high field strengths and experienced corona and arc discharges near the burner tip.
findings.safety_implication: High electric fields near a flame can trigger corona and arcing.
findings.source_quote: these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration near the jet burner tip.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Electric fields can act as sensors (ion current tracks combustion behavior) or actuators (ion-driven wind changes flame shape); applications include flame control.
findings.equipment_implication: Ion-current flame sensors and electric-field flame control are candidate fire detection/control technologies.
findings.source_quote: The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated with combustion behavior) or actuator (ion-driven wind changes the flame shape and characteristics).
findings.earth_application: Electric-field sensing and control of flames in combustors and burners.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames was found to be a common event in ISS testing — predicted computationally but never conclusively observed in ground tests because of short microgravity durations.
findings.safety_implication: In microgravity, slow-growing gas flames can self-extinguish by radiative heat loss at large size; long-duration low-g data are needed to predict this.
findings.source_quote: Surprisingly, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event in ISS testing, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Characteristically sooty flames were not achieved; follow-on tests are proposed with CO2 as inert and propane (C3H8) as fuel to study sooting flames and soot radiation effects on extinction.
findings.source_quote: experimentation with C3H8 is of utmost importance if we are to achieve our original objectives with respect to characteristically sooty flames
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air showed both extinction modes: kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low Damköhler number) and radiative extinction at high flow rates.
findings.equipment_implication: Cutting the fuel supply (flow ramp-down) drives gas flames to kinetic extinction — supports isolating leak sources quickly.
findings.source_quote: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air seem to demonstrate kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low system Da) and radiative extinction at high flow rates (high system Da).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Ethylene flames, which soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity; soot appeared only briefly during hot-wire ignition and then dissipated.
findings.safety_implication: Some microgravity gas fires may produce little or no smoke, so smoke-only detection could miss them.
findings.equipment_implication: Pair smoke detectors with gas/combustion-product or radiation sensors.
findings.source_quote: Ethylene flames which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions did not soot under microgravity conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction, making the chamber size an important parameter.
findings.source_quote: Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction, making the chamber size an important parameter.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames must grow to very large sizes before self-extinguishing; radiative extinction was not observed even at lower H2 concentration, though kinetic extinction appeared during flow ramp-down.
findings.safety_implication: Hydrogen leak flames in microgravity are unlikely to self-extinguish by radiation; stopping the fuel flow is needed.
findings.source_quote: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seem to need to be at very large characteristic sizes to self- extinguish.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Helium-diluted cases had shifted extinction limits versus nitrogen dilution; ignition was severely affected by helium, and its high thermal conductivity affects ignition and heat transfer.
findings.equipment_implication: Diluent choice (He vs N2) changes ignition and extinction limits in spacecraft atmospheres.
findings.source_quote: Ignition was also severely affected by using He as diluent.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (combustion intensity).
findings.safety_implication: A dim or invisible flame can still be intense; visual judgement of a fire's severity is unreliable.
findings.equipment_implication: Use radiometers/UV or chemiluminescence sensing, not only visible cameras, to judge flame state.
findings.source_quote: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Predicted pulsating instabilities (fuel/diluent mixtures above a critical Lewis number) were not conclusively observed in ISS video; radiometer and PMT data still need analysis.
findings.source_quote: However, such instabilities were not conclusively observed in the ISS tests, at least from the video images.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.statement: Understanding diffusion-flame dynamics and extinction improves power, efficiency, pollutant emissions and reliability of engines and combustion devices on Earth.
findings.source_quote: Engines and devices on Earth can be improved in efficiency, pollutant emissions, and dependability from such products.
findings.earth_application: More efficient, lower-emission and more dependable engines and combustion devices.
findings.investigation_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames

findings.material: SIBAL fabric (75 percent cotton and 25 percent fiberglass)
findings.conditions_text: low-speed concurrent forced flows; Ambient O2 was varied from 21 percent down to 16 percent
findings.statement: In microgravity, a 75 percent cotton and 25 percent fiberglass SIBAL fabric sample burning in concurrent forced flow quenched at flow speeds between 1 and 5 cm/s, with the quenching speed higher at lower oxygen concentrations of 16 to 21 percent.
findings.safety_implication: The reported quenching range identifies low-flow conditions where this fabric's flame may extinguish, but the higher quenching speed at lower oxygen shows that the limit depends on oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower O2 atmosphere.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Steady flame spread rates in different flow speeds and O2 percentages; both 2.2- and 1.2-cm samples
findings.statement: In microgravity, SIBAL fabric flames spread more slowly on narrower samples, at lower flow velocities, and at lower oxygen percentages.
findings.source_quote: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 2.2-cm sample; 5-cm/s flow; 21 percent O2
findings.quantity: total burn time; steady spread duration
findings.statement: A 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric sample in 21 percent oxygen and 5 cm/s flow took more than 60 s to burn completely and had a steady spread period of about 21 s.
findings.source_quote: Because the flow speed is lower, it took more than 60 s to burn the whole sample. Steady spread time lasts for about 21 s, much longer than the 10-cm/s flow case.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: thin fabric fuel in concurrent flow; quenching flow velocities were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher velocity at lower O2 percentage
findings.statement: For SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow in microgravity, quenching flow velocities were between 1 and 5 cm/s, with higher quenching velocities at lower O2 percentages.
findings.safety_implication: Ventilation and oxygen conditions should be considered together when assessing whether a SIBAL-like fabric flame can persist or be quenched in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: The measured quenching range can inform low-flow suppression assessments, but does not establish a universal shutdown threshold.
findings.source_quote: Quenching flow velocities were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher velocity at lower O2 percentage. This trend of the quenching boundary supports the prediction by earlier theoretical models (Refs. 1 and 8).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: concurrent flow in microgravity; 1.2-cm-wide sample compared with 2.2-cm-wide sample
findings.statement: The 1.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric sample had a smaller flammable domain than the 2.2-cm-wide sample in concurrent-flow microgravity tests; its quenching limit was not resolved.
findings.safety_implication: The unresolved limit means these tests do not establish a reliable quenching threshold for the narrower sample.
findings.source_quote: But it can be seen that the narrow sample has a smaller flammable domain, as expected.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 2.2-cm-wide sample in 18.7 percent O2; ignited at 10-cm/s flow; flow reduced to 2.2 cm/s
findings.quantity: flame dimensions and heat-loss behavior during quenching
findings.statement: In the typical SIBAL fabric quenching sequence, reducing flow caused flame length and width to decrease; the shrinking flame lost heat through radiation and, when sufficiently small, conduction before extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Reducing flow was the means used to approach extinction in this test.
findings.source_quote: As the flow speed was reduced, both flame length and flame width dropped accordingly with flow. After 25 s, flow velocity was reduced to 2.2 cm/s and held there for the remainder of the test. As shown in Figure 7.5, both the flame length and flame width continued to decrease approaching a circular-shaped blue flame seen from the top.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: low-speed purely forced flows
findings.statement: In microgravity low-speed purely forced flows, thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric flames had quenching extinction velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
findings.safety_implication: Microgravity fire assessments should account for flame persistence and extinction behavior at forced-flow velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
findings.source_quote: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: low flow velocities; radiative and conductive losses
findings.statement: Microgravity experiments with thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric qualitatively supported theoretical predictions that radiative and conductive losses produce solid-fuel flammability limits at low flow velocities.
findings.source_quote: The experimental data obtained supports earlier theoretical predictions (at least qualitatively) of solid flammability limits at low flow velocities due to radiative and conductive losses.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: at quenching
findings.statement: In microgravity, a quenching thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric flame shrank in both length and width before extinguishing in a three-dimensional manner.
findings.safety_implication: Flame monitoring and extinction assessments in microgravity should account for three-dimensional flame contraction during quenching.
findings.source_quote: The flame image sequence at quenching shows the flame shrinks both in length and width and the flame goes out in a three-dimensional manner.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Opposed; fan pot 1.3 (5cm/s), 0.4, 0.36, 0.32
findings.statement: The 12.7-mm black rod flame extinguished when the fan potentiometer was set to 0.32 in the reported opposed-flow test.
findings.source_quote: Fan pot 1.3 (5cm/s), 0.4, 0.36, 0.32; flame out when pot turned to 0.32
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.material: PMMA slab, 4 mm thick and 1 cm wide
findings.conditions_text: flame self-extinguished at 8 cm/s after almost 10 min
findings.statement: A 4-mm-thick, 1-cm-wide PMMA slab in microgravity self-extinguished at an airflow of 8 cm/s after almost 10 minutes of burning.
findings.safety_implication: A PMMA flame may persist for minutes in microgravity before extinguishing at reduced airflow, so it should not be assumed to go out quickly.
findings.source_quote: flame self-extinguished at 8 cm/s after almost 10 min;
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.material: PMMA, 1 cm wide and 5 mm thick
findings.conditions_text: 29-min burn; extinguished at 12 cm/s
findings.statement: A 5-mm-thick, 1-cm-wide PMMA sample in microgravity burned for 29 minutes and extinguished at an airflow of 12 cm/s.
findings.safety_implication: A PMMA fire can burn for an extended period in microgravity and extinguish only under a specific airflow condition.
findings.source_quote: 29-min burn; extinguished at 12 cm/s., HCl 0.5 > 5.0
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.material: PMMA, 2 cm wide and 3 mm thick
findings.conditions_text: 26-min burn; flow briefly at 15 cm/s but flame was too strong so turned down; extinguished 8 cm/s
findings.statement: A 2-cm-wide, 3-mm-thick PMMA sample in microgravity burned for 26 minutes and extinguished at an airflow of 8 cm/s.
findings.safety_implication: A PMMA flame can persist for many minutes in microgravity, and the tested flame was reported as too strong at 15 cm/s.
findings.source_quote: 26-min burn; flow briefly at 15 cm/s but flame was too strong so turned down; HCl 0 > 3.1,  extinguished 8 cm/s
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: a wide range of initial O2 concentrations, forced opposed or concurrent flow velocities, and using various sample geometries
findings.quantity: O2 depletion to CO2 production stoichiometric ratio
findings.statement: PMMA combustion tests in microgravity, across a wide range of initial O2 concentrations, opposed or concurrent flow velocities, and sample geometries, produced O2 depletion and CO2 production consistent with the 6:5 stoichiometric ratio.
findings.source_quote: The data, taken over a wide range of initial O2 concentrations, forced opposed or concurrent flow velocities, and using various sample geometries, is compared with this 6:5 stoichiometric ratio of O2 to CO2 in Figure 1.3. As shown, the data agrees very well with stoichiometric ratios for the wide range of test conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: concurrent rods
findings.statement: Concurrent PMMA rods burned in microgravity produced an average of 550 ppm CO for every 1 percent CO2.
findings.safety_implication: CO production during concurrent PMMA rod burns is a combustion-product hazard that should be accounted for when assessing cabin air quality.
findings.source_quote: Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed thick slabs
findings.statement: Opposed thick PMMA slabs burned in microgravity produced an average of 370 ppm CO for every 1 percent CO2.
findings.safety_implication: CO production during opposed thick-slab burns is a combustion-product hazard that should be accounted for when assessing cabin air quality.
findings.source_quote: The opposed thick slabs fall somewhere in between, producing on average 370 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: very low velocities; opposed-flow flames
findings.quantity: flame tail opening and incomplete combustion product escape
findings.statement: At very low flow velocities, opposed-flow PMMA flames developed an open tail, presumably allowing incomplete combustion products to escape the flame zone.
findings.safety_implication: Incomplete combustion products may escape the flame zone during very-low-velocity opposed-flow burns, so combustion-product exposure should be considered in fire assessments.
findings.source_quote: At very low velocities, the tail region of the opposed-flow flames opened up, which presumably allowed incomplete combustion products to escape the flame zone.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: concurrent flame; throughout the burn
findings.quantity: flame tail condition and incomplete combustion product escape
findings.statement: Concurrent PMMA flames had an open tail throughout the burn, allowing incomplete combustion products to exit.
findings.safety_implication: Incomplete combustion products can leave concurrent PMMA flames throughout burning, which may contribute to cabin contaminant exposure.
findings.source_quote: Interestingly, the concurrent procedure was very similar, but the concurrent flame always had an open tail, allowing incomplete combustion products to exit throughout the burn.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: MSG working volume V = 0.25 m3; gaseous N2 flow r = 0.0005 m3/min maximum; Cin = 0 (pure N2)
findings.quantity: O2 concentration in the work volume as a function of time
findings.statement: For pure-nitrogen dilution of the 0.25 m3 MSG work volume, the CSTR model predicts that oxygen concentration decreases exponentially with time according to c(t) = Co·exp(−(r/V)t).
findings.equipment_implication: The model calculates how nitrogen flow changes the glovebox work-volume O2 concentration over time.
findings.source_quote: The rate of change of the O2 concentration c(t) with time t within the work volume V equation is given by the flow of gaseous N2 (r) multiplied by the difference between the inlet (Cin) and outlet O2 concentrations (Cout)
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: during a high-flow blowoff attempt with a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample
findings.statement: During a high-flow blowoff attempt, a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample briefly ejected flame through the open sides of its holder toward the window before extinguishing.
findings.safety_implication: Blowoff can briefly direct flame beyond the sample holder, so nearby surfaces and windows may need protection from flame and soot during suppression.
findings.source_quote: During operations on GMT 205, during a high-flow blowoff attempt with a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample, some flame briefly vapor-jetted out from the open sides of the sample holder toward the window before the flame was extinguished.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: At 30 cm/s
findings.statement: For a modeled worst-case thick PMMA slab at 30 cm/s flow, the predicted peak regression rate is 3.13 mm/min.
findings.source_quote: At 30 cm/s, peak regression rate is estimated to be 3.13 mm/min.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: The sample is 8.5 cm long, so at 3.05 mm/min
findings.quantity: time for flame base to regress the sample length
findings.statement: The analysis estimates that an 8.5 cm PMMA slab sample would take approximately 28 minutes for the flame base to regress its full length at 3.05 mm/min.
findings.source_quote: The sample is 8.5 cm long, so at 3.05 mm/min, it will take ~28 min for the flame base to regress the entire length of the sample.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.quantity: time for flame to grow to steady-state size
findings.statement: The analysis estimates that a PMMA slab flame will grow to steady-state size in approximately 2.5 minutes.
findings.source_quote: To estimate the growth rate, we use an expected power law growth rate (Ref. 3) and estimate the flame will grow to a steady-state size in approximately 2.5 min, as shown in Figure D.3.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Worst-case assumptions; maximum burn time of 30.5 min.
findings.statement: Under the assumed 30.5-minute worst-case burn, the BASS-II exhaust heat sink was estimated to reach 434 °C, below the lowest-melting hardware material's 660 °C melting point; the entire experiment assembly was estimated to reach 62 °C, and hardware damage was not expected.
findings.safety_implication: The analysis indicates the largest expected BASS-II sample flames should not damage the experiment hardware under the stated assumptions.
findings.equipment_implication: The exhaust heat sink and experiment assembly were estimated to remain below the lowest hardware melting temperature.
findings.source_quote: The maximum temperature if all of the combustion energy is only deposited in this heat sink under these worst-case assumptions, is 434 °C, which is below the melting point of the lowest melting material (aluminum at 660 °C) so this absolute worst-case maximum temperature will not cause damage to the hardware.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: One-sided PMMA slab burned at a slow flow; 1-cm-wide sample.
findings.statement: A one-sided PMMA slab burned at slow flow had a reported spread rate of 0.037 mm/s, with its flame reaching a steady size of about 15 mm in about 3 min.
findings.source_quote: In Figure D.6, a one-sided PMMA slab was burned at a slow flow. The 1-cm-wide sample took 7.5 min for the total test time, with the ignition taking over 1 min. Flame reached steady size in about 3 min and was only 15 mm long. The spread rate was 0.037 mm/s (0.0037 cm/s or 2.2 mm/min).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 1-cm PMMA sphere; consumed in four tests at various high- and low-flow speeds; rate calculated from total burn time and sphere surface area.
findings.statement: A 1-cm PMMA sphere consumed over four tests had a reported average burning rate of 1.9 mg/s, corresponding to an estimated surface regression rate of 0.005 mm/s.
findings.source_quote: Sample 19 (1-cm PMMA sphere) was completely consumed in four tests (various high- and low-flow speeds) with the burn durations in Table D.2. The total burn time was 5 min and 25 s (325 s). The average burning rate was 617.5/325 = 1.9 mg/s.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: BASS–II microgravity flames
findings.statement: BASS-II microgravity flames had CO-to-CO2 ratios well above the less-than-0.004 ratio typical of efficiently burned flue gases, indicating comparatively inefficient combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Inefficient combustion can produce elevated CO, so fire safety assessment should account for toxic combustion products as well as flame behavior.
findings.source_quote: For efficiently burned flue gases (boilers, furnaces, etc.), this ratio is typically less than 0.004. As can be seen, most of our data is well above that, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: a fire of the scale of a BASS–II test diluted within the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume)
findings.statement: The estimated CO concentration from a BASS-II-scale fire diluted within the U.S. Lab would be 1.5 ppm, below the stated long-term 10 ppm and 1 hour 55 ppm SMAC values.
findings.safety_implication: The estimate indicates this fire scale would remain below the cited CO exposure limits after dilution in the U.S. Lab, but does not establish concentrations near the fire or in other volumes.
findings.source_quote: Since the ISS is quite large, the combustion products from a fire of the scale of a BASS–II test would quickly be diluted, so that even within just the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume), the CO levels in the lab would only be 1.5 ppm, well below spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) values for even long-term exposure (10 ppm), let alone the 1 hour SMAC of 55 ppm (Ref. 12).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: small microgravity fires; duct flows varied between and within tests
findings.statement: Estimated heat release rates for the tested small microgravity fires were typically well below 100 W, increased with ambient O2 concentration, and varied with duct flow.
findings.safety_implication: The reported rates characterize these small tests only; the observed dependence on oxygen and flow means fire heat release should not be assumed constant across ventilation conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: Duct flow affected the scatter in estimated heat release rates.
findings.source_quote: Using his constant of 13.1 kJ/g O2, we estimate the HRRs to be typically well below 100 W, as shown in Figure 1.6. There is a trend of increasing HRR with increasing ambient O2 concentration, and the scatter is attributed to the different duct flows between and even within the tests.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: one long opposed thick slab test; one relatively brief concurrent rod test
findings.quantity: heat release rate and observed window damage
findings.statement: A long opposed thick slab test released close to 100 W and damaged the lower downstream corner of the front window, while a relatively brief concurrent rod test releasing almost 110 W caused no damage.
findings.safety_implication: The contrast indicates that exposure duration and heat direction or location can matter to hardware damage, not just peak heat release.
findings.equipment_implication: The prolonged slab burn damaged the lower downstream corner of the front window; the brief rod burn did not cause damage.
findings.source_quote: The one long opposed thick slab test that caused the lower downstream corner of the front window damage released close to 100 W. A prior relatively brief concurrent rod test that released almost 110 W did not cause any damage.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: remaining 19 samples used for global equivalence ratio estimates
findings.statement: In the usable BASS-II samples, CO generation generally increased with fuel mass loss and O2 consumption; the test with 7-g fuel mass loss exceeded 1,000 ppm CO, above the sensor range.
findings.safety_implication: CO can exceed the measurement range during substantial fuel consumption, so monitoring systems need adequate range to characterize high-CO events.
findings.equipment_implication: The CO sensor was exceeded in the 7-g fuel mass loss test.
findings.source_quote: The CO data is more scattered, but CO generation generally increases with increasing fuel mass loss and O2 consumption. The 7-g fuel mass loss test had over 1,000 ppm of CO (above the range of the sensor).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: low-velocity forced-flow conditions; effective equivalence ratio estimated using the observed slope of 0.4582 O2 vol% per gram of fuel and PMMA molecular weight of 100 g/gmol
findings.statement: BASS-II tests had an estimated average global equivalence ratio of 1.3, indicating fuel-rich burning under low-velocity forced-flow conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel-rich burning under these tested conditions left some vaporized fuel incompletely burned, contributing to soot, CO, and unburned hydrocarbons.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported low-velocity forced flow was associated with fuel-rich burning.
findings.source_quote: Using the observed slope of 0.4582 O2 vol% per gram of fuel, and the molecular weight for PMMA of 100 g/gmol for the majority of the data, we can use the above equations to solve for the effective equivalence ratio for the tests: Φglobal = 1.3, which is fuel rich. So, in general, the flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: tests with different geometries, flow velocities, and initial O2 concentrations
findings.statement: BASS-II sensor data showed nearly stoichiometric conversion of O2 to CO2, while CO levels depended on geometry and in some cases the flow-velocity and geometry combination.
findings.safety_implication: Combustion-product yields vary with fuel geometry and ventilation conditions, so CO production should not be inferred from oxygen consumption alone.
findings.equipment_implication: Flow velocity combined with geometry affected CO levels in some tests.
findings.source_quote: Sensor data from the tests showed that the O2 was burning nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, and that CO levels appear to be a function of geometry and, in some cases, the flow velocity and geometry combination.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 100-μm sample; forced flow abruptly cut off after steady flame spread across half the sample length
findings.quantity: time to extinction after flow cutoff
findings.statement: In BASS-II microgravity tests, a steady flame spreading across a 100-μm PMMA film at 2.2 mm/s extinguished within 2 s after the forced flow was abruptly cut off.
findings.source_quote: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s, as shown by the radiometer signal drop in Figure 2.2.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 100, 200, and 300 μm films: about 1 cm/s; 400 μm film: about 1.5 cm/s
findings.statement: In BASS-II microgravity tests, the extinction flow velocity was about 1 cm/s for 100-, 200-, and 300-μm PMMA films and about 1.5 cm/s for a 400-μm film; the report concludes that extinction velocity does not depend on fuel thickness.
findings.source_quote: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: About 16 percent O2; 100-μm sample width 20 mm and 200-μm sample width 10 mm
findings.statement: In BASS-II microgravity tests at about 16 percent O2, PMMA films extinguished at about 2.6 cm/s for a 100-μm film and about 4 cm/s for a 200-μm film, and the report states that extinction velocity significantly increases as O2 level is reduced.
findings.source_quote: Tests were also conducted at a lower O2 level of about 16 percent for two different thicknesses and the extinction velocities were found to be about 2.6 cm/s for 100 μm and about 4 cm/s for 200 μm.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposing flow velocity as the control variable
findings.quantity: boundary-layer effect on flame spread rate and blowoff extinction; correlation for cellulosic fuel
findings.statement: In experiments with ashless filter paper, boundary-layer development was an important parameter in flame spread and blowoff extinction; the experiments were repeatable and produced a correlation for cellulosic fuel.
findings.source_quote: To establish the boundary layer effect on flame spread rate, experiments were carried out with ashless filter paper with the opposing flow velocity as the control variable. While the blowoff extinction velocity is assumed to be only a function of chemical kinetics, these experiments clearly establish the boundary layer development as an important parameter. The experiments are quite repeatable, and a correlation has been obtained for cellulosic fuel.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: critical opposed-flow velocity at which radiative extinction occurs in a microgravity environment
findings.quantity: dependence of critical opposed-flow velocity on fuel thickness
findings.statement: In microgravity, the critical opposed-flow velocity for radiative extinction was reported to be independent of solid fuel thickness.
findings.source_quote: RTDFS vindicated the theoretical and computational findings that the critical opposed-flow velocity at which radiative extinction occurs in a microgravity environment is independent of fuel thickness, the manuscript published in Combustion and Flame is included in its entirety in Section 2.2.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: in the microgravity regime, where the opposing flow can be very mild or even completely absent in the absence of buoyancy-induced flow
findings.quantity: flame spread rate and extinguishment as opposing flow is reduced
findings.statement: For thin solid fuels in the microgravity regime, flame spread rate decreases as opposing flow is reduced, and under certain conditions the flame can extinguish at sufficiently low flow velocity.
findings.source_quote: While spread rate over thin fuels is independent of the opposing flow velocity in the thermal regime, in the microgravity regime, where the opposing flow can be very mild or even completely absent in the absence of buoyancy-induced flow, the spread rate is known to decrease as the opposed flow is reduced. Under certain conditions, this can lead to flame extinguishment at a low enough flow velocity.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread in a microgravity environment
findings.quantity: critical flow velocity for radiative extinction
findings.statement: The report predicts a critical flow velocity for flame extinction using scaling arguments and computational results; a limited number of space-based tests seem to confirm the prediction and closed-form formula.
findings.source_quote: This report combines scaling arguments with computational results to predict a critical flow velocity for such flame extinction. Results from the recently conducted limited number of space-based tests, presented in this report, seem to confirm the prediction validating the closed-form formula for the critical extinction velocity.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: ambient conditions of 21/79 (percent by volume) mixture of O2 and N2 at 1 atm pressure
findings.statement: In the authors’ computations for thin polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) at 21 percent O2 and 1 atm, the extinction velocity was 1.5 cm/s for each of the four fuel thicknesses studied.
findings.safety_implication: The consistent modeled threshold across thicknesses suggests airflow-based extinction criteria may apply across these thin PMMA fuel thicknesses under the stated conditions.
findings.source_quote: Moreover, the extinction velocity is identical at 1.5 cm/s for all the four thicknesses studied.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 100-µm-thick sheet of PMMA; 16 percent O2; comparison at 21 percent O2
findings.statement: For a 100-µm-thick PMMA sheet at 16 percent O2, the computational extinction velocity was 3.5 cm/s, compared with 1.5 cm/s at 21 percent O2.
findings.safety_implication: Lower oxygen concentration does not necessarily make low-flow extinction easier for this modeled configuration; suppression design should account for the higher extinction velocity reported at reduced oxygen.
findings.source_quote: The extinction velocity is found to be 3.5 cm/s as opposed to 1.5 cm/s at 21 percent O2.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment; 21 percent O2
findings.statement: In the model for downward flame spread over PMMA in quiescent normal gravity at 21 percent O2, steady spread rates were 2.8, 1.6, 1.2, and 0.9 mm/s for thicknesses of 100, 200, 300, and 400 µm, respectively.
findings.source_quote: It should be mentioned that when the computational model is used (Ref. 15) for downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment, a steady spread results for 21 percent O2 with spread rates of 2.8, 1.6, 1.2, and 0.9 mm/s, for 100, 200, 300 and 400 µm, respectively, as shown in Figure 2.11.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment; 16 percent O2
findings.statement: In the model for downward PMMA flame spread in quiescent normal gravity, the buoyancy-created flow at 16 percent O2 was strong enough to cause blowoff extinction.
findings.source_quote: At 16 percent O2, however, the buoyancy-created flow is strong enough to cause blowoff extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: at 1 atm; various fuel thicknesses and two O2 levels
findings.statement: For PMMA at 1 atm, the experimentally determined critical opposing-flow velocity below which steady flame spread cannot be sustained was independent of fuel thickness across four tested thicknesses and increased when the O2 level decreased across the two tested levels.
findings.safety_implication: Under the reported conditions, fuel thickness did not change the critical velocity, while lower O2 increased it.
findings.source_quote: A critical flow velocity below which steady spread cannot be sustained is experimentally determined for various fuel thicknesses and two O2 levels. Results from four different fuel thicknesses indicate that fuel thickness does not affect the critical velocity, which increases if the O2 level is decreased.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: FOR THIN POLYMETHYLMETHACRYLATE AT 1 atm; Experiment: 10±5 mm/s
findings.statement: For thin polymethylmethacrylate at 1 atm and 21 percent O2, the measured critical extinction velocity was 10±5 mm/s.
findings.source_quote:
