findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: thin fuel in the thermal limit; opposed-flow flame spread
findings.quantity: flame spread rate dependence on opposing-flow velocity
findings.statement: For thin-fuel opposed-flow flame spread, the experimental results were independent of opposing-flow velocity in the identified thermal limit.
findings.source_quote: A comparison between the two datasets allow us to establish the thermal limit for thin fuel for which the spread rate is independent of the opposing flow velocity.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread data over varying thicknesses; ISS microgravity data and downward-spread normal-gravity data
findings.quantity: fit of classical thin-fuel spread-rate formula
findings.statement: For polymethylmethacrylate, the classical thin-fuel spread-rate formula fit the experimental results well when the adiabatic flame temperature was used in its flame coefficient.
findings.source_quote: The classical thin fuel spread rate formula is shown to fit well with the experimental results provided the adiabatic flame temperature is used in the flame coefficient that appears in the formula.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: In the thermal regime; if the O2 level is reduced
findings.statement: In the thermal regime, reducing oxygen decreases the fuel consumption rate and increases the gas-phase combustion timescale; extinction occurs when that timescale becomes comparable to the gas residence time.
findings.safety_implication: Lower oxygen can still lead to flame extinction, but the document does not provide a numerical oxygen limit for this condition.
findings.source_quote: If the O2 level is reduced, the fuel consumption rate F′′′ decreases increasing tg,chem and finite-rate chemistry becomes important, leading to flame extinction, when tg,chem becomes comparable to tg,res.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: If Vg is high enough
findings.quantity: gas residence time at blowoff extinction
findings.statement: In the thermal regime, a sufficiently high opposing-flow velocity shortens gas residence time until it is comparable to the combustion timescale, causing blowoff extinction.
findings.source_quote: Even if there is sufficient O2, if Vg is high enough, tg,res can decrease to the point that it becomes comparable to tg,chem and finite-rate kinetics becomes important leading to blowoff extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: For thermally thin and thermally thick fuels, respectively, under the expressions in Equation (2.9).
findings.quantity: flame spread rate dependence on opposing-flow velocity
findings.statement: Under the reported spread-rate expressions, thermally thin fuels have a flame spread rate independent of opposing-flow velocity, whereas thermally thick fuels have a spread rate proportional to opposing-flow velocity.
findings.source_quote: One of the remarkable aspects of these expressions is that the spread rate is independent of opposing flow velocity Vg for thin fuels while it is proportional to Vg for thick fuels.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Downward flame spread over a 50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sheet in forced opposed airflow.
findings.quantity: flame spread rate dependence on forced opposing airflow
findings.statement: For downward flame spread over 50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sheets, spread rate remained relatively independent of forced opposing airflow until the airflow reached 40 cm/s.
findings.source_quote: To illustrate this, average spread rate data acquired in a vertical combustion tunnel (Ref. 18) for various opposing airflow velocity for spread over a thin sheet of PMMA (50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide) is plotted in Figure 2.15. The spread rate can be seen to remain relatively independent of the forced opposing flow velocity until it reaches a value of 40 cm/s.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Downward flame spread; computational work used a one-step second-order global kinetics model.
findings.statement: A cited computational study suggested that kinetic effects may be present during downward flame spread at 21 percent O2, but the report states that this conclusion cannot be established definitively from the computational results alone.
findings.source_quote: The independence of spread rate with opposing flow velocity was interpreted as a constant kinetic effect by the buoyancy-generated flow. However, given the simplicity of the chemical kinetic model (one-step overall reaction) used in the computational model, a definitive conclusion cannot be made from computational results alone.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.
findings.statement: For PMMA flame spread in microgravity, high opposing-flow velocity caused kinetically driven blowoff extinction, while very low velocity at about 1 cm/s caused radiative extinction.
findings.safety_implication: PMMA can extinguish through different mechanisms at opposing-flow extremes, so ventilation changes may affect flame persistence as well as spread.
findings.source_quote: At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit; 10-cm-wide sample
findings.statement: For downward flame spread over thick PMMA in the thick limit, the selected average spread rate was 0.044 mm/s; the reported 10-cm-wide sample value was 0.042 mm/s.
findings.source_quote: Although for thicker fuels, the spread rate is slightly width dependent, a value of 0.042 mm/s for a 10-cm-wide sample (Ref. 23) as opposed to 0.044 mm/s for the 2-cm-wide sample, an average value of 0.044 mm/s is selected as the average spread rate for downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: downward flame spread in ambient air
findings.statement: The calculated transition thickness between thermally thin and thick fuels for downward PMMA flame spread in ambient air was 5.19 mm.
findings.safety_implication: Fuel thickness can change which spread-rate regime applies, so flammability assessments of PMMA should account for thickness rather than extrapolate thin-sheet behavior to thicker parts.
findings.source_quote: The transition thickness (2τtransition) can be calculated from this expression as 5.19 mm for downward flame spread in ambient air.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.statement: In the BASS-II tests, the three Nomex samples did not ignite.
findings.safety_implication: Nomex used as an ISS fire barrier did not ignite in these tests.
findings.equipment_implication: Nomex is used aboard the ISS as a fire barrier.
findings.source_quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed flow; initial 3 cm/s; five different flow velocities
findings.quantity: flow velocities at which the candle burned
findings.statement: A wax candle ignited and burned in opposed flow at five flow velocities in the BASS-II test.
findings.source_quote: The wax candle test successfully ignited in an opposed flow (akin to holding a candle upside down) and burned at five different flow velocities corresponding to the test matrix potentiometer settings as shown in Figure 3.1.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed flow; wick ejects droplet of wax directly upstream
findings.statement: In microgravity opposed-flow tests, a burning candle wick ejected a wax droplet directly upstream, illustrating a possible ignition hazard from burning droplets ejected by low-viscosity melt.
findings.safety_implication: Burning droplets from low-viscosity melting plastics may travel and ignite other materials in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: The ejected wax droplet shown in Figure 3.1(b) typifies the flame spread hazard associated with melting plastics in microgravity. If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.material: black cast PMMA rods (0.00635 m and 0.009525 m diameter)
findings.conditions_text: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested; opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s
findings.quantity: opposed-flow velocity below which sustained flame spread was not observed
findings.statement: For black cast PMMA rods of 0.00635 m and 0.009525 m diameter, sustained microgravity opposed-flame spread was not observed below approximately 4 mm/s opposed-flow velocity under the tested conditions.
findings.safety_implication: Under the tested conditions, sustained flame spread was not observed below approximately 4 mm/s for these two rod diameters.
findings.source_quote: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 0.00635- and 0.009525-m-diameter rods.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: average flame spread rate; opposed-flow velocity within the small range of flow velocities tested
findings.statement: For black PMMA rods in microgravity, average opposed-flame spread rate increased with opposed-flow velocity over the tested range.
findings.source_quote: As can be seen in Figure 4.1(a), the average flame spread rate increases with opposed-flow velocity, even within the small range of flow velocities tested.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread; results particularly marked for 6.35-mm-diameter rods
findings.statement: For black PMMA rods in microgravity, flame spread rate trended upward as oxygen concentration increased, particularly for the 6.35-mm-diameter rods.
findings.source_quote: In Figure 4.1(b), the data exhibits an upward trend in spread rate with increasing O2 concentration, which is especially marked in the results of the 6.35-mm-diameter rods.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: in the absence of external radiant heating
findings.quantity: minimum O2 concentration for flame spread
findings.statement: Black PMMA rods spread flame at oxygen concentrations as low as 17.5 percent in microgravity, while flame spread was not observed below 19 percent in normal gravity; the authors attributed the difference probably to lower opposed-flow velocity in the microgravity tests.
findings.safety_implication: Normal-gravity flammability tests may not establish a conservative oxygen threshold for flame spread in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Account for microgravity flame spread when using normal-gravity flammability test results to set spacecraft material limits.
findings.source_quote: The most important result of the comparison is that of the minimum O2 concentration for flame spread in normal and microgravity. While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.statement: Decreasing the diameter of PMMA rods increased flame spread rate in both normal gravity and microgravity, and flame spread was appreciably faster in microgravity than in normal gravity for cylindrical rods.
findings.source_quote: Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments, as shown in Figure 4.3. It is also apparent that flame spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1g for cylindrical rods of PMMA.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: classic limiting O2 index test; a small sample is burned like a candle flame in a 4-cm/s oxidizer flow velocity
findings.statement: The distinction between flame spread and regression affects interpretation of the limiting O2 index test: near the extinction limit in normal gravity, small flames sit at the top of the sample instead of spreading down it.
findings.safety_implication: A limiting oxygen index result based on top-burning behavior may not represent a material's ability to sustain flame spread along its surface.
findings.equipment_implication: Interpret limiting O2 index results with the distinction between top burning and surface flame spread in mind.
findings.source_quote: The distinction between flame spread and regression is important when one considers the classic limiting O2 index test (Ref. 9), where a small sample is burned like a candle flame in a 4-cm/s oxidizer flow velocity, and the O2 concentration is reduced until the flame extinguishes. The small flames in 1g sit at the top of the sample instead of spreading down the sample near the extinction limit.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: concurrent rod geometry; premixed flame oscillations persisted longer in microgravity than in normal gravity
findings.statement: For concurrent PMMA rods, hot material could continue producing fuel vapors after extinction, and the authors recommend maintaining spacecraft fire suppression until the material cools and stops emitting vapors.
findings.safety_implication: Stopping suppression immediately after visible extinction may leave hot material capable of supplying fuel for renewed burning.
findings.equipment_implication: Maintain suppression until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
findings.source_quote: After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools. Premixed flame oscillations along the rod have been observed for the concurrent rod geometry that persist much longer in microgravity than in normal gravity due to the lower rate of convective cooling of the rod. This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 1 mm thick; 2.2 cm wide; two sides burning; opposed flow; flow velocities 5, 3, and 2 cm/s
findings.statement: For 1 mm thick, 2.2 cm wide PMMA burned on two sides in opposed flow, the measured flame spread rates were 0.144, 0.1309, and 0.1062 mm/s at flow velocities of 5, 3, and 2 cm/s, respectively.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: microgravity; model employs the same test sample and MSG geometry as the experiment
findings.statement: The FDS model of flat PMMA samples in microgravity predicted a higher flame spread rate than the experiments observed.
findings.source_quote: The model employs the same test sample and MSG geometry as the experiment. The model predicts a higher flame spread rate than that observed in experiments.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Spread rates decrease as thickness increases, and also decrease as forced-flow velocity decreases (Ref. 10).
findings.statement: For flat PMMA slabs in microgravity, flame spread rate decreased as sample thickness and forced-flow velocity decreased.
findings.source_quote: Spread rates decrease as thickness increases, and also decrease as forced-flow velocity decreases (Ref. 10).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: one-sided samples; thickness increased
findings.quantity: extinction oxygen concentration and forced-flow velocity
findings.statement: For one-sided PMMA slabs in microgravity, increasing thickness was associated with a lower oxygen concentration for extinction and a higher forced-flow velocity for extinction.
findings.safety_implication: Material screening should account for thickness because a thicker one-sided slab may remain burning at a higher forced-flow velocity even as its extinction oxygen concentration decreases.
findings.source_quote: For the one-sided samples, there was a clear trend that as thickness increased, the O2 concentration for extinction decreased but the forced-flow velocity for extinction increased.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: two-sided samples that spread across the surface compared with one-sided samples
findings.statement: For PMMA slabs that spread across the surface on both sides, extinction velocities were significantly lower than for one-sided samples, indicating greater heat loss to the substrate for one-sided flames.
findings.safety_implication: Flammability assessments of mounted materials should account for substrate heat loss, since it can change the flow conditions at which burning is sustained.
findings.source_quote: For the two-sided samples that spread across the surface, there was not a clear trend with thickness, but the extinction velocities were significantly lower than for the one-sided samples, indicating that heat loss to the substrate for the one-sided flame was significantly greater than the two-sided flame without a substrate.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: 1.2-cm-wide versus 2.2-cm-wide regressing samples
findings.statement: For the regressing PMMA samples, 1.2-cm-wide samples extinguished at approximately 1 percent higher O2 than 2.2-cm-wide samples.
findings.source_quote: There was no clear dependence on thickness for the extinction limits for both the 1- and 2.2-cm-wide regressing samples, but the 1.2-cm-wide samples did extinguish approximately 1 percent O2 higher than the 2.2-cm-wide samples, most likely due to increased relative heat losses to the sample holder.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: two-sided burns; thin fuels (1-mm-thick)
findings.statement: In the BASS-II two-sided PMMA experiments, higher flow velocity or a thinner sample corresponded to a higher flame spread rate; for 1-mm-thick samples, 2-cm-wide samples spread faster than 1-cm-wide samples.
findings.safety_implication: Width as well as thickness should be represented in material flammability tests, since sample geometry affected measured spread behavior.
findings.source_quote: As you see, the graph illustrates that the higher the flow velocity, or the thinner the sample, the higher the spread rate is. The triangles represent the two model data points, which show a much higher spread rate than experiments (Refs. 9 and 10). On further observation, we can see that the plot exhibits a clear width effect.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: one-sided samples compared with two-sided samples
findings.quantity: flame spread rate and opposed-flow rate required to sustain burning
findings.statement: In BASS-II microgravity tests, one-sided PMMA samples burned more slowly than two-sided samples and required a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.
findings.safety_implication: Test configurations that expose fuel on both sides may be more conservative for sustaining flame spread than one-sided mounted samples.
findings.source_quote: As shown in Figure 5.9, the one-sided samples burned more slowly than the two-sided samples, and also needed a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: most of the tests
findings.statement: Most BASS–II tests had heat release rates below 100 W.
findings.safety_implication: The generally low heat release rates indicate that many microgravity fires in these tests may develop relatively low thermal output, which is relevant to fire detection and suppression design.
findings.source_quote: We calculated the heat release rates during each test from the O2 consumption and burn times, using the constant 13.1 kJ of heat released per gram of O2 consumed. The results showed that most of the tests had heat release rates well below 100 W.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: using mass loss and O2 consumption data
findings.statement: The estimated global equivalence ratio for BASS–II tests was fuel rich, averaging 1.3 based on mass loss and O2 consumption data.
findings.source_quote: Lastly, the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be fuel rich, 1.3 on average using mass loss and O2 consumption data.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: for some datasets; different geometries of fuel and flow
findings.statement: The relationship between CO and CO2 was linear for some BASS–II datasets but not for all combinations of fuel geometry and flow.
findings.safety_implication: CO2-based interpretation of combustion completeness may not reliably characterize CO production across all fuel geometries and flow conditions.
findings.equipment_implication: CO and CO2 monitoring should account for fuel geometry and flow dependence.
findings.source_quote: The CO versus CO2 followed a linear trend for some datasets, but not for all the different geometries of fuel and flow tested.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: For thin fuels
findings.statement: For thin fuels in the BASS experiments, sample width affects flame spread rate.
findings.source_quote: The two-sided summary graphs show that for thin fuels, sample width affects the spread rate.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: At low flows
findings.statement: Prior microgravity tests of PMMA, POM, and HDPE rods reported that flames survived at airflow below 1 cm/s.
findings.source_quote: Flames survived at airflow less than 1 cm/s.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns
findings.statement: In the BASS experiments, flames spread faster during two-sided burns than during one-sided burns.
findings.source_quote: In general, the flames spread faster for two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: different thicknesses that we have tested
findings.statement: In the BASS experiments, increasing solid fuel thickness increased the time for flame spread and reduced the spread rate.
findings.source_quote: The greater the thickness of the fuel, the greater is the time taken for the flame to spread and so the lower is the spread rate.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.statement: The model used for the BASS experiments predicted much higher spread rates than the experiments measured.
findings.source_quote: The model currently predicts much higher spread rates than those obtained in the experiment.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: ambient O2 concentration in the Microgravity Science Glovebox was varied from 13.6 to 22.2 percent; higher O2 concentrations and as the minimum O2 concentration is approached
findings.statement: In ISS microgravity tests of clear and black PMMA rods, flames were globally stoichiometric at higher oxygen concentrations and became more globally fuel rich near the minimum oxygen concentration because excess pyrolyzate leaked from the open flame tail.
findings.source_quote: O2, CO2, and CO gas sensors provided initial and final readings for each test and indicate that the flames are globally stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations, but become more globally fuel rich as the minimum O2 concentration is approached due to excess pyrolyzate leakage out of the open tail of the hemispherical flames.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: at very low forced flows; quenching and blowoff extinction
findings.statement: For PMMA rods in microgravity, quenching extinction occurred at very low forced flows as the flame shrank to an oscillating hemispherical blue flame; blowoff began when a hole formed in the flame sheet at the stagnation region.
findings.source_quote: Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out. Blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: surface energy balance model; along the flammability boundary
findings.statement: For PMMA rods in microgravity, the surface-energy-balance model's calculated rod regression rates agreed favorably with experimental measurements.
findings.source_quote: The rod regression rates calculated from this model compare favorably with the experimental measurements.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: along the blowoff branch; in the quenching region
findings.statement: For PMMA rods along the blowoff branch of the microgravity flammability boundary, heat losses were negligible, while surface radiative loss dominated in the quenching region.
findings.source_quote: The surface energy balance reveals that along the blowoff branch, heat losses are negligible whereas in the quenching region, surface radiative loss dominates.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: At the bottom of the flammability map
findings.statement: For PMMA rods at the bottom of the microgravity flammability map, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurred when convective flows became comparable in magnitude to diffusive flows, shifting the critical Damköhler number limitation from residence time to diffusion time.
findings.source_quote: At the bottom of the flammability map, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the convective flows become the same order of magnitude as diffusive flows, shifting the critical Damköhler number from residence time limitations to diffusive time limitations.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2
findings.statement: Clear cast PMMA cylindrical rods in microgravity could not achieve sustained ignition below an initial oxygen concentration of approximately 14.5 percent, despite flames being observed while the igniter was on and briefly after it was turned off.
findings.safety_implication: The ignition limit depends on the ignition conditions and should not be treated as the oxygen concentration below which an already burning PMMA rod will necessarily extinguish.
findings.source_quote: Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2, a sustained ignition could not be achieved even though flames were observed when the igniter was on and briefly after the igniter was turned off before extinguishing.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Flames ignited at a higher O2 concentration and survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2
findings.quantity: minimum final oxygen concentration sustaining a flame
findings.statement: In microgravity, clear cast PMMA rods that ignited at higher oxygen concentrations sustained flames as the final ambient oxygen concentration fell to 13.6 percent O2.
findings.safety_implication: A PMMA rod that cannot be ignited at a given oxygen level may still continue burning at a lower oxygen level after it has been ignited.
findings.source_quote: Despite this limiting O2 concentration for ignition, flames ignited at a higher O2 survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2, indicating that the high heat loss to the initially cold rod will quench a postignition flame while a developed solid phase temperature profile allows a sustained flame down to these low ambient O2 concentrations.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Ignition generally occurred at a forced flow of 5 cm/s; below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, ignition delay increased significantly, with larger rods taking longer to ignite
findings.statement: For clear cast PMMA rods in microgravity, ignition generally occurred within approximately 40 seconds at higher oxygen concentrations, but ignition delay increased significantly below 16 percent O2 and reached as long as 230 seconds for larger rods.
findings.safety_implication: A short ignition exposure may fail to ignite PMMA even when a longer exposure could establish a sustained flame, particularly at lower oxygen concentrations and for larger rods.
findings.equipment_implication: Ignition procedures with short exposure times may not reveal whether PMMA can sustain combustion after a longer ignition attempt.
findings.source_quote: At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s. Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly. Larger rods take longer to ignite, especially at lower O2 concentrations (up to 230 s).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: NASA’s Test 1 is an upward flame spread test that has a fixed ignition time of ~25 s
findings.statement: The report concludes that NASA Test 1's fixed ignition time of approximately 25 seconds may be too short for a flammability test and may instead function as an ignition test.
findings.safety_implication: Passing NASA Test 1 after its fixed ignition period may not establish that a material cannot ignite under a longer exposure.
findings.equipment_implication: The report warns that the fixed ignition time may make NASA Test 1 an ignition test rather than a sufficient flammability test.
findings.source_quote: NASA Test 1 25-s ignition time may be too short for flammability test and so may be an ignition test.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.material: clear cast PMMA cylindrical rod (r = 0.476 cm)
findings.conditions_text: The initial O2 setting was 14.8 percent O2 (by volume) and the final O2 reading was 13.6 percent O2; flow changed from 2 to 1.5 cm/s
findings.statement: During a microgravity quenching test of a clear cast PMMA rod with radius 0.476 cm, at a final oxygen concentration of 13.6 percent, the rod reached an apparently steady-state regression rate of 0.0385 mm/s after the flow changed from 2 to 1.5 cm/s.
findings.source_quote: The flow was incrementally decreased throughout the test, as shown by the red stepped line. The flame length stopped growing at the 2- to 1.5-cm/s flow change, and shortly thereafter the rod regression reached an apparently steady-state regression rate of 0.0385 mm/s.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: lowest O2 quenching test; approximately 1-cm/s convective flow
findings.statement: For the 0.476-cm-radius rod in the lowest-O2 quenching test, the radiometer detected flame oscillations at approximately 1.1 Hz before the flame extinguished.
findings.source_quote: The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz as shown in the inset to Figure 6.6, and drops to a value of 1.05 over a period of a few seconds followed by a large oscillation.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: lowest O2 quenching test; measurements just before each flow change
findings.quantity: relationship between flame length and clear bubble layer length
findings.statement: For the 0.476-cm-radius rod in the lowest-O2 quenching test, flame length minus standoff distance matched the clear bubble layer length just before flow changes, indicating that flame heat flux formed the bubble layer.
findings.source_quote: The flame length minus the standoff distance matches the clear bubble layer length just before each flow change, as shown in Figure 6.5, indicating that the bubble layer formation is due to heat flux from the flame, as shown in the flame image inset in Figure 6.5 (at 1,100 s).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread; at any flow
findings.quantity: minimum oxygen concentration for observed flame spread
findings.statement: For opposed-flow flame spread over rods in BASS-II, spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.
findings.safety_implication: Materials and operating conditions should be assessed for fire spread risk at oxygen concentrations above this observed no-spread range.
findings.source_quote: This is consistent with tests for opposed-flow flame spread over rods that were also done as part of BASS–II (Ref. 14), where opposed-flow flame spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: as the initial O2 concentration decreases; low ambient O2 levels in microgravity
findings.statement: For PMMA burning in microgravity at low ambient O2 concentrations, the CO-to-CO2 ratio increased as initial O2 decreased and was an order of magnitude greater than the 1g cone-calorimeter values, indicating less efficient burning.
findings.safety_implication: Higher CO production relative to CO2 under low-O2 microgravity conditions may increase crew exposure to carbon monoxide.
findings.source_quote: The CO to CO2 ratio is plotted against the initial O2 concentration in Figure 6.15, and shows that as the initial O2 concentration decreases, the CO to CO2 ratio increases. These values are an order of magnitude greater than the 1g values found in the cone calorimeter for PMMA (Ref. 24), indicating very inefficient burning at low ambient O2 levels in microgravity.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: At higher O2 concentrations; at lower O2 concentrations
findings.statement: For PMMA burning in microgravity, flames were nearly stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations, while the global equivalence ratio increased at lower O2 concentrations, indicating that O2 rather than fuel was the limiting reactant.
findings.source_quote: At higher O2 concentrations, the flames are nearly stoichiometric. At lower O2 concentrations, the global equivalence ratio increases. This indicates that the limiting reactant is the O2 rather than the fuel.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: along the flammability boundary; for quenching extinction (a < ~10 s–1)
findings.statement: In the analyzed flammability-boundary model, the predicted critical flame temperature for the fuel decreases as stretch rate a decreases, with a more rapid drop for quenching extinction at a < ~10 s–1.
findings.source_quote: The resultant critical flame temperature along the flammability boundary is shown in Figure 6.17 as a function of a. The critical temperature drops as a decreases. For quenching extinction (a < ~10 s–1), the critical flame temperature drops more precipitously.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: along the flammability boundary; stagnation region of the rod
findings.quantity: convective heating rate dependence on stretch rate
findings.statement: The analysis predicts that convective heating rate to the PMMA rod's stagnation region depends linearly on stretch rate a along the flammability boundary.
findings.source_quote: The convective heating rate is linear with a, as shown in Figure 6.17. This is an interesting combination of a terms in Equation (6.4): the square root Nu flow dependence (Eq. (6.3)), the approximate minus cube root s dependence (0.334 power from Figure 6.12), and the approximate seventh root temperature difference (Tcrit – Ts) dependence on a (0.16 power from Figure 6.17).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: for a given a; 3D cylindrical geometry
findings.statement: For the 3D cylindrical geometry, the two-zone model predicted higher burning rates than the 1D solution at a given stretch rate because it has more surface area for heat transfer and fuel vaporization.
findings.safety_implication: Using a 1D model alone could underestimate burning rates for fuels with cylindrical geometry.
findings.source_quote: The burning rates for the two-zone model are significantly higher than the 1D solution for a given a due to the increased surface area for heat flux and fuel vaporization in the 3D cylindrical geometry.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: flow and O2 varied during each test
findings.statement: The two-zone model's predicted average rod regression rates were of the correct magnitude compared with measured average regression rates, although the measured values had significant scatter.
findings.source_quote: There is significant scatter in the measured average regression rates since the flow and O2 varied during each test, but the values are of the correct magnitude compared to the predicted 3D rod regression rates.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Along the flammability boundary; at unity a
findings.statement: Along the flammability boundary at unity stretch rate, the minimum flame heat flux to the surface was 1.57 W/cm2, within the range of literature values for the critical heat flux for PMMA ignition.
findings.source_quote: The minimum heat flux at unity a is 1 W/Ah = 1.57 W/cm2, which is in the range of literature values for the critical heat flux for ignition of PMMA (Ref. 31).
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: Along the quenching branch
findings.statement: Along the modeled PMMA flammability boundary's quenching branch, fuel vaporization drops sharply as flame-to-surface heat flux falls and heat losses become a significant fraction of that flux.
findings.source_quote: Along the quenching branch, fuel vaporization drops precipitously as the total heat flux to the surface drops and the losses become a significant fraction of the total heat flux to the surface.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at a of 8 to 12 s–1, where the a is modified to account for the various rod sizes tested through the gas-phase ℓ scale.
findings.statement: For clear and black PMMA rods tested in microgravity, the minimum of the flammability boundary occurred at a stretch rate of 8 to 12 s–1, with the stretch rate modified for the different rod sizes using the gas-phase length scale.
findings.safety_implication: This boundary identifies conditions near the lowest oxygen flammability limit that should be considered when assessing PMMA fire risk in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at a of 8 to 12 s–1, where the a is modified to account for the various rod sizes tested through the gas-phase ℓ scale.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached
findings.statement: In the BASS-II microgravity tests, ignition delay for the tested rods increased as the minimum limiting oxygen concentration was approached, and could reach almost 10 times the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
findings.safety_implication: An ignition test duration based on the standard igniter on time may not capture the longer ignition delays observed near the limiting oxygen concentration.
findings.equipment_implication: The NASA STD–6001 igniter on time is a comparison benchmark; observed delays could be almost 10 times longer.
findings.source_quote: Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached. Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition. The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition
findings.quantity: oxygen concentration at ignition limit relative to flammability limit
findings.statement: In the BASS-II microgravity tests, ignition limits for the tested rods occurred at higher oxygen concentrations than their flammability limits because the initially cold rod added heat loss during ignition.
findings.safety_implication: Flammability limits alone do not represent the higher oxygen concentrations needed to ignite the initially cold rods under these test conditions.
findings.source_quote: Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: ISS experiments and Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits
findings.statement: The BASS-II ISS experiment's PMMA rod blowoff extinction limits agreed well with limits from Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop tests.
findings.source_quote: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: On the quenching branch of Figure 6.22, as the U is reduced
findings.quantity: ambient O2 concentration at the quenching limit
findings.statement: For PMMA rods near the quenching branch in microgravity, reducing flow required higher ambient oxygen concentration at the flammability limit to provide an adequate oxygen gradient for diffusion to the flame.
findings.safety_implication: The minimum oxygen condition for flame persistence depends on flow; lower flow near quenching was associated with a higher required ambient oxygen concentration.
findings.source_quote: On the quenching branch of Figure 6.22, as the U is reduced, the ambient O2 concentration at the limit has to increase to create an adequate O2 gradient for diffusion of O2 to the flame.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: for this geometry; U/UD = 1
findings.quantity: transition from blowoff to quenching relative to diffusive velocity
findings.statement: For the tested PMMA rod geometry, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurred when forced-flow velocity became the same order as the diffusive velocity, with the reported diffusive velocity UD equal to 2 cm/s.
findings.equipment_implication: The reported transition is associated with forced-flow velocity becoming comparable to diffusive velocity.
findings.source_quote: The transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the forced-flow velocity becomes the same order as the diffusive velocity (U/UD = 1) for this geometry.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.conditions_text: at low a
findings.quantity: effect of gas-phase radiative feedback on flammability
findings.statement: For the tested PMMA rods, gas-phase radiative feedback became an important heat-transfer process at low stretch rates and extended flammability to lower a.
findings.safety_implication: Radiative feedback can sustain PMMA flammability at lower stretch rates than would occur without that heat-transfer contribution.
findings.source_quote: Gas-phase radiative feedback becomes an important heat transfer process that extends the flammability limit to lower a.
findings.investigation_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

findings.statement: ISS droplet experiments (FLEX/FLEX-2/CFI) showed that large n-alkane droplets can keep burning quasi-steadily as invisible 'cool flames' at about 700–900 K after the visible hot flame (>1200 K) goes out.
findings.safety_implication: A fire that looks extinguished may continue as an invisible cool flame, so visual confirmation of extinguishment is not enough in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Post-suppression checks should use gas/temperature sensing, not only cameras or the crew's eyes.
findings.source_quote: FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Over two hundred CFI tests (Jan–Sep 2017) covered n-dodecane at 0.5–5 atm, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, helium dilution (29%, 59% at 21% O2) and the renewable jet fuel farnesane, with ~4 mm droplets.
findings.source_quote: Over two hundred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Low-temperature chemistry controls fuel autoignition; CFI data help validate kinetic mechanisms for low-temperature HCCI engines (less pollution, higher efficiency), and cool flames may aid fuel reforming to hydrogen for fuel cells.
findings.source_quote: The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications.
findings.earth_application: Cleaner, more efficient HCCI engines and fuel reformulation to produce hydrogen for fuel cells.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: CFI data are not yet fully analyzed; researchers are invited to propose further analysis to NASA.
findings.source_quote: All the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Cool-flame combustion ends abruptly at a finite droplet diameter, leaving unburned fuel to vaporize; a vapor cloud of partially oxidized fuel forms right after cool-flame extinction.
findings.safety_implication: After flame-out, unburned and partially oxidized fuel vapor remains in the cabin and could reignite or be toxic.
findings.equipment_implication: Plan post-fire atmosphere monitoring and cleanup for fuel vapor and partial-oxidation products.
findings.source_quote: A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Cool flames need long residence times and cannot be observed with droplet flames in normal gravity — they are a microgravity-specific phenomenon.
findings.source_quote: the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Above about 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles occurred: the hot flame went out by radiative loss, became a cool flame, then reignited to a hot flame, repeating until the droplet was consumed — unexpected from earlier FLEX results.
findings.safety_implication: At elevated pressure a flame that appears extinguished can spontaneously reignite to a hot flame, repeatedly.
findings.equipment_implication: Keep suppression active and monitor for reignition until fuel is consumed or cooled, especially above 2 atm.
findings.source_quote: as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Adding iso-dodecane to n-dodecane reduces the tendency to form cool flames — fuel molecular structure controls cool-flame behavior.
findings.source_quote: The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: More helium dilution makes the cool flame extinguish earlier (larger extinction diameter) for n-dodecane droplets.
findings.equipment_implication: Helium (high thermal diffusivity) dilution promotes earlier cool-flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger extinction diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Cool-flame extinction is controlled mainly by chemical kinetics: as the droplet shrinks, residence time drops until the cool flame becomes statically unstable; a 40 µm support fiber has little effect on extinction diameter.
findings.source_quote: It is interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: Warm flames appear at higher pressures after radiative extinction and are not visible in the color camera; helium addition seems to strengthen the heat-release/heat-loss balance in the NTC region.
findings.equipment_implication: Visible-light cameras miss warm/cool flames; UV (OH*) imaging or radiometers are needed.
findings.source_quote: Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: At low pressure a stable spherical soot shell forms; as pressure rises it becomes diffuse, and residual soot stays around the droplet even after hot-flame extinction — not yet understood.
findings.source_quote: when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction.
findings.investigation_title: Cool Flames Investigation

findings.statement: DAFT demonstrated that a modified COTS TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter (redesigned condenser using capillary flow instead of gravity) works reliably in microgravity, retiring a key risk for the SAME smoke experiment.
findings.equipment_implication: Gravity-dependent COTS instruments (e.g., alcohol-recycling particle counters) can be adapted for spacecraft by replacing gravity drainage with capillary wicking.
findings.source_quote: The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity. This retired a significant risk that was being carried by the SAME project.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: Large particles can build up in the P-Trak optics chamber; on orbit the count/mass ratio declined with run time (Bag #3), consistent with this build-up.
findings.equipment_implication: Optical particle counters in microgravity may foul faster because more large particles stay airborne; plan cleaning/maintenance.
findings.source_quote: a buildup of particles can occur within the optics chamber of the P-Trak
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: The key failure mode — alcohol pooling in the optics chamber and blocking readings — did not occur; both instruments operated in microgravity for an extended time with no apparent failure.
findings.equipment_implication: Condensation particle counters can be used on spacecraft once gravity-dependent fluid handling is redesigned.
findings.source_quote: The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: The team considers the optimal P-Trak reading range to be 30,000–100,000 particles/cc and DustTrak 20–80 mg/m³; the DAFT-3 data were inside this range.
findings.equipment_implication: Operate particle instruments within 30,000–100,000 pt/cc (P-Trak) and 20–80 mg/m³ (DustTrak) for reliable readings.
findings.source_quote: The project team believes that the optimal reading range for the P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: SAME later flew in Increment 15 with flawless operation of the P-Traks over the entire test matrix.
findings.source_quote: SAME flew successfully in Increment 15 with flawless operation of the PTraks over the entire test matrix.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: Operational lessons: a fill-assembly HEPA filter broke in launch packing (soft foam gave no support), a laptop COM port mismatch blocked data transfer, and an alcohol wick container could not be opened.
findings.equipment_implication: Package small hardware with rigid support, verify laptop/port compatibility and container opening before flight.
findings.source_quote: Damage to fill assembly observed
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: The report states DAFT has no tangible Earth benefits.
findings.source_quote: There are no tangible Earth benefits from this experiment.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: The P-Trak condenser was modified to move liquid alcohol back to the evaporator with capillary forces, replacing the downward slope that relied on gravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Capillary-driven condenser redesign for the particle counter.
findings.source_quote: a modification to the condenser tube was developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the evaporator using capillary forces
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors were designed from smoke particle data measured in 1g, while earlier on-orbit data (CSD) showed microgravity smoke can differ appreciably.
findings.safety_implication: Current spacecraft smoke detectors may be mismatched to the smoke actually produced in microgravity.
findings.equipment_implication: Next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors need microgravity smoke data (the goal of SAME).
findings.source_quote: The design of the smoke detectors currently in use aboard the ISS and the NASA Space Shuttle are based on test results from the measurement of the smoke particulate created in a 1-g environment.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: First measurement of ISS particulate air quality: US Lab air was about ten times cleaner than normal US office air (P-Trak readings of only 2–5 particles/cc), consistent with HEPA filtration.
findings.safety_implication: Very low background particle levels mean a rise in particle count is a strong early-fire signal on the ISS.
findings.equipment_implication: Background levels allow sensitive, low-threshold particle-based smoke detection in spacecraft cabins.
findings.source_quote: Test point #1 data (Figures 1 and 2) shows that the overall particulate levels in the US Lab atmosphere are very low, about a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: Mating and de-mating Velcro on orbit produced particle readings above 30,000 particles/cc, showing the P-Trak responded normally; common cabin activities generate measurable particulates.
findings.safety_implication: Routine non-fire activities (Velcro use) can produce high particle counts, a nuisance-alarm source for particle-counting smoke detectors.
findings.equipment_implication: Smoke detector algorithms should discriminate dust from crew activities (e.g., Velcro) from smoke.
findings.source_quote: Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: On orbit the count/mass ratio was lower than in ground tests, meaning the average particle was heavier: without gravitational settling, more large particles stay suspended.
findings.safety_implication: Smoke/dust aerosols in microgravity keep more large particles airborne, which changes what smoke detectors see.
findings.equipment_implication: Detectors and particle samplers for spacecraft must handle larger particles than in 1g.
findings.source_quote: This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on-orbit is higher than that determined on Earth. This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: In 1g ground tests, particle levels in the sample bag dropped over time together, consistent with gravitational rainout of particles.
findings.source_quote: Overall, in the 1-g testing scenario, the particulate levels drop together with time, consistent with gravitational rainout of the particles in the sample bag.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: Average on-orbit particle mass was 2.5e-12 g (range 2–3e-12 g) and average diameter 1.65 µm (1.56–1.7 µm), uniform across sample bags.
findings.source_quote: The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron.
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: The DAFT impactor that should remove large particles is only about 50% efficient, so many large particles reached the instruments.
findings.equipment_implication: Particle-size pre-separators for spacecraft sampling must be validated; a ~50% efficient impactor passes many large particles.
findings.source_quote: although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only about 50% efficient
findings.investigation_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

findings.statement: In burning methanol droplets, water produced by the flame diffuses back to the droplet surface, condenses and builds up in the droplet during the second half of burning, which drives extinction.
findings.source_quote: During the second half of the burning period the water is absorbed and gradually builds up in the droplet
findings.investigation_title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

findings.statement: FLEX tested methanol droplets on the ISS at 13–21% O2 with CO2/N2 diluent mixtures; theory suggests extinction diameter grows linearly with initial droplet diameter.
findings.equipment_implication: CO2-diluted atmospheres (as from a CO2 extinguisher) at 13–21% O2 were mapped for droplet extinction.
findings.source_quote: Recent FLEX testing with a range of O2 concentrations from 13% to 21% w/ diluent mixtures of CO2 / N2
findings.investigation_title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

findings.statement: Example ISS test FLEX-145 (1 atm, 20% O2 / 75% CO2 / 5% N2): a 3.38 mm methanol droplet burned to visible flame extinction at 1.66 mm.
findings.investigation_title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

findings.statement: OH* chemiluminescence images from the FLEX UV camera identify the water-flux transition point in methanol droplet burning; a simple color camera may give a reasonable approximation.
findings.equipment_implication: UV (OH*) imaging tracks dim methanol flames; inexpensive color cameras may approximate it.
findings.source_quote: Similar analysis using a simple color camera may provide reasonable approximation of the same phenomena
findings.investigation_title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

findings.statement: Methanol is a good proxy fuel: simple kinetics, very little soot and small flame standoff that minimizes radiative effects.
findings.source_quote: Only trace amounts of CH3 resulting in very little soot production
findings.earth_application: Better understanding of methanol combustion as a practical fuel.
findings.investigation_title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

findings.statement: Before Saffire, all spacecraft fire experiments used samples no larger than 10 cm, while a serious spacecraft fire would be much larger — leaving designers without large-scale low-g fire data.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire safety designs rest on small-sample or terrestrial data; uncertainty grows for long missions far from Earth.
findings.source_quote: Prior experiments have been limited to samples no larger than 10 cm in length and width whereas a serious spacecraft fire would likely be much larger and consume much more material.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Using terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems carries inherent risk because of significant uncertainty, which increases for exploration missions with long return times.
findings.safety_implication: Exploration vehicles (Moon/Mars transit) need fire safety validated in low gravity, not only by 1g standards.
findings.equipment_implication: Supplement 1g material screening (NASA-STD-6001) with low-g large-scale data.
findings.source_quote: The use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Saffire-I/III burn a 0.94 m x 0.4 m SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric sample — at least an order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any prior low-g flame spread test — at 20 cm/s (I) and 30 cm/s (III) airflow.
findings.source_quote: Saffire-I will be conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s while Saffire-III will be run at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Drop tower tests show maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) flammability limits can differ in low-g from normal gravity; Saffire-II tests 9 samples (silicone, SIBAL, Nomex, PMMA) chosen to burn just above/below 21% O2 in 1g, at NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 size.
findings.equipment_implication: Material acceptance by 1g MOC (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) may not hold in low gravity.
findings.source_quote: Drop tower testing has demonstrated the MOC flammability limits of a material can be different in low-g than in normal gravity
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Saffire runs in the uncrewed Cygnus after it unberths from ISS, so large fires can be tested without risk to crew; the major hazard (inadvertent igniter activation exposing crew to toxic gases) is controlled by four ground-commanded latching relays.
findings.equipment_implication: Large fire tests in vehicles need multiple independent inhibits on the igniter and ground-commanded enabling.
findings.source_quote: Igniter activation requires that all four relays be closed.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Remaining needs identified for exploration spacecraft: flame behavior in exploration atmospheres (elevated O2, lower pressure), multi-moment smoke sensors rejecting nuisance alarms, hybrid smoke/gas detection, post-fire gas decay, smoke-eater cleanup and low-momentum water mist suppression — planned for Saffire-IV to VI.
findings.equipment_implication: Next-gen spacecraft fire systems: multi-moment smoke detectors, combustion product monitors, smoke-eaters, water mist suppression.
findings.source_quote: Demonstrate fire detection with multi-moment sensors
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Only a small number of tests (two large and nine small samples) is planned; thorough evaluation needs many more samples and materials, supported by ground parametric experiments anchored by flight data.
findings.source_quote: A thorough evaluation of these phenomena would require many more samples and range of materials.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

findings.statement: Full-scale fire tests of vehicles, buildings and homes are common on Earth; Saffire brings the same full-scale approach to spacecraft.
findings.source_quote: Tests on full-scale transportation vehicles, buildings, homes, and habitats have been common on earth
findings.earth_application: Large-scale low-g flame spread data on cotton fabric and plastics can improve fire models used for fabric/plastic fire spread in buildings and vehicles on Earth.
findings.investigation_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
